title: force quoting strings in write_csv (and similars)
description:
Is there any plan to add a 'forced-quoting' option for strings in `write_csv` (and variants)?
The use case is this: some identifiers appear as numbers (e.g. integers), but should be _treated_ in code as strings.
When writing these strings out from one program (using `write_csv`), then reading those strings into another program (using `read_csv`), they may get read as numerics, despite careful formatting options for their string representation in the first program (e.g. not relying on the standard numeric-as-a-string formatting).

To be clear, this option would simply force quoting strings (instead of the current check `write_csv` makes to decide whether or not to quote a particular string).

title: write_* choose escaping method
description:
`read_delim` has `escape_backslash` and `escape_double` to read backslashed escape characters and quotes escaped by doubling them.

`write_delim` by default escapes quotes by doubling them and does not offer other options. There should be an option to use backslash escaping. See `qmethod` argument of `write.table`.

title: write_tsv() needs the option to never quote any fields
description:
This is in the spirit of @cboettig's comment in #844:

> @jimhester I think this issue also impacts `write_tsv()`?  Looks like `readr` cannot write a IANA valid tsv file with quoted text, since there's not even an option(?) to not double-quote quotations?

Indeed, the main feature of the .tsv is that tab characters are disallowed in fields, thereby making quoting totally unnecessary.

So, I would argue that the problem isn't that `write_tsv()` needs an "option(?) to not double-quote quotations," but rather that `write_tsv()` needs an option to never quote anything. Setting `quote_escape = "none"` does not accomplish this, though I realize that this wasn't the intent behind it:

```r
library(tidyverse)

foo <- 
  tribble(
    ~name, ~catch_phrase,
    "Jane", 'I am 72" tall.',
    "John", '"No" means "no."'
  )

tmp <- tempfile()

write_tsv(foo, path = tmp, quote_escape = "none")

writeLines(readLines(tmp))

#> name	catch_phrase
#> Jane	"I am 72" tall."
#> John	""No" means "no.""
```

One has to resort to `write.table()` in order to obtain an IANA-compatible .tsv file out of a data frame like `foo`:

```r
tmp_base <- tempfile()
write.table(foo, file = tmp_base, quote = FALSE, sep = "\t", row.names = FALSE)
writeLines(readLines(tmp_base))

#> name	catch_phrase
#> Jane	I am 72" tall.
#> John	"No" means "no."
```

So for `write_tsv()`, there should be an option to never quote any fields. Perhaps there could also be an option to throw an error if a tab character is detected, but that's not my main concern in this issue.

title: suggest to change default quote parameter for tsv
description:
In IANA's definition of TSV at https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types/text/tab-separated-values , no mention is made of string quoting. In fact, the reason for the use of TSV was to avoid having to deal with confusing string quoting at all by simply stating the tab character may not be used in the values of fields. 

Currently, the default value of "quote" parameter in readr::read_tsv is ```\"```. 

To follow the spirit of TSV, suggest to change the default value of the "quote" parameter in readr:read_tsv (and accompanying methods) to an empty value.

title: selective quoting causes Excel to treat .csv as UTF-16 (.txt) on next save
description:
I'm using `readr::write_csv` to dump a comma-delimited file out for my Excel-using friend. A couple of cells have commas in the cell value, so those are escaped with double quotes. So far so good.

My friend opens the file and hits Ctrl-S, without making any edits.

Oddly, what Excel writes out is now delimited by *tabs*, not commas. 

Digging a little deeper, I try the same thing myself, but "Save As" instead of Ctrl-S ... and see that Excel is suggesting "UTF-16 Unicode Text (.txt)" in the "Save As" dialog. WTF?

- `csvclean` (from `csvkit`) reports no errors in the file on disk.
- I'm on a Mac, so the line endings are not CRLF. But I can convert them to CRLF (using `unix2dos`) and the same thing happens.
- The problem is avoided by using `base::write.csv` with `quote = TRUE`.

Can we have a `quote =` option in `write_csv`? Maybe the default should be `FALSE`. But why not allow it?

I like the efficiency of selective quoting but we have to share the world with Excellers.

Thanks!

title: Parsing Failure caused by Space before New Line
description:
I may have found a possible bug in `readr` version 1.3.1, which may relate to #823 

Assume you have a file named `test_case.csv`:
```
"Name      ","Age      ","Color      " 
"Joe       ","12       ","Red        " 
"Bob       ","23       ","Blue       " 

```
Note that there is a `\s` at the end of each line prior to the `\n` and an empty final line.

If you attempt to parse with `readr` it will fail:
```
> read_csv('test_case.csv')
Parsed with column specification:
cols(
  Name = col_character(),
  Age = col_double(),
  `Color      " 
"Joe` = col_character(),
  `12` = col_double(),
  `Red        " 
"Bob` = col_character(),
  `13` = col_character(),
  `Blue       " 
` = col_character()
)
Warning: 5 parsing failures.
row                   col                     expected    actual            file
  1 Color      " 
"Joe delimiter or quote                     'test_case.csv'
  1 Color      " 
"Joe delimiter or quote           B         'test_case.csv'
  1 Red        " 
"Bob delimiter or quote                     'test_case.csv'
  1 Red        " 
"Bob closing quote at end of file           'test_case.csv'
  1 NA                    7 columns                    5 columns 'test_case.csv'

# A tibble: 1 x 7
  Name    Age `Color      " \r\n"Joe`    `12` `Red        " \r\n"Bob` `13`  `Blue       " \r\n`
  <chr> <dbl> <chr>                     <dbl> <chr>                   <chr> <chr>              
1 Joe      12 "Red        \" \r\n\"Bob"    13 "Blue       \" \r\n"    NA    NA                 
```
But this same file is valid to the base-R parser.
```
> read.csv('test_case.csv')
  Name...... Age......  Color......
1 Joe               12 Red         
2 Bob               13 Blue        
```
As well as `data.table`

```
> fread('test_case.csv')
   Name       Age       Color      
1: Joe        12        Red        
2: Bob        13        Blue  
```

I have several thousand csv's, some unpredictably serialized in this format. If the issue cannot be easily remedied in `readr`, is it at least possible to add a more precise message in the parsing failures?

Thank you package maintainers!

title: read_csv does not fail gracefully if tempdir is filled/full when reading gzipped files.
description:
R version 3.5.3 (2019-03-11)
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)
readr: 1.3.1.9000

I compiled readr from source (hence at version 1.3.1.9)  to see if the problem went away, but it did not make any difference. 


Hi,

This problem stumped me for a few days as I thought I had hardware and or system library problems.

I was using readr::read_csv() to open a large gzipped CSV file with about 500,000 rows and 300 columns. I regularly check the size of the returned data.frame as I've been performing multi-stage processing/cleaning and save the data between stages.

For example:

```r
df <- readr::read_csv('mydata.csv.gz', guess=10000)
```

On one occasion, I found that the data frame was only about 200,000 rows and I was getting one or two warnings about parsing the file. 

I thought I might have accidentally removed too many rows in a previous stage or used the wrong delimiter somehow. I unzipped the csv.gz file from a bash terminal and read the file in using base R read_csv(). Much to my relief I found that all the expected number of rows and columns were present, so the csv.gz file was fine.

The odd thing was that almost every time I ran the readr::read_csv() function to read the csv.gz file, the row and column that produced the parsing error was different. It was never consistent. Hence, I thought I had some sort of hardware problem or an odd system library issue.

I eventually found that my /tmp directory was almost full. Such that readr:read_csv() would fill the /tmp folder and I would get the parsing errors and a smaller tibble than expected.

Below is a reproducible example for a GNU/Linux system. 

We can create a small temporary directory using tmpfs as root to illustrate the problem.

```shell
# mkdir /tmp_r
# mount -t tmpfs -o size=1M tmpfs /tmp_r/
# df
Filesystem           Type      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
...
tmpfs                tmpfs     1.0M     0  1.0M   0% /tmp_r

```

From my understanding, readr decompresses files to the tempdir() location so it can parse the file and guess the column types. To manually override the tempdir() location, I found the [unixtools](https://github.com/s-u/unixtools) library to be the easiest approach. We'll also change the temporary session path (R_SESSION_TMPDIR) for good measure.

```r
library(devtools)
devtools::install_github("s-u/unixtools")
library(unixtools)
unixtools::set.tempdir('/tmp_r')
tempdir()
# [1] "/tmp_r"
Sys.setenv(R_SESSION_TMPDIR = '/tmp_r')
Sys.getenv('R_SESSION_TMPDIR')
# [1] "/tmp_r"
```

Create a sufficiently large data.frame and save it as a CSV file.

```r
df <- data.frame(matrix(0, nrow=1000000, ncol=20))
write.csv(df, 'mytable.csv', row.names = F, quote = T )

```

Read the csv file back into R to check if it worked 

```r
df_csv <- read.csv( 'mytable.csv' )
dim(df_csv)
# [1] 1000000      20
```

I could have used write.csv(gzfile()) to compress the file, but it's easier do it manually in the terminal.

```shell
$ gzip -c mytable.csv > mytable.csv.gz
```

Base read.csv() and gzfile() has no problem reading the file. This is important because readr also uses gzfile() and I wanted to rule out gzfile() being the cause of the problem.

```r
df_csv_gz <- read.csv( gzfile('mytable.csv.gz') )
dim(df_csv_gz)
# [1] 1000000      20
```

However, running readr:read_csv() produces warnings and a tibble with fewer rows than expected.
```r
df_csv_gz <- readr::read_csv( 'mytable.csv.gz' )
# Parsed with column specification:
#   cols(
#     .default = col_double()
#   )
# See spec(...) for full column specifications.
# Warning: 1 parsing failure.
# row col   expected     actual         file
# 26212  -- 20 columns 13 columns <connection>
dim(df_csv_gz)
# [1] 26212    20

```
The tempdir() is not completely filled on the first run as you would expect.
If you re-running the above command two times tempdir is filled with three files.

```shell
# ls -l /tmp_r
total 1.0M
-rw-r--r-- 1 user1 user1 1016K Dec 26 12:12 file45439fd235a
-rw-r--r-- 1 user1 user1  8.0K Dec 26 12:12 file4544bae6c09
-rw-r--r-- 1 user1 user1     0 Dec 26 12:12 file454604032cd
```

Running the read_csv() for a forth time results in an empty data.frame and no messages at all.
```r
df_csv_gz <- readr::read_csv( 'mytable.csv.gz' )
dim(df_csv_gz)
# [1] 0 0
```

If we increase the \tmp_r directory size, the problem is solved.

```shell
# rm -rf /tmp_r/*
# mount -t tmpfs -o remount,size=50M tmpfs /tmp_r/
# df
Filesystem           Type      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
...
tmpfs                tmpfs     50M     0  50M   0% /tmp_r
```

```r
df_csv_gz <- readr::read_csv( 'mytable.csv.gz' )
# Parsed with column specification:
#   cols(
#     .default = col_double()
#   )
# See spec(...) for full column specifications.
dim(df_csv_gz)
# [1] 1000000      20

```
I would have expected readr:readr() to check if gzfile() successfully decompressed the file before trying to parse it. 

If you need any further information, please let me know.

title: support for 64 bits integer using bit64 and integer64
description:
Hi,

would it be possible to have a support for 64 bits integer right out of the box. It is very common nowadays to have nanoseconds time stamps precision and therefore, they are encoded as 64 bits.
For example, these are the kind of values I use all the time: 1487811688746493361 and they are read by default as doubles.

Example of code:
```
> read_csv("a\n1487810827837636484",col_types="i")
Warning: 1 parsing failure.
row col   expected              actual
  1   a an integer 1487810827837636484

# A tibble: 1 × 1
      a
  <int>
1    NA
> read_csv("a\n1487810827837636484",col_types="n")                                                                
# A tibble: 1 × 1
             a
         <dbl>
1 1.487811e+18
> read_csv("a\n1487810827837636484",col_types="d")                                                                
# A tibble: 1 × 1
             a
         <dbl>
1 1.487811e+18
```

The first example fails. If a `col_types` for 64 bits integer (like `l`), it would work and would return a vector of integer64 (from the bit64 package). The other example suffers a loss of accuracy.

For the time being, I am forced to read the column as characters and convert them after to integer64.
```
> x<-read_csv("a\n1487810827837636484",col_types="c")
> x
# A tibble: 1 × 1
                    a
                <chr>
1 1487810827837636484
> x$a=as.integer64(x$a)
> x
# A tibble: 1 × 1
                    a
      <S3: integer64>
1 1487810827837636484
```

title: Support remote reading for read_rds()
description:
Currently, it is possible to read remote files using most `read_*()` functions. But for `read_rds()`, that really only calls `readRDS()`, this does not work, which hinders downloading remote data sets from e.g. repositories. 

Would it be an idea to support downloading prior to reading RDS files? As an example:

```r
read_rds <- function(file) {
  if (grepl("^http", file, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
    # temp location
    file_local <- file.path(tempdir(), basename(file))
    # download the data set
    download.file(file, file_local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    file <- file_local
  }
  readRDS(file)
}
```

title: Consider using Fast CPP csv parser
description:
The [Fast C++ CSV Parser](https://github.com/ben-strasser/fast-cpp-csv-parser) is a header only implementation that seems quite fast, although it requires some C++11 features.

A proof of concept using it is at https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/compare/master...jimhester:fast-cpp-csv-parser, which gives performance similar to the multi-threaded *data.table* readr for a reasonably big input.

title: CollectorFactor should only create CHARSXP for the levels
description:
Calling `makeCharLenCE()` can be expensive, so it is best to avoid and only call it when a level is sure to be in the final result, rather than for every value as is currently being done.

https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/blob/9a92f23d747e7937dcc2096829e78b46dcc11d69/src/Collector.cpp#L221-L225

parsing the same repeated value to a factor should theoretically be _much_ faster than reading to a character vector.

Thanks in advance!

title: Improved description of fwf_* functions
description:
I recently ran into fixed with files and was happy to find that ```readr``` support importing such files into R. 

The documentation around these functions are however a bit lacking. Specifically it is not described what ```fwf_empty```, ```fwf_widths```, ```fwf_positions``` and ```fwf_cols``` actually do. 

Some of them you can guess, but the lack of documentation is a shame - especially for ```fwf_empty()``` which might be the most useful but also the one where people (or at least I) cannot guess what does form its name and usage. I actually though I had to implement such a function myself until I stumbled upon it in a comment for a stackoverflow post.

A short description of each function, like you have for ```?read_table``` would improve the usage of these functions.

Cheers
Kristoffer

title: `type_convert()` ignores `cols()` specification without warning when not able to convert
description:
### Overview
It appears that the function `type_convert()` will not convert a column unless it is `character`. It would be helpful to have a warning message or a `verbose` argument in the function to control warnings when `type_convert()` is unable to enforce the supplied `cols()` specification.

----
### Reproducing the issue

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
library(readr)

# Specify the desired data structure, a 2-column data frame with one column a 
# double and the other a datetime
desired_column_spec <- cols(v1="d", v2="T")

# SITUATION 1 (GOOD): Enforce desired spec on load, even when values are all NA
read_csv("v1,v2\nNA,NA\nNA,NA", col_types = desired_column_spec)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>      v1 v2                 
#>   <dbl> <dttm>             
#> 1    NA NA                 
#> 2    NA NA

# SITUATION 2 (GOOD): Use a "generic spec", essentially forcing specific columns as 
# character, which type_convert supports to convert to numeric and datetime
df <- read_csv("v1,v2\nNA,NA\nNA,NA", col_types = cols(v1="c", v2="c"))
df %>% type_convert(col_types = desired_column_spec)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>      v1 v2                 
#>   <dbl> <dttm>             
#> 1    NA NA                 
#> 2    NA NA

# SITUATION 3 (NOT GOOD): Load without spec, which causes columns to be logical, then 
# you can't use type_convert() at all, and what's worse is that there is no warning message 
# that nothing was converted
df <- read_csv("v1,v2\nNA,NA\nNA,NA")
df %>% type_convert(col_types = desired_column_spec)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   v1    v2   
#>   <lgl> <lgl>
#> 1 NA    NA   
#> 2 NA    NA
```

In SITUATION 3 you can't convert a logical column back to a double or character, even if that is a possible datatype to cast from the existing values in the column. It is important to note that warnings do appear when trying to cast a `character` to another datatype when it is not possible (e.g. `character` to `numeric` column). One could hope to get a similar type of warning if the `logical` column is specified in `cols()` but not actually being converted.

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
library(readr)

df <- read_csv("v1,v2\nhi,NA\nNA,NA")
# this prints an warning message at least!
df %>% type_convert(col_types = cols(v1="d", v2="c"))
#> Warning in type_convert_col(char_cols[[i]], specs$cols[[i]], which(is_character)
#> [i], : [0, 1]: expected a double, but got 'hi'
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>      v1 v2   
#>   <dbl> <lgl>
#> 1    NA NA   
#> 2    NA NA
```

----
### Discussion of potential solutions

I'm starting to confuse myself a bit on whether the desired behavior for `type_convert()` is to essentially replicate `type.convert` in the sense that only character columns will be converted `vs.` being able to use the `col_types` argument like we do with `read_csv()` to enforce a specific datatype for each column. The latter seems like useful functionality for `type_convert()` to have, and if not, then potentially in a separate function.

----
### Current Workaround

If you can't enforce the column datatypes on load (e.g. via read_csv), then convert all columns to strings and then use type_convert from there.

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
library(readr)
df <- read_csv("v1,v2\nNA,NA\nNA,NA") # assume you can't enforce spec here on load
# cast the columns
df %>% 
  mutate_at(c("v1"), ~parse_double(as.character(.x))) %>% 
  mutate_at(c("v2"), ~parse_datetime(as.character(.x)))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>      v1 v2                 
#>   <dbl> <dttm>             
#> 1    NA NA                 
#> 2    NA NA
```

**Why you need to use this workaround**
You have to use this workaround if you're not sure whether the column will contain all `NA` values. In the example below, the columns in `df2` are not all `NA`, so we don't really need to use the `mutate_at`, but if we don't know ahead of time, then we still have to do it this way. Otherwise, we'll get trapped into uncastable `logical` column types.

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
library(readr)

df1 <- read_csv("v1,v2\nNA,NA\nNA,NA")
df1 %>% 
  mutate_at(c("v1"), ~parse_double(as.character(.x))) %>% 
  mutate_at(c("v2"), ~parse_datetime(as.character(.x)))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>      v1 v2                 
#>   <dbl> <dttm>             
#> 1    NA NA                 
#> 2    NA NA

df2 <- read_csv("v1,v2\n1,1979-10-14T10:11:12\nNA,NA")
df2 %>% 
  mutate_at(c("v1"), ~parse_double(as.character(.x))) %>% 
  mutate_at(c("v2"), ~parse_datetime(as.character(.x)))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>      v1 v2                 
#>   <dbl> <dttm>             
#> 1     1 1979-10-14 10:11:12
#> 2    NA NA

bind_rows(df1, df2)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>      v1 v2                 
#>   <dbl> <dttm>             
#> 1    NA NA                 
#> 2    NA NA                 
#> 3     1 1979-10-14 10:11:12
#> 4    NA NA
```

title: `readr::read_delim()`: delim argument accepts >1 character
description:
`readr::read_delim()` seems to accept more than one character for the `delim` argument without giving an error or appropriate warning (on the reprex below the warning is for another issue). In the help it states delim is "Single character used to separate fields within a record". Base R `read.delim()` gives an error when `sep`` is not one byte.

```
library(tidyverse)

delimFile <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
delimSpace <- c('Date , City , Temp
"18/06/2017" , "Lisbon, Portugal" , 23
"18/06/2017" , "Rome, Italy" , 25
"18/06/2017" , "Oslo, Norway" , 12')
write_file(delimSpace, delimFile)

# I didn't expect this outcome or the warning message 
  space_delim_3 <- readr::read_delim(delimFile, delim = " , ")
  glimpse(space_delim_3)

# Base R read.delim() gives an error when sep is not one byte.
# Not run.
#   space.delim.3 <- read.delim(delimFile, sep = " , ", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

It would be a nice to be able to use more than one character for the `delim` argument to handle CSV files like the one above.

title: read_fwf and pipe connections
description:
Similar to #552, a `pipe(...)` connection is not recognized in `read_fwf`:

```r
read_fwf(system("c:/Rtools/bin/echo -e 'a b\nc d'", intern = TRUE),
         fwf_widths(c(2, 1)))
# # A tibble: 2 x 2
#   X1    X2   
#   <chr> <chr>
# 1 a     b    
# 2 c     d    
read_fwf(pipe("c:/Rtools/bin/echo -e 'a b\nc d'"),
         fwf_widths(c(2, 1)))
# Error in isOpen(con) : invalid connection
```

On linux:

```r
readLines(pipe("/bin/echo -e 'a b\nc d'"))
# [1] "a b" "c d"

readr::read_fwf(pipe("/bin/echo -e 'a b\nc d'"), readr::fwf_widths(c(2,1)))
# Error in isOpen(con) : invalid connection
```

`readr-1.3.1` on both systems.

title: The is.character() check in parse_number() seems unnecessary.
description:
If you give parse_number() a vector that includes numbers in both numeric and character format, it returns an all-numeric vector without complaint.

> readr::parse_number(c(10,'15','12,345'))
[1]    10    15 12345

If you give it a vector that's all numeric, it throws an error:

> readr::parse_number(c(10,15,20))
Error in parse_vector(x, col_number(), na = na, locale = locale, trim_ws = trim_ws) : 
  is.character(x) is not TRUE

In the following real-world example, reading the sample county-by-county election results in Pennsylvania results in a list of dataframes where the Votes column is usually in character format, since they contain comma-delimited vote totals but some of the smaller counties have Votes columns in integers. Ideally, you want them all to be integers for analysis, but running parse_number() on them produces the error because of the few that are in integer format.

What's the issue the is.character() test is designed to prevent?

``` r
library(tidyverse)

payload <- xml2::read_html("https://electionreturns.pa.gov/electionFeed.aspx?ID=23&FeedName=2020+Primary+Election+by+County")

df <- payload %>%
  rvest::html_nodes("table") %>%
  rvest::html_table(header = TRUE, fill = TRUE)

df <- purrr::imap(df, ~mutate(.x, Votes = readr::parse_number(Votes)))
#> Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `Votes`.
#> x is.character(x) is not TRUE
#> i Input `Votes` is `readr::parse_number(Votes)`.
```

title: Read files with skip until regex match
description:
### The feature request
It would be really great if file reading would work with a variable `skip` argument based on a regex match. When reading many files from certain sources, some files may have different number of lines in the descriptor (header? metadata?) at the top of the file. 

### Reprex:
```r
content_1 <- "descriptor of file 1\n#----\ncol1;col2\n1;2\n2;3\n4;5\n6;7\n"
content_2 <- "descriptor of file 2\nanother line in the descriptor\n#----\ncol1;col2\n1;2\n2;3\n4;5\n6;7\n"

writeLines(content_1, file_1 <- tempfile())
writeLines(content_2, file_2 <- tempfile())

# different skips needed for different files
readr::read_delim(file_1, delim = ";", skip = 2)
readr::read_delim(file_2, delim = ";", skip = 3)
```

### Proposed user interface: a character accepted in the skip argument
```r
# Specify the end of the header using a regex pattern
readr::read_delim(file_2, delim = ";", skip = "#----")
```

With some guidance, I would also be happy to try an implementation in a pull request!

title: write_csv (and any other in the write_delim family) can't export NaN anymore
description:
Hi,
I have an issue with the commit ccc4dea68fe8c0cb1e19d3e279c532ccebed5775 for readr 1.4.0:
* `write_*()` functions now output any NaN values in the same way as NA values,
  controlled by the `na=` argument. (#1082).

I can't export `NaN` anymore, which I was using for my work.
Since this was is in line with `write.csv()` and `data.table::fwrite()`, I can't export `NaN` in any user friendly function right now.

This would add back the functionality while keeping the latest change intact.

title: Expose `num_threads` for the `vroom` backend
description: The 2nd edition of `readr` uses `vroom` as a backend, which by default utilizes `parallel::detectCores()` unless the user sets  `num_threads` argument or `VROOM_THREADS` environment variable. This can overwhelm the resources when reading multiple files in parallel. So, it would be useful to expose `num_threads`, defaulting to `1L` or `vroom::vroom_threads()`.

title: Memory usage of `read_csv_chunked()` in conjunction with a gzip compressed file
description:
Recently I have been running into `Error: vector memory exhausted (limit reached?)` errors when reading large gzip compressed .csv files using the chunked API. IIRC, earlier versions of readr would explicitly create a temporary file, containing the full uncompressed data, which then was fed into `read_csv_chunked()`.

Looking at reported memory usage, this no longer seems to be the case.  If this change was intentional, I apologize for having missed that, but I could not find any announcement hinting at this (neither from NEWS nor docs). Also, I feel this takes away some of the convenience of the chunked API. Of course, this can easily be resolved outside of readr by decompressing files manually beforehand (using for example `R.utils::gunzip()`).

title: Allow "skip" to specify multiple ranges
description:
Brief description of the problem

I'm trying to read in old US Census data from the 1860's.  Here's an example file:

http://us-census.org/pub/usgenweb/census/xtn/cheatham/1860/indx-a-b.txt

I've tried to read in the data using read_table:

    data <- read_table("http://us-census.org/pub/usgenweb/census/xtn/cheatham/1860/indx-a-b.txt", skip = 25)

The problem is, they use a long "VVVVVVV" line to delineate the header row, so if I start reading at row 25, the long "VVVV" string prevents read_table from defining the col_types correctly.

It would be useful if I could specify multiple skip ranges.   So to skip the first 25 lines, read one line, then skip the next line, something like "skip = c(25, 1)", or whatever makes sense.    

Or otherwise, tell read_table to skip any line that has "VVVVV" in it.  I tried to do this using the "comment" function but it didn't work.   It correctly plucks out the comment, but still auto-creates the col_types using the "VVVVV" line instead of the following lines.

    data <-   read_table("http://us-census.org/pub/usgenweb/census/xtn/cheatham/1860/indx-a-b.txt", skip = 25, comment = "VVVVV")

Hope that makes sense.

title: read_delim: unable to parse thorn delimiter - þ
description:
I've tried a variety of things but read_delim seems unable to parse this particularly nasty character.

Character encoding is latin1 (ISO-8859-1) and two bytes. `\xfe` is unicode representation.

All of the following fail:

`invalid multibyte string in col_name`
read_delim('thorn_test.txt', 'þ')

`parses all into one column`
read_delim('thorn_test.txt', '\xfe')

`correct columns - appends (¾) char in every column/value`
read_delim('thorn_test.txt', 'þ', locale=locale(encoding='latin1'))
read_delim('thorn_test.txt', 'þ', locale=locale(encoding='ISO-8859-1'))

`one column - appends  (Ã¾) in every column/value`
read_delim('thorn_test.txt', '\xfe', locale=locale(encoding='latin1'))

Conversely, in Python using Pandas the following works:

`pandas.read_csv('~/thorn_test.txt', delim='\xfe', engine='python')`

However, it doesn't work if the default C engine is used. Therefore, I'm thinking it has to do with how C/C++ handles this character.

title: read_file() %>% other_stuff() %>% write_file() has unexpected results
description:
I noticed this when switching from readr 1.3.1 to 1.4.0, but as shown below there is some unexpected behavior in 1.3.1 too. Basically you get weird behavior (usually an empty file) when you have a sequence of functions connected by a `%>%` that:

* reads something in with `read_file()`
* modifies the resulting string 
* writes something out with `write_file()`

# Reprex 1

This is a version of what my original code was doing: using `stringr::str_replace()` to modify the contents of a file.

```r
# This works as expected: foo is replaced by bar in the file
> library(readr)
> library(stringr)
> packageVersion("readr")
[1] ‘1.3.1’
> packageVersion("stringr")
[1] ‘1.4.0’
> write_file("foo", "foo.txt")
> read_file("foo.txt")
[1] "foo"
> read_file("foo.txt") %>% str_replace("foo", "bar")
[1] "bar"
> read_file("foo.txt") %>% str_replace("foo", "bar") %>% write_file("foo.txt")
> read_file("foo.txt")
[1] "bar"
```
But when I do this with 1.4.0 I get a blank file:
```r
> library(readr)
> library(stringr)
> packageVersion("readr")
[1] ‘1.4.0’
> packageVersion("stringr")
[1] ‘1.4.0’
> write_file("foo", "foo.txt")
> read_file("foo.txt")
[1] "foo"
> read_file("foo.txt") %>% str_replace("foo", "bar")
[1] "bar"
> read_file("foo.txt") %>% str_replace("foo", "bar") %>% write_file("foo.txt")
> read_file("foo.txt")
[1] ""
```

# Reprex 2

I tried to simplify this example by using `paste()` instead, and now I get unexpected behavior in _both_ 1.3.1 and 1.4.0. Hopefully this helps instead of confusing the issue further. Either way, I would expect the result of `read_file("foo.txt") %>% paste("second")` to the same thing that ends up in the file when I pipe it to `write_file()` but that's not the case in either version.

```r
> library(readr)
> packageVersion("readr")
[1] ‘1.3.1’
> write_file("first", "foo.txt")
> read_file("foo.txt")
[1] "first"
> read_file("foo.txt") %>% paste("second")
[1] "first second"
> read_file("foo.txt") %>% paste("second") %>% write_file("foo.txt")
> read_file("foo.txt")
[1] " second"
```
And also here
```r
> library(readr)
> packageVersion("readr")
[1] ‘1.4.0’
> write_file("first", "foo.txt")
> read_file("foo.txt")
[1] "first"
> read_file("foo.txt") %>% paste("second")
[1] "first second"
> read_file("foo.txt") %>% paste("second") %>% write_file("foo.txt")
> read_file("foo.txt")
[1] " second"
```

title: readr::write_file()'s text mode does not work on Windows
description:
Readr version 1.4.0, Windows 10 Home.

```
library(tidyverse)

fileObj <- file("test.txt", "wt") # text mode not working
msg <- "test message\n" # cannot automatically convert \n to \r\n
readr::write_file(msg, fileObj, append = TRUE)
close(fileObj)
```
The above code generates an error message:
```
 Error in (function (object, con, size = NA_integer_, endian = .Platform$endian,  : 
  can only write to a binary connection 
```

For the time being the temporary workaround is:
```
library(tidyverse)

fileObj <- file("test.txt", "wb") # use binary mode
msg <- "test message\r\n" # explicit Windows style
readr::write_file(msg, fileObj, append = TRUE)
close(fileObj)
```

title: read_csv column read as numeric loses accuracy for some numbers
description:
Some numbers (e.g. 0.66) read as numeric aren't imported precisely.
Specifying double seems to fix the problem, but shouldn't numeric have the same result?

``` r
library(readr)
library(tibble)

test_source <- tribble(
  ~num, ~dbl,
  0.65,   0.65,
  0.66,   0.66,
)

write_csv(test_source, 'test.csv')

test <- read_csv('test.csv', col_types = 'nd')

# Note addtional zero at end of numeric 0.66
test
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>     num   dbl
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 0.65   0.65

# Works as expected for 0.65

#> [1] TRUE
test$dbl[1] == 0.65

# Works as expected for 0.66 read as double
test$dbl[2] == 0.66

In particular, when using `AccumulateCallback` in conjunction with `read_delim_chunked`, is there a way to modify the accumulator in place (i.e., by reference) to avoid making deep copies? title: `write_csv2` adds leading space in numeric column to keep a fixed width
description:
Starting from a simple data frame:

```r
(bla <- data.frame(A = 1:3, B = c(12, 123, 0)))
```
```
  A   B
1 1  12
2 2 123
3 3   0
```
Export to a CSV file using `write_csv2` adds leading space to format the second column to 3 characters:

```r
write_csv2(bla, "bla.csv")
```
```
A;B
1; 12
2;123
3;  0
```
I don't think this is intended since 1) I didn't see it documented and you wouldn't expect it in a proper CSV file, and 2) `write_csv` and `write_delim` do not add them:

```r
write_delim(bla, "bla.csv")
```
```
A B
1 12
2 123
3 0
```

```r
write_csv(bla, "bla.csv")
```
```
A,B
1,12
2,123
3,0
```

Also, a fun side effect happens in case of a simple column with only 0–9 and `NA`s:

```r
(bla <- data.frame(A = 1:3, B = c(NA, NA, 0)))
```
```
  A  B
1 1 NA
2 2 NA
3 3  0
```
```r
write_csv2(bla, "bla.csv")
```
```A;B
1;NA
2;NA
3; 0
```
where the column is defined to two characters to match the length of `NA`. Even if we explicitely ask to use an empty cell (`na = ""`) for missing values, the leading space is kept:

```r
write_csv2(bla, "bla.csv", na = "")
```
```
A;B
1;
2;
3; 0
```

title: write_csv does not write output correctly
read_delim() fails when sample of parsing problems contains non-ASCII characters
description:
When a non-ASCII file is read using `read_delim()` or its friends *and* there are parsing failures *and* the text used by `warn_problems()` contains non-ASCII characters, the following error is returned:

```
## Error in nchar(x) : invalid multibyte string, element 3
```

This is quite hard to debug because the error makes it seem like the encoding was set incorrectly or the file has problems. (In my case it only occurred with 2 out of about 6000 CSV files read using `map_dfr()` even though all contained non-ASCII text.)

In fact the error occurs in `warn_problems()`: 

https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/blob/05890c3b493458ad4699654ceed58d2515939e94/R/problems.R#L83

where `nchar()` throws an error if one of the problems "sampled" for display contains a non-UTF-8 string. The data is in fact read correctly inside `read_delimited()`; the call only fails once `warn_problems()` is called.

Once I supplied the column specification and the non-ASCII text no longer appeared in the list of reported problems, the error no longer occurred (see reprex).

Possibly related to #1111 where the same error is thrown by `parse_number()`; this may have a similar root cause though I haven't investigated specifically.

Reprex:

```r
tf <- tempfile()
download.file("https://vdp.cuzk.cz/vymenny_format/csv/20200930_OB_547999_ADR.csv.zip", destfile = tf)
read_csv2(tf, locale = locale(encoding = "Windows-1250"))

## Error in nchar(x) : invalid multibyte string, element 3
```

Inspecting this in the debugger, the `probs_f` variable used inside `warn_problems()` does indeed contain non-ASCII text.

This works as expected:

```
read_csv2(tf, locale = locale(encoding = "Windows-1250"),
          col_types = cols(.default = "c"))

```

The file referenced in the reprex above was correctly read using `read.csv2` also using the "WINDOWS-1250" encoding. Likewise it can be read in python using the pandas CSV reader with the same encoding.

System:

Mac OS
R 4.0.2
readr 1.4.0 from CRAN

title: version bump to avoid cpp11 serialization error?
description:
Hi,

we've had the problem where `save` would fail trying to serialize `cpp11_preserve_env`. What was confusing that the problem still occured, even though it was fixed in cpp11 and we had the right version of cpp11 installed. But of course `readr` links statically against cpp11 and since we've built `readr` before the fix, it was still using the old code. As it wasn't very obvious that the problem was caused by `readr`, I thought maybe one could bump the version on CRAN so other people who might have the same problem would trigger rebuilding their `readr` package. Duno if this is the best solution but might save some people from a little headache.

Regards, Dominik

title: Empty strings disappear when reading a single-column data.frame
description:
Empty strings are discarded when reading a single column data.frame. This happens with both `read_delim` or `read_table`.

See the example below where the second row just disappears, despite being written correctly.

``` r
df <- data.frame(x = c("a", "", "c"))
readr::write_csv(df, "test.csv")
readr::read_lines("test.csv")
#> [1] "x" "a" ""  "c"
readr::read_csv("test.csv", col_types = "c")
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>   x    
#>   <chr>
#> 1 a    
#> 2 c
readr::read_table("test.csv", col_types = "c")
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>   x    
#>   <chr>
#> 1 a    
#> 2 c
```

<sup>Created on 2020-11-25 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

This happens across several column types:

``` r
readr::write_lines(c("x", "1", "", "3"), "test_num.csv")
readr::read_csv("test_num.csv", col_types = "c")
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>   x    
#>   <chr>
#> 1 1    
#> 2 3
readr::read_csv("test_num.csv", col_types = "d")
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>       x
#>   <dbl>
#> 1     1
#> 2     3
readr::read_csv("test_num.csv", col_types = "i")
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>       x
#>   <int>
#> 1     1
#> 2     3
```

<sup>Created on 2020-11-25 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

Interestingly, the bug only appears when the data contains one column. As soon there's a second column, it works:

 ``` r
df2 <- data.frame(x = c("a", "", "c"), 
                  y = 1:3)
readr::write_csv(df2, "test2.csv")
readr::read_csv("test2.csv")
#> 
#> ── Column specification ─────────────────── ...
#> cols(
#>   x = col_character(),
#>   y = col_double()
#> )
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   x         y
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 a         1
#> 2 <NA>      2
#> 3 c         3
```

<sup>Created on 2020-11-25 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

I just noticed this with `readr` 1.3.1 but it is still present in the latest github version. Tested with R 3.6 and `vctrs` 0.3.5.

Shout-out to the new `vctrs` consistency check which forced me to discover the bug :+1:

title: Memory errors when using Rscript with read_tsv_chunked() with trailing tab
description:
Sorry for the bizzare problem. When using `read_tsv_chunked()` on a large enough malformed file, R throws random memory issues. When running this in Rstudio I get the classic bomb with unexpected termination. But when running via Rscript on console I get a random sample of

address 0x55fd97fb94f8, cause 'memory not mapped'
```
or
```
malloc(): unsorted double linked list corrupted
```
or
```
*** recursive gc invocation
*** recursive gc invocation
*** recursive gc invocation
*** recursive gc invocation
*** recursive gc invocation
...many more
```
and potentially other memory errors that I have not noted down.

The code below is the minimal triggering condition on Pop!OS 20.04 LTS (Ubuntu 20.04).  Run via Rscript with R4.0.3 and readr 1.4.0.

```r
writeLines(paste("x", 1:6, sep = "", collapse = "\t"), "test.txt")
write(
    rep(paste0(paste(letters[1:6], collapse = "\t"), "\t"), 1e7), # trailing tab
    "test.txt",

)

title: readr fails to interpret gzip multibyte string
description:
Given a g'zipped file that does not have a file extension, `readr` complains that it has detected an invalid multibyte string.  Note that in contrast, vroom correctly detects the gzip type:

```r
readr::write_tsv(mtcars, "mtcars.tsv.gz")
fs::file_copy("mtcars.tsv.gz", "mtcars")
# works
vroom::vroom("mtcars")

# error invalid multi-byte string
readr::read_tsv("mtcars")

# works once we manually use gzfile, ick
readr::read_tsv(gzfile("mtcars"))

## works with extension from file name
readr:::read_tsv("mtcars.tsv.gz")
```

My understanding is that it would be best for readr to identify the compression from the multibyte string instead of relying on the convention of a filename extension.

title: Need option to ignore terminator at end of each line instead of parsing failure per line?

```

I took care of the phantom column created by the unexpected terminators in this kludgy way:

```
organizations <- 
  read_delim(
              filename, 
              delim = "|",                       # pipe delimiter
              quote = "",                        # not quote delimited
              na = character(),                  # no missing values
              col_types = cols(.default = "c")   # all character types for now

```

title: wchar_t Unicode warning on Solaris
description:
Filing this issue since @cpsievert saw the same thing for htmltools and figured out the problem and thought you'd want to know. 

On Solaris, readr currently has this warning:

```
checking for unstated dependencies in ‘tests’ ... WARNING
Warning in deparse(e[[2L]]) :
  it is not known that wchar_t is Unicode on this platform
Warning in deparse(e[[2L]]) :
  it is not known that wchar_t is Unicode on this platform
Warning in deparse(e[[2L]]) :
  it is not known that wchar_t is Unicode on this platform
Warning in deparse(e[[2L]]) :
  it is not known that wchar_t is Unicode on this platform
```

We had that warning for htmltools when checked with `--as-cran` on Solaris.

We found that it happens when a high-valued Unicode character is printed. For example:

```
> "\U0001F937"
[1] "\U0001f937"
Warning message:
it is not known that wchar_t is Unicode on this platform 
```

However, for lower-valued Unicode characters, it seems to be OK.

```
> "\Uff \U4E2d"
[1] "ÿ 中"
```

In htmltools, we didn't print the weird character in the tests, but it probably happened when the test fails (because perhaps Solaris isn't representing the character correctly), and then it tries to print the character. We worked around it by just disabling the relevant test on Solaris.

title: write_* formats badly numbers over 1e15
description:
Hallo,
I have a tibble whose numeric columns contain values ranging over several magnitude orders, partly in exponential notation.
Upon saving with `write_delim` (or similar), all numbers higher than $10^15$ are written in a very unusual exponential notation, which refers to the position of the _last_ significant digit. This is yet correct in strict mathematical meaning, but goes again common scientific practice and creates some confusion when the saved file is opened with a text editor such as Notepad++.
A reproducible example:
```
library(tidyverse)
u <- tibble( name=c("Planck constant","Avogadro number","Loschmidt constant",
                    "Faraday constant"),
            numValue=c(6.62607015e-34,6.02214076e+23,2.65e+25,96485.33289),
            stdUncertainty=c(0,0,1.5e+19,5.9e-4) )
u           # the numbers are displayed correctly, apart from truncation
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   name               numValue stdUncertainty
#>   <chr>                 <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 Planck constant    6.63e-34       0.      
#> 2 Avogadro number    6.02e+23       0.      
#> 3 Loschmidt constant 2.65e+25       1.50e+19
#> 4 Faraday constant   9.65e+ 4       5.90e- 4
write_delim(u,"u1.tsv",delim="\t")
write.table(u,"u2.tsv",sep="\t",quote=FALSE,row.names=FALSE)
```
Here is the output of `write_delim`, opened with Notepad++:
> name               numValue       stdUncertainty
Planck constant    6.62607015e-34 0
Avogadro number    602214076e15   0
Loschmidt constant 265e23         15e18
Faraday constant   96485.33289    5.9e-4

whereas the old `write.table` correctly formats the numbers in scientific notation (even the zero values, which actually don't need!):
> name               numValue        stdUncertainty
Planck constant    6.62607015e-34  0e+00
Avogadro number    6.02214076e+23  0e+00
Loschmidt constant 2.65e+25        1.5e+19
Faraday constant   9.648533289e+04 5.9e-04

title: Loss of precision in decimal places in write_csv2
description:
`write_csv2` and `write_excel_csv2` don't preserve the precision of decimal numbers in exported csv files, regardless of the current value of the `getOption("digits")`, as opposed to `write_csv` and `write_excel_csv`.

Since this is happening because of the transformation performed by `change_decimal_separator`, I hope this counts as a reproducible example:

``` r
digits <- getOption("digits")

df <- data.frame(value = 1234567.1)

options(digits = 7)
readr:::change_decimal_separator(df)
#>     value
#> 1 1234567

options(digits = 8)
readr:::change_decimal_separator(df)
#>       value
#> 1 1234567,1

options(digits = digits)
```

For reference, both `utils::write.csv2` and `data.table::fwrite` with arguments `dec = ","` and `sep = ";"` also preserve the decimal numbers.

title: Build fails on IBM i due to invalid '-rpath' linker flag

https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/commit/5e30b32ce22526ba1f227ad02aa6bc216ce182ea

If something like rpath is needed, the closest thing on AIX would be `-blibpath`

One could check UNAME for `OS400` (or `AIX`) and condition the `PKG_LIBS` syntax accordingly. 

I'd be willing to help develop/test a fix.

title: Add optional End Of Line (EOL) parameter for write functions
description: One challenge for using readr for writing files to be processed by other software is the lack of ability to define a Windows or Unix end of line characters. Adding a parameter for defining the EOL, like in read.table, would allow scripts to have consistent output regardless of the operating system the script is executed on.

title: write_csv2/format_csv2 adds leading whitespace to numbers
description:
When using write_csv2 or format_csv2, leading whitespace is added to values in a number column if the numbers are of different length:

```r
readr::format_csv(tibble(x = c(6, 66)))
# "x\n6\n66\n"
readr::format_csv2(tibble(x = c(6, 66)))
# "x\n 6\n66\n"
```
This is against the csv format (whitespace is significant). Perhaps add `trim = TRUE` to `format` in `change_decimal_separator`?

title: Partial reading from gzipped files
description:
Using readr 1.3.1, if I wanted to read just a few lines from a gzipped table, I find myself waiting quite a long time to get results.

```{r}
library(readr)

df <- data.frame(
    x = 1:1e7,
    y = 1:1e7
)

temp_file <- paste0(tempfile(), ".gz")

write_tsv(df, temp_file)

# Almost instant
system.time(
    read.table(temp_file, nrows = 10, header = TRUE)    
)

# Takes a few seconds
system.time(
    read_tsv(temp_file, n_max = 10)
)
```

I think this is readr fully decompressing the gzipped file, whereas the read.table is streaming the decompression.

title: parse_guess doesn't ignore NA values, thus rendering the na parameter less useful.
description:
I'd expect that `parse_guess` would first remove NA strings prior to guessing the type. Otherwise anything with an NA encoded as a string (rather than `_NA_character`) would not be guessed correctly, as `guess_parser` does not filter NA strings.

---

```r
> parse_guess(c("123", NA))
[1] 123  NA
> parse_guess(c("123", "NA"), na="NA")
[1] "123" NA  
```

Notice that it is converting the `"NA"` to `NA`, but not prior to parsing.

title: should `type_convert()` erase the 'spec' attribute?
description:
When [`readr::type_convert()`](https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/blob/master/R/type_convert.R) is applied to a data.frame, should it update the 'spec' attribute?  Currently, it does not, and potentially returns a misleading result.

```r
library(magrittr); library(readr)
d1 <- 
  read_csv(
    readr_example("mtcars.csv"),
    col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
  )
str(d1)
```

After the initial creation, the data.frame's spec attribute is correct (*i.e.*, all columns are character).
```
Classes ‘spec_tbl_df’, ‘tbl_df’, ‘tbl’ and 'data.frame':	32 obs. of  11 variables:
 $ mpg : chr  "21" "21" "22.8" "21.4" ...
 ...
 $ carb: chr  "4" "4" "1" "1" ...
 - attr(*, "spec")=
  .. cols(
  ..   .default = col_character(),
  ..   mpg = col_character(),
  ..   cyl = col_character(),
  ...
  ..   carb = col_character()
  .. )
```

Then  `type_convert()` correctly converts everything to doubles.

```r
d2 <- data %>% 
  type_convert()
```

```
Parsed with column specification:
cols(
  mpg = col_double(),
  cyl = col_double(),
  ...
  carb = col_double()
)
```

But the spec still shows the character vectors.

```r
spec(d2)
```
```
cols(
  .default = col_character(),
  mpg = col_character(),
  cyl = col_character(),
  ...
  carb = col_character()
)
```

BTW, I really like this function.  It was nice when I was stacking a bunch of dataframe on top of each other, but some columns in some sub-dataframes were empty to the data types weren't compatible during the stack.

I appreciate the work you've already done and are doing!

Best,

Trent

title: read_csv fails with cryptic error when trying to read a csv with > 2 billion rows
description:
I'm trying to use read_csv to read a CSV with 2.5 billion rows, and am greeted with the following error message:

`Error in read_tokens_(data, tokenizer, col_specs, col_names, locale_,  : 
  invalid value`

Browsing through the read_delim source file clued me in to the idea that the problem might be related to having a number of rows greater than the 32-bit integer limit.

So one question is whether there is any way around the integer limit. Obviously reading 2.5 billion row CSVs isn't a common use case, but I've got the RAM to handle the files.

The second question is whether a more informative error could be thrown, since a relatively easy workaround (at least for cases where total rows are under 2 * integer limit) is to use n_max and skip to read the file in pieces. But it's hard to arrive at this solution without knowing what is causing the error.

title: Issue with write_csv/read_csv on fractional seconds
description:
write_csv uses the display option digits.secs to determine the precision of timestamps when writing csv's and will cut off decimal seconds when exporting without any sort of warning (write.csv appears to do the same). Also there seems to be minor precision issues with reading and writing timestamps.
```

library(lubridate)
library(readr)
Sys.setenv(TZ='UTC')
options(digits.secs=6) #Set to display 6 decimal places
packageVersion("readr")
#[1] ‘1.3.1’

t1<- tibble(time= mdy_hms("1/1/2019_12:30:05", tz = "UTC")+microseconds(500))
t1$time[1] #"2019-01-01 12:30:05.0004 UTC" #Displayed incorrectly
t1$time[1] == ymd_hms("2019-01-01 12:30:05.0005") #TRUE (Actually equal to .0005 despite incorrect display)
write_csv(t1, "test_time.csv") #write csv with display set to 6 decimal places

options(digits.secs=2) #Set to only display 2 decimal places
write_csv(t1, "test_time2.csv") #write csv with display set to 2 decimal places

options(digits.secs=6) #Reset back to display 6 decimal places

test1<- read_csv("test_time.csv")
test1_text<- read_csv("test_time.csv", col_types= "c") #read in as character
test2<-  read_csv("test_time2.csv")
test2_text<- read_csv("test_time2.csv", col_types= "c") #read in as character


t1$time[1]==ymd_hms("2019-01-01 12:30:05.0005") #TRUE
test1_text$time[1] #"2019-01-01T12:30:05.000499Z" (6 digits but slightly off)
test1$time[1]==ymd_hms("2019-01-01 12:30:05.000499") #TRUE
test2_text$time[1] #"2019-01-01T12:30:05.00Z" (Only written 2 decimal places)
test2$time[1]==ymd_hms("2019-01-01 12:30:05.00") #TRUE
```

This feature if available or could be made possible will be very helpful.

Thanks,

Ashu

title: parse_number() on hexadecimal, binary numbers
description:
Playing around with `parse_number()`, I realized it has strange behavior with respect to non-decimal numbers. `as.numeric()` can parse hexadecimal properly, but not binary, both are probably reasonable.

On hexadecimal:
``` r
readr::parse_number("0x1f")
#> [1] 0
as.numeric("0x1f")
#> [1] 31
```

<sup>Created on 2019-10-15 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

On binary:
``` r
readr::parse_number("0b1011")
#> [1] 0
as.numeric("0b1011")
#> Warning: NAs introduced by coercion
#> [1] NA
Rcpp::evalCpp("0b1011")
#> [1] 11
```

<sup>Created on 2019-10-15 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

The result of `readr::parse_number("0x1f")` seems strange; it appears to parse the first "number" it finds with no warning. Is that expected?
``` r
readr::parse_number("asdf123.12asdf234")
#> [1] 123.12
```

title: Provide custom logical format in col_logical()
description:
(Read feature request)

It would be cool if you could provide the character format for logical variables (like you can for dates).

The [`batman::to_logical()`](https://github.com/Ironholds/batman/blob/master/R/batman.R) function is pretty good for this after the fact, but it would be _awesome_ if you could do it all in the initial `readr` function.

Something like this:

```
read_csv(
  file = "x\nY\nN\nY\nY\nN",
  col_types = cols(x = col_logical(true = "Y", false = "N"))
)
```

Or maybe this:

```
read_csv(
  file = "x\nY\nN\nY\nY\nN",
  col_types = cols(x = col_logical(format = "Y/N"))
)
```

title: guess_parser returns character when passed a factor?
description:
I recently found that `guess_parser` returns a character when passed a factor - this seems to be something that has changed recently - this is used internally in `visdat` to visualise possible types of values for each value.

This now means that factors are not returned, and I just thought I should check if that is intended behaviour. It makes sense to me to not worry about factors in `readr`, but just thought I would double check.

``` r
library(readr)

guess_parser("1")
#> [1] "double"
guess_parser("1.1")
#> [1] "double"
guess_parser("a")
#> [1] "character"
guess_parser("b")

# This seems unexpected - I would expect factor?
guess_parser(factor("a"))

title: `recode_na` argument in `col_*` functions ?
description:
I'm working on a csv that has a column that is either missing or `1`. missing means `FALSE ` and `1` means `TRUE`.

It would have been convenient to be able to map these missing values to `FALSE ` directly in the `read_*` call for this specific column. As far as I understand this is not possible at the moment.

For character columns it can also be convenient to set specific values for missing.

Maybe something like this : 

```
read_csv(
  csv_path,
  col_types = cols(is_foo = col_logical(na_recode = FALSE),
                   bar = col_character(na_recode = "unknown bar"))
```

By the same token, these could have a parameter `na` that overrides the `na` parameter of `read_*` functions for specific columns ?

title: Allow read_csv() to determine column types using all rows
description:
I'm using `read_csv()` to read data files.  However, I receive parsing failures because `read_csv()` is trying to guess the column types based on the first 1000 rows (the default value for the `guess_max` argument).  This leads to parsing failures because my values in the later rows of the data frame (e.g., 2s and 3s) do not conform to the binary variable (0s/1s) that is guessed from the first 1000 rows.

Ideally, we'd be able to set `guess_max` to `Inf` or (automatically) to the number of rows in the dataframe.  But these are not an option—`read_csv()` throws an error when trying to set `guess_max` to `Inf`: see issue https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/588.  A successful workaround is to manually set `guess_max` to an arbitrarily large number.  But this is not elegant, and it can lead to system crashing or errors if the value is too large (see issue https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/588).  And it's not always practical to specify all column types manually.  It would also be nice not to have to use two steps (read in the data as characters and use `type_convert()`).

title: Fixed-width file import should have option to ignore single spaces
description:
`readr` has a number of helpful functions — `read_table()`, `read_table2()` and `fwf_empty()` — that can examine whitespace in a fixed-width file and estimate where column breaks should be. 

However, this can behave poorly in cases where columns contain unquoted strings with spaces in them. To give some common examples, "New York" or "Cook County". 

As an example, I've loaded the first few lines of a U.S. Census file showing county-to-county migration (original, very large file [here](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/tables/geographic-mobility/2016/county-to-county-migration-2012-2016/county-to-county-migration-flows/CtyxCty_US.txt)) into a [gist](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/dhmontgomery/b43b0bd09c80ac4ec0659aa8e8b0201b/raw/2d476575e02486d14cb263fd831bdf2c29e47fe1/fwf_text.txt). 

All three of the options below produce the same output: detecting the space in "Autauga County" as reflecting separate columns:

```r
url <- "https://gist.githubusercontent.com/dhmontgomery/b43b0bd09c80ac4ec0659aa8e8b0201b/raw/2d476575e02486d14cb263fd831bdf2c29e47fe1/fwf_text.txt"
read_table(url, col_names = FALSE)
read_table2(url, col_names = FALSE)
read_fwf(url, col_positions = fwf_empty(url))
```

Obviously there are some cases where we *want* these functions to treat a single space as reflecting separate columns in a fixed-width data. So changing the default behavior here would be bad. My thought was that the functions could be improved by adding an option to ignore single spaces when calculating columns.

title: [Feature Request] Print column specification with write_csv
description:
When a csv created by `write_csv()` is read into another script, it would be helpful to have the column specification already produced as a side-effect of the `write_csv()` call that produced it.

Here's one way that could look. 

After `write_csv()` is used, a message is printed with the column specification matching the datatypes of the dataframe that was input to `write_csv()`.

``` r
library(tibble)
library(lubridate)
library(readr)

df <- data_frame(ID = c("01", "42"),
                 Date = ymd(c("2018-10-31", "2010-10-30")))

write_csv(df, path = "Data.csv")

#> To read "Data.csv", you can use the following column specification:
#> cols(
#>      ID = col_character(),
#>      Date = col_date(format = "")
#>      )
```

This would make it easier to integrate `write_csv()` into a data-processing pipeline that plays nicely with Git.

title: Enable writing to textConnection objects
description:
I am writing an API that can return data formatted as CSV, and for that I want to be able to save CSV data in a string (that I can put in a request) rather than a file.

I am aware I could write to a temporary file then read the file as a string, however it seems more natural to write directly to a string.

With `write.csv`, this can be achieved with a `textConnection`

``` r
write.csv(head(mtcars), textConnection("str1", open = "w"))
str1
#> [1] "\"\",\"mpg\",\"cyl\",\"disp\",\"hp\",\"drat\",\"wt\",\"qsec\",\"vs\",\"am\",\"gear\",\"carb\""
#> [2] "\"Mazda RX4\",21,6,160,110,3.9,2.62,16.46,0,1,4,4"                                            
#> [3] "\"Mazda RX4 Wag\",21,6,160,110,3.9,2.875,17.02,0,1,4,4"                                       
#> [4] "\"Datsun 710\",22.8,4,108,93,3.85,2.32,18.61,1,1,4,1"                                         
#> [5] "\"Hornet 4 Drive\",21.4,6,258,110,3.08,3.215,19.44,1,0,3,1"                                   
#> [6] "\"Hornet Sportabout\",18.7,8,360,175,3.15,3.44,17.02,0,0,3,2"                                 
#> [7] "\"Valiant\",18.1,6,225,105,2.76,3.46,20.22,1,0,3,1"
```

<sup>Created on 2019-09-06 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>


This however does not work with `readr::write_csv`

``` r

Why not? Can it be enabled?

title: write_csv should have an option to specify end of line character
description: There should be an option to specify what character should be on the end of a line.  I am dealing with a process of loading data to a database from .csv files, and it only works when the eol is a Carriage Return Line Feed (as is done when Windows Excel saves a .csv file).  The current function saves with a Line Feed, and I do not see any option to change this, unless I missed it.

title: write_csv (and any other in the write_delim family) can't handle NaN values
description:
Hi, working with *readr* version 1.3.1.  In this and previous versions, I've found that whenever there are NaN's in the data, `write_csv` presents no options for handling them.  They are always written out as NaN, no matter what is passed to the parameter "na".  

Within R, of course, NaN's function as a type of NA's, and can sometimes emerge organically from normal operations where "true" NA's are present, as shown in the reprex.   

The complimentary reading functions within R (`read_csv` and `read.csv`) can recognize the NaN's and thus maintain them and any expected behavior, but this presents problems for moving data to any outside environment where the user would expect that data to be marked as missing.  

I could see preserving NaN's for some users if that avoids information loss in their data, but I'd love to at least have a choice of behavior.  And if I'm being opinionated, I think the reasonable default behavior would handle NaN's uniformly with writing all the other classes/types of NA, fitting the expectations of most users who are reasoning from the fact that `is.na(NaN)` evaluates to `TRUE`.

```r
is.na(NaN) # NaN's are considered missing data, 
# Data with some NA's and NaN's
dat <- 
  tibble(a = c(NA, 1:10),
         b = c(NA, 11:20),
         c = c(NA, 21:25, NaN, 27:30),
         d = c(NA, 31:35, NA, 37:40)
  ) %>% 
  # NaN's can derive from NA's in some operations:
  mutate(e = rowMeans(., na.rm=T))

# write_csv leaves NaN's:
write_csv(dat, "./file.csv")

# Explicitly specifying the na parameter does nothing:
write_csv(dat, na = "XXX", "./file2.csv")

```

title: read_csv fails on zipped empty csv files
description:

While read_csv directly supports reading .gz zipped files, if you try and open an empty text file that is first "gz" zipped you get an error.

It seems like this edge case should have a catch?

title: warnings from read_* functions are not tryCatch:able
description:
Hello,

Thanks for the great library, I use it nearly day in my PhD studies 👍 . Today though, I came across a small issue trying to automate some document reading (I now know about stop_for_problems()).

Using tryCatch with parse_number, the warnings emitted are caught as expected.
```r
tryCatch(parse_number(c("12", "13", "ABC")), warning = function(w) parse_character(c("12", "13", "ABC")))
```
However, with the read_* functions warnings emitted are not caught.
```r
test_data <- readr_example("fwf-sample.txt")

tryCatch({
    # Explicitly wrong column specification
    read_table(test_data, col_types = cols(col_number(), col_number(), col_number(), col_number()))
}, warning = function(w) {
    # Let readr guess the column specificaiton
    read_table(test_data)
})
```

title: encoding = "ISO-8859-1" much slower than encoding = "UTF-8"
description:
I found that the readr function configured with encoding = "UTF-8" is almost 15 times faster than with encoding = "ISO-8859-1".

Would it be possible to speed up the reading when the encoding is different from "UTF-8"?

OBS: The file "[K3241.K03200DV.D00124.L00001](https://onedrive.live.com/download?resid=758C804985145E0F!480632&authkey=!AE444CSMQcWi3rE&e=KIWKUl)" used in the reprex has the encoding "ISO-8859-1" and can be [downloaded here](https://onedrive.live.com/download?resid=758C804985145E0F!480632&authkey=!AE444CSMQcWi3rE&e=KIWKUl). title: write_excel_csv inserts 'U+FEFF' (Byte Order Mark) when append = TRUE
description:
`write_excel_csv` inserts 'U+FEFF', Byte Order Mark (BOM) when append = TRUE, `write_csv` doesn't. I believe it would be preferable if neither did.

From the docs:

> All columns are encoded as UTF-8. `write_excel_csv()` and `write_excel_csv2()` also include a UTF-8 Byte order mark which indicates to Excel the csv is UTF-8 encoded.

However, `write_excel_csv` doesn't include the BOM if there is no "append"ing. 

I discovered this problem because a vlookup in Excel wasn't matching the values in the first row of each appended section.

I've included session info, but can confirm that this behavior is the same on Windows and Mac.

**Note:** reprex creates 2 csv files that are necessary to demonstrate problem.

``` r
library(reprex)
library(tidyverse)

simple_tbl <- tibble(
  Region = c("West", "East", "North", "South"),
  Sales = c(50, 100, 73, 28)
)

simple_write <- function(rgn, sales, out_file, use_excel_csv) {
  
  out <- tibble(
    region_summary = paste0("Sales for the ", rgn, " region: ", sales)
  )
  
  append_flag <- file.exists( out_file )
  
  if (use_excel_csv) {
    write_excel_csv(
      out,
      out_file,
      append = append_flag,
      col_names = !append_flag
    )
  } else {
    write_csv(
      out,
      out_file,
      append = append_flag,
      col_names = !append_flag
    )
  }
}

# sales_excel.csv will have U+FEFF (Byte Order Mark)
# at start of each "append"
simple_tbl %>%
  select(Region, Sales) %>%
  pwalk(~simple_write(..1, ..2, "sales_excel.csv", TRUE))

# sales_no_excel.csv will not have any U+FEFF
simple_tbl %>%
  select(Region, Sales) %>%
  pwalk(~simple_write(..1, ..2, "sales_no_excel.csv", FALSE))
```

title: Unexpected handling of multiple input files in readr::read_lines
description:
I am attempting to get readr::read_lines to read in multiple files. 
Works fine for one file, but when filepath is a vector n>1, it does not return the contents of all of the files. 

---

Brief description of the problem

```r
library(tidyverse)

text1 = "12345"
text2 = "abcde"

# read a single file
#
file1 = "file1.csv"
file2 = "file2.csv"

write(text1, file1)
write(text2, file2)
bothfiles=c(file1, file2)


#works fine
readr::read_lines(file=file1)
#works fine
readr::read_lines(file=file2)

#now try to read both ..
readr::read_lines(file=bothfiles)
# fails

# Expected result:
# "12345"
# "abcde"

# This fails also
map_df(bothfiles, readr::read_lines)

sessionInfo()
```
I suspect user error, of course, but seems worth documenting.

title: Why parse_number() removes decimal digits if there are at least 7 digits in the number?
description:
See the code from the examples section of `readr::parse_number` documentation (https://readr.tidyverse.org/reference/parse_number.html#examples): 

``` r
readr::parse_number("1,234,567.78")
#> [1] 1234568
```

<sup>Created on 2019-07-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

I noticed two digits `7` and `7` which were around `.` are gone. I expect 1234567.78 as the answer. The further investigation gave these results:

``` r
readr::parse_number("12,345.12") # OK
#> [1] 12345.12
readr::parse_number("12345.12") # OK
#> [1] 12345.12
readr::parse_number("123456.12") # 2 is missing
#> [1] 123456.1
readr::parse_number("1234567.12") # .12 is missing
#> [1] 1234567
readr::parse_number("1,234,567.12") # rounded, NOT OK
#> [1] 1234567
readr::parse_number("12,345.123456789") # rounded, NOT OK
#> [1] 12345.12
readr::parse_number("0.123456789") # rounded, NOT OK
#> [1] 0.1234568
```

<sup>Created on 2019-07-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

 It seems that some rounding is taking place if more than 7 digits are present in the number. Is it expected? How can it be controlled? I expect warning in case the precision of the data is changed. At least, this behavior should be well documented. 

Is number 7 somehow magical? 

`readr` version 1.3.1

title: read_delim (and friends) looks for file when given literal data
description:
The `read_delim` function accepts literal data when the `file` argument contains a newline, however, it will still attempt to access a file whose name is the literal data. This is because `read_delimited` will call `empty_file` on the literal data, which will (on Linux) end up calling the `stat` syscall.

Easily reproduced with:
```
[bash] strace -e trace=stat R
[r] library ('readr')
[r] read_delim ('this\nshould\nnot\nhappen', delim = ',')
[console] stat("this\nshould\nnot\nhappen", 0x7ffd6298e220) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
```
The function works in that it then correctly parses the literal data, but it is still strange that it should use the literal data to access the file system. (In general, it feels like doing autodetect on the `file` argument rather than distinguishing files, links and literal data through different arguments is somewhat fragile, and perhaps even not very useful.)

title: More helpful error when trying to write out data frames with list columns
description:
``` r
library(tidyverse)
#> Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 3.5.1
#> Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 3.5.1
diamonds %>% nest(-cut) %>% write_csv('test.csv')
#> Error in stream_delim_(df, path, ...): Don't know how to handle vector of type list.
```

Created on 2018-12-06 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).

It would be more useful (especially in non-interactive use) if the `write_` functions reported _which_ column it was unable to handle. My feeling is this error either happens because:

* Someone forgot to drop an intermediate list column (eg. nested source data or a list of models) before exporting;
* They accidentally used regular `map()` instead of a type-coercive variety like `map_dbl` to extract a parameter; or
* They don't understand that flat files can't store more complex list columns.

I understand that there's some discussion in #303 about potentially handling simple list columns, but given the variety of objects that end up in list columns accidentally, I imagine this problem will still exist even if that issue gets resolved. Actually implementing a PR for this might be a little out of my depth, but I'm willing to give it a go over Xmas.

title: Use of utils::unzip with default "internal" method prevents read_csv from effectively reading .zip files > 4 GB
description:
When I try to use read_csv to read a .zip file which is larger than 4 GB, the import appears to succeed, but is accompanied by a warning:

```
Warning message:
In (function (con, what, n = 1L, size = NA_integer_, signed = TRUE,  :
  possible truncation of >= 4GB file

```

And indeed only the first 4 GB of the file has been read. It appears that read_csv is using the utils::unzip function with its default unzip = "internal" argument.

Would it be possible to add some method for passing through the `unzip` argument to utils::unzip? Without being able to pass through unzip = "unzip" (or whatever else), read_csv effectively can't read from large zip files, which is ironic given the utility of storing large CSVs in a compressed format!

title: Why does readr::read_csv need timezone data and Olson database?
description:
This issue is closed, but I see no resolution: https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/320

I just ran into a similar situation today when teaching on a server. We were trying to use `readr::read_csv` to load this file: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UBC-DSCI/dsci-100/master/materials/worksheet_01/marathon_small.csv

On one server which has tzdata installed, it works fine, on another that does not have this installed the following error message is given:

```
library(tidyverse)
marathon_small <- read_csv("marathon_small.csv")
```

```
Warning message in OlsonNames():
“no Olson database found”
Error: Unknown TZ UTC
Traceback:

1. read_csv("marathon_small.csv")
2. read_delimited(file, tokenizer, col_names = col_names, col_types = col_types, 
 .     locale = locale, skip = skip, comment = comment, n_max = n_max, 
 .     guess_max = guess_max, progress = progress)
3. col_spec_standardise(data, skip = skip, comment = comment, guess_max = guess_max, 
 .     col_names = col_names, col_types = col_types, tokenizer = tokenizer, 
 .     locale = locale)
4. guess_header(ds_header, tokenizer, locale)
5. guess_header_(datasource, tokenizer, locale)
6. default_locale()
7. locale()
8. check_tz(tz)
9. stop("Unknown TZ ", x, call. = FALSE)
```

This csv file is very simple (see snippet below). Why does `readr::read_csv` need timezone data and Olson database? This GitHub issue, appears to tracking down  `readr::read_csv` depending on `tzdata` but why? Naively, it doesn't seem necessary, and `read.csv` works fine on either server.

`.csv` snippet:
```
age,bmi,km5_time_seconds,km10_time_seconds,sex
25.0,21.6221160888672,NA,2798,female
41.0,23.905969619751,1210.0,NA,male
25.0,21.6407279968262,994.0,NA,male
35.0,23.5923233032227,1075.0,2135,male
34.0,22.7064037322998,1186.0,NA,male
45.0,42.0875434875488,3240.0,NA,female
33.0,22.5182952880859,1292.0,NA,male
58.0,25.2340793609619,NA,3420,male
```

The smallest reproducible example I can get down to is this: 

```
library(tidyverse)
default_locale()
```

which on the problematic server gives: 
```
Warning message in OlsonNames():
“no Olson database found”
Error: Unknown TZ UTC
Traceback:

1. default_locale()
2. locale()
3. check_tz(tz)
4. stop("Unknown TZ ", x, call. = FALSE)
```

So the problem likely stems from the [`read_*` functions depending on `default_locale()` for the `locale` argument by default](https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/blob/a0fbe94c742be204f2cc4d823a0ed37613906059/R/read_delim.R#L118). Is this really necessary? Naively, I think not, but I could be very wrong. Is there a way to say `locale = None/NA/etc`?

This is not just a problem for me, as I have come across others experiencing the same problem...
- https://github.com/swirldev/swirl/issues/603
- https://github.com/jupyter/docker-stacks/issues/502
- https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/320
