description:
when read_lines() is used with longish text files (1000s of lines), the use of skip and n_max is unreliable. to demonstrate this issue i created a github repository (since the demo needs a file). it's here: https://github.com/dan-reznik/read_lines_bug

I am also including a "reprex", but you will need to download [text_file.zip](https://github.com/dan-reznik/read_lines_bug/blob/master/test_file.zip) from the above github repo to reproduce it.

The text file within the .zip has some 31.6k lines, all well-formed (CR+LF at the end of every line). It is a UTF-8 file. Still, via binary search (see code below) we notice that for k>=7379, read_lines("text_file.zip", skip=k, n_max=1) no longer equals to read_lines("text_file.zip")[k+1], though they should!

After hrs on this issue, I have failed to identify what could be present in lines of the input file prior to the problem line (a ghost character of some kind) to cause read_lines w/ a nonzero skip to lose sync. In any case, read_lines() should not care, as its only separator is the end-of-line.

``` r
suppressMessages(library(tidyverse))

# Confirm UTF-8 encoding of included zip file (it contains a larger .txt)
fname <- "test_file.zip" # get it from: https://github.com/dan-reznik/read_lines_bug/blob/master/test_file.zip
guess_encoding(fname)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   encoding     confidence
#>   <chr>             <dbl>
#> 1 UTF-8              1   
#> 2 Shift_JIS          1   
#> 3 windows-1252       0.68
#> 4 windows-1250       0.31

# Read all lines from zip (approx. 31.6k)
all_lines <- read_lines(fname)
length(all_lines)
#> [1] 31695

# Notice all lines have "well-formed" terminations with a carriage-return followed by a newline.
{
  s <- read_file(fname)
  print(s %>% str_count("\\r"))
  print(s %>% str_count("\\n"))
  print(s %>% str_count("\\r\\n"))
  print(s %>% str_count("\\n\\r"))
}
#> [1] 31695
#> [1] 31695
#> [1] 31695
#> [1] 0

# For this file, the separator is ";" (irrelevant for read_lines()), there should be 45 per line.
# However, notice a few lines have a non-standard number of separators (';'), namely: 46 and 48.
all_lines %>%
  str_count(";") %>%
  table
#> .
#>    45    46    48 
#> 31678    14     3

# List which lines have the wrong number of separators, as this will drive us to the bug.
all_lines %>%
  str_count(";") %>%
  {which(.!=45)}
#>  [1] 14579 24268 24269 26000 26792 26793 27535 29736 29737 29738 29755
#> [12] 29764 29936 29937 30383 30384 30385

# With `read_lines()`  read only the first line with the wrong number of separators,
# shown above to be line 14579. So "skip" that number minus one.
line1 <- read_lines(fname,
                    skip=14578,
                    n_max=1)

# Notice its content not only has a different number of separators,
# it's a different line altogether! (herein lies the bug)
all_lines[14579] %>% str_count(";")
#> [1] 48
line1 %>% str_count(";")
#> [1] 45
all_lines[14579] == line1
#> [1] FALSE

# BUG IS HERE: the line retrieved by `read_lines(skip=14578,n_max=1)` appears
# much later in the file, suggesting the reading under this skip+n_max has lost "sync".
(all_lines==line1)%>%which
#> [1] 17923

# find first line to cause loss of sync via binary search
find_weird_row <- function(n0,n_min,n_max) {
  l_skip <- read_lines(fname,skip=n0,n_max=1)
  l_all <- all_lines[n0+1]
  l_eq <- l_skip==l_all
  print(n0)
  #browser()
  if(n0%in%c(n_min,n_max)) {
    print(sprintf("line %d with l_eq=%s",
                  n0,
                  l_eq%>%as.character()))
    n0
  } else {
    if (!l_eq)
      find_weird_row(as.integer((n0+n_min)/2),n_min,n0)
    else
      find_weird_row(as.integer((n0+n_max)/2),n0,n_max)
  }
}

# IMPORTANT: binary search identifies that beyond line 7379, i.e.:
# read_lines(skip=7379,n_max=1) is no longer equal to all_lines[7380],
# recalling the latter is the complete read of the file via read_lines()
find_weird_row(15000,1,length(all_lines))
#> [1] 7379
```

Notes: 
- when skip and n_max are not defined (complete read), read_lines() works correctly
- this bug is not caused by the .zip (same behavior if started from the uncompressed txt)
- this is not related to encoding, in fact, I made sure the file inside the zip is UTF-8
- this issue seems to manifest itself with longer files only. potentially there's a character within this file being interpreted as a carriage return.
- this is an important bug to be solved because skip+n_max allows us to look at files progressively and debug problems without loading the entire file.

title: parse_* no longer useful for handling factors that represent numbers
description:
2be9285a5a585e7b2dc4c662875f14f1b39eb606 breaks using `parse_*` as a way to collapse factor levels that represent numbers back into those numbers.

Here is a situation that is common in surveys: Via a drop-down menu ask for a number, where one of the options is "x or more". I then want to map that "x or more" into a number for analysis.

The working solution looks weird to me. I would expect that whenever `parse_integer` takes a factor, it converts the factor values according to their labels, and then parses those labels as integers.

So I want to ask if this the intended behavior of `parse_*`?

``` r
library(tidyverse)
x <- factor(c(4:6, '7 or more'))
x <- fct_collapse(x, '10' = '7 or more')

# Does not work
as.integer(x)
#> [1] 1 2 3 4
parse_integer(x)
#> Error in parse_vector(x, col_integer(), na = na, locale = locale, trim_ws = trim_ws): is.character(x) is not TRUE

# Works, but looks weird
parse_integer(as.character(x))
#> [1]  4  5  6 10
```

title: read_builtin
description:
Something like this:

```R
read_builtin <- function(x, package = NULL) {
  x <- data(list(x), package = package, envir = environment())
  get(x[[1]], envir = environment)
}
```

Makes `data()` consistent with the other reading functions.

title: safer guessing on missing data?
description: I believe readr infers a literal NA in csv/tsv files as type logical, consistent with R's own behavior.  However, this seems to be asking for trouble when reading large tables with large amounts of missing data, where readr is frequently inclined to guess these columns as logicals and create coercion parsing errors.  Would it not be safer to default to the assumption that NA is a `as.character(NA)` instead of a logical NA?

Old version (1.1.0) yields `2018-01-01T00:00:00Z` in the newer versions (since 1.2.0) I get `2018/01/01 00:00:00`.

```r

library(lubridate)

df <- data_frame(a=ymd_h(2018010100, 2018120112), b = 1:2)
write_excel_csv(df, "temp.csv")
devtools::session_info()

devtools::dev_mode()

library(readr)
```

title: type_convert cannot convert characters "t"/"f" to logical type
description:
postgres' copy command (i.e. `COPY ... TO STDOUT WITH ...`) converts boolean columns to the characters "t" and "f" by default. There seems to be no flag to avoid this behaviour in postgres, unless manually casting to text first.

Would it be possible to add an option for `readr::type_convert` to guess columns solely consisting of the values `t` and `f`. Currently those are kept characters:

```
readr::type_convert(dplyr::data_frame(bool = c("t", "f")))

```

title: New `spec_tbl_df` class cannot be written to SQLite database
description:
The recent introduction of the `spec_tbl_df` class seems to create a regression of bug #317 

```r
library("readr")
library("RSQLite")
fwf_sample <- system.file("extdata/fwf-sample.txt", package = "readr")
d1 <- read_fwf(fwf_sample, fwf_widths(c(2, 5, 3)))
db <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
dbWriteTable(conn = db, name = "table", value = d1)
Error in (function (classes, fdef, mtable)  : 
  unable to find an inherited method for function ‘dbWriteTable’ for signature ‘"SQLiteConnection", "character", "spec_tbl_df"’
```

It appears this can be resolved in the same way, e.g. in this case, 

```  
setOldClass(c("spec_tbl_df", "data.frame"))
```

which I guess could be done in `readr` (since the class is defined here) but maybe should be done on the `tibble` end once again instead?  cc @krlmlr ?

title: readr 1.2.1 incompatible with Bioconductor package GEOquery 2.50.0
description:
Apologies in advance if it would be more relevant to raise this issue with Bioconductor but I thought it was worth highlighting the different behavior of packages that rely readr.

I had been working on some scripts that used the GEOquery Bioconductor package to read in microarray data from GEO using GEOquery::getGEO. GEOquery requires readr. Everything was working fine until I installed some new packages (which I suspect upgraded readr). I think this was from version 1.1.1 to 1.2.1. It took a while to work out the issue was with readr. Rolling back from 1.2.1 to 1.1.1 resolved the issue.

Essentially getGEO loads in a large matrix with unique row and column names as well additional metadata. When readr 1.2.1 is installed, column names are not parsed correctly, resulting in duplicate column names and metadata is no longer correctly referenced to the columns. 

**Example of the issue**
I am using 64 bit R version 3.5.1 on Windows 10 Pro. This issue is also present with 64 bit R 3.4.4 on Unbuntu 16.04.5. I am using GEOquery 2.50.0.
The examples below use my Windows version, the only difference is the readr version:

title: read_csv() creates "spec" attributes which don't get updated nor lost by some tibble transformations
description:
`read_csv()` (and probably the other read_delim funtions, though I haven't tested it) creates `"spec"` attributes which do not get updated nor lost when the tibble gets transformed and thus can end up being in total mismatch with the tibble they are associated with.

This does not create any problem, but it makes for very weird outputs to `str()` and creates unnecessarily lengthy outputs to `dput()`.

---

**Example:**

I read a .csv file with `read_csv()` to create a tibble. I change its names, I select one variable out, I replace the remaining variables with vectors of different types and I end up with this tibble:

``` r
tbl <- structure(list(
  A = c("a", "b", "c"),
  B = 1:3),
  row.names = c(NA, -3L),
  spec = structure(list(
    cols = list(
      date = structure(list(format = ""), class = c("collector_date", "collector")),
      species = structure(list(), class = c("collector_character", "collector")),
      abundance = structure(list(), class = c("collector_double", "collector"))),
    default = structure(list(), class = c("collector_guess", "collector"))),
    class = "col_spec"), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))
```
So now, this is my tibble:

```r
tbl
#>   A B
#> 1 a 1
#> 2 b 2
#> 3 c 3
```

And it gives these `str()` and `dput()` outputs:

```r
str(tbl)
#> Classes 'tbl_df', 'tbl' and 'data.frame':    3 obs. of  2 variables:
#>  $ A: chr  "a" "b" "c"
#>  $ B: int  1 2 3
#>  - attr(*, "spec")=List of 2
#>   ..$ cols   :List of 3
#>   .. ..$ date     :List of 1
#>   .. .. ..$ format: chr ""
#>   .. .. ..- attr(*, "class")= chr  "collector_date" "collector"
#>   .. ..$ species  : list()
#>   .. .. ..- attr(*, "class")= chr  "collector_character" "collector"
#>   .. ..$ abundance: list()
#>   .. .. ..- attr(*, "class")= chr  "collector_double" "collector"
#>   ..$ default: list()
#>   .. ..- attr(*, "class")= chr  "collector_guess" "collector"
#>   ..- attr(*, "class")= chr "col_spec"
```
(Now the `"spec"` attribute has a wrong number of variables, wrong variable names, and wrong variable types :rofl: )

```r
dput(tbl)
#> structure(list(A = c("a", "b", "c"), B = 1:3), row.names = c(NA, 
#> -3L), spec = structure(list(cols = list(date = structure(list(
#>     format = ""), class = c("collector_date", "collector")), 
#>     species = structure(list(), class = c("collector_character", 
#>     "collector")), abundance = structure(list(), class = c("collector_double", 
#>     "collector"))), default = structure(list(), class = c("collector_guess", 
#> "collector"))), class = "col_spec"), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", 
#> "data.frame"))
```

(That's a long `dput()` output for such a simple tibble :flushed: )

Of course, using the result of `dput()` to create the object in the first place in this example makes it look very circular and kind of silly, but I have to do that to demonstrate the idea without forcing you to download a .csv file or create one. But this is not just a theoretical point: a real life and very common scenario where this kicks in is this:

You create a tibble with `read_csv()`, you want to create a reprex, so you transform your tibble to make it very simple, then you use `dput()` to create the data of your very basic tibble and you end up with a ton of silly attributes in the output. Of course, you can simply get rid of the `"spec"` attribute from the result of `dput()` and all is good:

```r
structure(list(
  A = c("a", "b", "c"),
  B = 1:3),
  row.names = c(NA, -3L))
```
gives the same tibble and it is easy enough to do. And even if you don't, those wrong attributes don't get in the way of anything. So not a big deal. But because it is somewhat hard to get new users to create good reproducible examples, it is a little quirk that doesn't help with explaining `dput()`.

title: read_lines(fname,skip=xxx) skipping empty lines causes unexpected, backward-incompatible behavior
description:
Let 'file.txt' contain the following 8 lines, with its 4th line empty:

```
L1
L2
L3
<empty line>
Hello,Weird,Behavior
1,2,3
3,4,5
6,7,8
```
Calling read_lines() with no skip parameter produces the expected results, with sk0's 4th element being the empty string:
```
library(tidyverse)
fname <- 'file.txt'
sk0 <- read_lines(fname)
sk0
#> "L1","L2","L3","","Hello,Weird,Behavior","1,2,3","3,4,5,"6,7,8"    
```
Skipping the first 3 lines also works, now with the 1st element being an empty string:
```
sk3 <- read_lines(fname,skip=3)
sk3
#> "","Hello,Weird,Behavior","1,2,3","3,4,5","6,7,8"               
```
However, and here lies the bug, skipping 4 lines misses the 5th line entirely! (in fact skip=4 will miss any sequence of empty lines). 
```
sk4 <- read_lines(fname,skip=4)
sk4
#> "1,2,3","3,4,5","6,7,8"
```
Though skipping empty lines is a documented feature of this version of readr, it seems inconsistent and unnecessary, and will result in backward incompatibilities.

title: write_tsv adds whitespace characters to NA
description:
Hi,

Using readr 1.2.1 I'm getting extra whitespace characters around NA values when I use write_tsv. Here's an example:

[example.txt](https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/files/2636161/example.txt)

```r
library(readr)
a <- read_tsv("example.txt")
write_tsv(a, path = "example2.txt")
```

In this example the `'NA'` values are written as `'\s\s\s\s\s\sNA'`

Let me know if you need any other info.

Thanks,

David

title: Benchmarks vs. data.table in README.md seem to be incorrect
description:
`readr`'s `README.md` claims that `readr` functions are currently "~1.2-2x" slower than `data.table::fread()`. Is this still correct? If not, I think `README.md` should be corrected.

I did some simple benchmarks of `readr::read_csv()` versus `data.table::fread()` as well as `readr::write_csv()` versus `data.table::fwrite()` and found that the `readr` functions are much slower on average than the claimed ~1.2-2x.

For csv files between 26 MB and 1.1 GB, `readr` is about 3.6-4x slower when reading and 3.9-5.1x slower when writing – when data.table is in single thread mode. When data.table uses up to 4 threads, readr is about 7.4-10.3x slower when reading and 8-11.4x slower when writing csv files between 26 MB and 1.1 GB.

```
    threads size_MB write_csv read_csv fwrite fread write_ratio read_ratio
 1:       4      26     0.775    0.489  0.097 0.049         8.0       10.0
 2:       4     106     2.614    1.703  0.264 0.166         9.9       10.3
 3:       4     268     6.417    3.615  0.565 0.423        11.4        8.5
 4:       4     537    12.749    6.985  1.181 0.862        10.8        8.1
 5:       4    1084    26.177   13.501  2.463 1.816        10.6        7.4
 6:       1      26     0.680    0.330  0.175 0.091         3.9        3.6
 7:       1     106     2.705    1.310  0.617 0.337         4.4        3.9
 8:       1     268     7.504    3.262  1.465 0.841         5.1        3.9
 9:       1     537    14.514    6.559  2.964 1.688         4.9        3.9
10:       1    1084    26.358   13.443  5.919 3.376         4.5        4.0
```

Here is my code:

```
library(data.table)
library(readr)

# Make readr silent
options(readr.num_columns = 0)

# Function for making test data
make_data <- function(n){
  data.frame(char = sprintf("%08d", 1:n),
             int = 1L:n,
             double_a = runif(n, -1000000, 1000000),
             double_b = runif(n, -1000000, 1000000),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

# n rows of data to generate
n_rows <- c(500000, 2000000, 5000000, 10000000, 20000000)

# vectors for storing results
size_MB <- c(); fwrite <- c(); write_csv <- c()
fread <- c(); read_csv <- c(); threads <- c()

# Function for benchmarking
benchmark <- function(threads){
  
  # Set threads
  setDTthreads(threads)
  
  # Benchmarking in a loop
  run <- 1
  for (i in n_rows) {
    
    df <- make_data(i)
    
    # Writing benchmarks
    fwrite[run] <- system.time(fwrite(df, "df_dt.csv", showProgress = FALSE))[[3]]
    write_csv[run] <- system.time(write_csv(df, "df_rdr.csv"))[[3]]
    
    # Write file with base R for neutral reading benchmarks
    write.csv(df, "df.csv", row.names = FALSE)
    
    # Calculate file size
    size_MB[run] <- round(file.size("df.csv") / 1e+6)
    
    # Reading benchmarks
    fread[run] <- system.time(df_dt <- fread("df.csv", showProgress = FALSE))[[3]]
    read_csv[run] <- system.time(df_rdr <- read_csv("df.csv", progress = FALSE))[[3]]
    
    threads[run] <- getDTthreads()
    run <- run + 1
  }
  
  # Bind and calculate results
  data.table(threads, size_MB, write_csv, read_csv, fwrite, fread)
}

# Run benchmarking
benchmarks <- rbind(benchmark(0), benchmark(1L))

# Calculate differences between fread and readr
benchmarks[, `:=`(write_ratio = round(write_csv / fwrite, 1),
                  read_ratio = round(read_csv / fread, 1))]
```

And some system info:
```
MacOS 10.14.1
MacBook Pro (Retina, 13-inch, Mid 2014)
2,8 GHz Intel Core i5
16 GB 1600 MHz DDR3
```

title: use_tidy_ci()
use_roxygen_md()
Build system cannot accomodate relative build locations: rpath setting wrong
description:
Debian builds have always relative to a current (possibly) temporary build directory.  The builds then happen in a set of subdirectories relative to the current directory: first `debian/`, then the package name and that location is taken to be `/` below which `/usr` etc are created -- and are at the end bundled up in a tarfile relative to the subdirectory which makes the lower-level directories believe it is actually  `/` and the root.

That works for as long as paths are in fact relative.  If an absolute path is constructed from the current directory, things fail.  That just happened here.   The log from my Debian upload of readr 1.2.1 shows

```
g++ -shared -L/usr/lib/R/lib -Wl,-z,relro -o readr.so Collector.o CollectorGuess.o Iconv.o LocaleInfo.o RcppExports.o Reader.o Source.o Tokenizer.o TokenizerDelim.o TokenizerFwf.o TokenizerWs.o connection.o datetime.o grisu3.o init.o localtime.o parse.o read.o type_convert.o write.o write_connection.o write_delim.o -L. -lrcon -L../inst/rcon -Wl,-rpath,/build/r-cran-readr-1.2.1/debian/r-cran-readr/usr/lib/R/site-library/readr/rcon -L/usr/lib/R/lib -lR
````

The key here is the `/build/r-cran-readr-1.2.1/debian/r-cran-readr/usr/lib/R/site-library/readr/rcon`. We see the build operating in a chroot cleanroom `/build` with the package, its `debian/` and package directory below it ... and then the supposed abolute path.  We get that for free from expanding

```
PKG_LIBS = -L. -lrcon -L../inst/rcon -Wl,-rpath,$(R_PACKAGE_DIR)/rcon
```

I just tried to fix it by overriding the fixed (known) path that would be used for the installed package.  That however failed for loading the package at the end of the build process -- so it is a bit of an issue.  If you could look into a scheme in which normal builds proceed as usual but we get to override this at build or install time I'd appreciate it.  This can't be a new issue for the build systems, but it has been a while since I last had to use `rpath` on a packaged library.

More context in [this Debian bug report](http://bugs.debian.org/914633) which was just filed again my r-cran-readr package for this issue.  I will follow up there with the respective Debian folks.

title: Read into a 'melted' structure
description:
Thank you for this fantastic package.

Would you consider a PR for reading into a 'melted' structure?

``` r
readr::tokenize_melt("1,as\n3.3,2017-01-03,5\n\n6")
#> # A tibble: 6 x 4
#>     row   col      value data_type
#>   <int> <int>      <chr>     <chr>
#> 1     0     0          1   integer
#> 2     0     1         as character
#> 3     1     0        3.3    double
#> 4     1     1 2017-01-03      date
#> 5     1     2          5   integer
#> 6     2     0          6   integer
```

This form is useful when the source is ragged and/or has mixed data types within columns.  Once it has been read into R in this form, it can be traversed and transformed into something tidier.

I realise the readr purpose is 'Read Rectangular Text Data', but since the implementation would be a thin wrapper around existing C++ code, it would seem to belong here.  Otherwise would it be possible to use the readr headers from another package?

title: accept PRs to enhance read_fwf to deal with decimal places and overlaping  columns
description:
as requested, following up on #534 in a new issue

@hadley,
we have been working on PRs to fix the two limitations of read_fwf

Can't deal with decimal places (issue #399). Proposed solution: add a new argument decimal_positions to fwf_positions, modifying the main read_fwf function (pull request #632, implemented in Rcpp, tks to @gutorc92)

Can't deal with overlapping columns (current issue). Proposed solution: parse the import dictionary into a list of dictionaries with no overlapping variables. Then import the data based on each dictionary and cbind the results (pull request #634, implemented in R, tks to @daniellima123). We implemented this as a separate function read_fwf2 (in the same spirit of how read.cvs2 is related to read.cvs), to avoid recursive calls. We could make the changes directly to read_fwf, defining it recursively. What do you think?

Please let us know if these suggestions are acceptable. We have been using them in our forked repos and they seem to work fine.

title: AccumulateChunkCallback
Have read_* functions parse non-traditional logicals
description:
Functions like `read_delim()` and `read_csv()` do not recognize columns with logical data coded as "0/1" or "true/false", but it does recognize "T/F". This behavior is different than `parse_logical()` which accepts all of the examples listed above. Is it possible to have these functions parse similar to `parse_logical()`?

**read_delim() Behavior**
```
lines <- "a,b
A,true
B,true
C,false
"
read_delim(lines, ",")
# A tibble: 3 x 2
  a     b    
  <chr> <chr>
1 A     true 
2 B     true 
3 C     false
```

**Desired Behavior**
```
lines <- "a,b
A,true
B,true
C,false
"
read_delim(lines, ",")
# A tibble: 3 x 2
  a     b    
  <chr> <lgl>
1 A     TRUE 
2 B     TRUE 
3 C     FALSE
```

**parse_logical() Behavior**
```
readr::parse_logical(c("T", "F", "true", "false", 0, 1))
[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE
```

Since #497 `parse_factor()` has the option to automatically figure out levels by setting `levels = NULL`. Shouldn't this be the default, so that, for example, a call to `col_factor()` without arguments would make use of this feature?

I came across this because I was intuitively expecting `col_factor()` to do this already. Seems it wouldn't break any existing code since currently `col_factor()` alone throws an error.

title: parse_factor() is the only parser that lacks a single character shortcode
description: Now that `parse_factor()` can operate without explicit levels (#497), it seems like it should have a single letter shortcode. It is the only parser that does not.

title: Support reading single line literal datasets
description:
If a literal dataset has only 1 line, it will be treated as a path to a file (rather than literal data), which causes an error to be thrown. This affects text data types with no header row.

My use case is that I have a lot of fixed width datasets extracted from a PDF document using `pdftools::pdf_text()`. Some of these datasets have only 1 row.

## Reproducible examples

Fixed width format example.

```r
library(readr)
library(purrr)
all_dataset_lines <- list(
  dataset_lines1 = c("1a", "2b"),
  dataset_lines2 = c("3c")
)
column_widths <- fwf_positions(start = c(1, 2), end = c(1, 2))
map(all_dataset_lines, read_fwf, column_widths)
## Error: '3c' does not exist in current working directory ('/path/to/wd').
```

This would also affect SQL Server-style CSV files that don't include a header row.

```r
all_dataset_lines <- list(
  dataset_lines1 = c("1,a", "2,b"),
  dataset_lines2 = c("3,c")
)
map(all_dataset_lines, read_csv, col_names = FALSE)
## Error: '3,c' does not exist in current working directory ('/path/to/wd')
```

## Ideas for a fix

If you could specify that the input is literal data, then `datasource()` could handle it accordingly.

For example, we could define

```r
as.literal_data <- function(x) {
  class(x) <- "literal_data"
  x
}
```

then in `datasource()`, you could have a logical block like

```r
if(inherits(file, "literal_data")) {
  datasource_string(paste(file, collapse = "\n"), skip, comment)
}
```

Then the datasets could be parsed using 

```r
library(purrr)
map(all_dataset_lines, compose(read_fwf, as.literal_data), column_widths)
```

or 

```r
map(all_dataset_lines, compose(read_csv, as.literal_data))
```

description:
cc @jimhester if you would like me to refactor the roxygen for this, please let me know and I'd be more than willing to help.

It would be extremely help if readr stated somewhere in the documentation that the read_csv and read_delim use UTF-8 as the default encoding, unless otherwise specified with the locale argument. And, if you are unsure about your file encoding:


```
#for mac os x
file -I <my_file>
#linux
file -i <my_file>
```
even use https://linux.die.net/man/1/enconv or https://www.gnu.org/savannah-checkouts/gnu/libiconv/documentation/libiconv-1.15/iconv.1.html
to go about fixing prior to uploading in R

```
library(readr)
read_tsv(
```

The column type for `ID` is `<dbl>`, but it should be `<int>`.

title: "read_table()" cannot read long strings?
description:
I have been using readr package for fast import for some time but after writing some analytic codes of my data, some unpredicted errors occur, and after debugging I found it is due to the incapability of read_table() to read long strings:

For my input file, I have long character strings in each line (and I need to separate them using functions such as str_split() ). Here is an example line: "gene_id_1 ABC-5%, DEFIOIAFDJO-18%, OISHDFU-77%". However, after processing all my genetic information, there were 28 errors, and I found that all these lines concluded long strings. In one of these imported lines, the import was not complete, and the line was truncated to something like "gene_id_1 ABC-5%, DEFIOIAFDJO-18%," which ended abruptly. 

This is my original code:
```{r}
  data[[species]] <- read_table(file = data.txt.names[index],
                                col_names = FALSE)
```

And the parsing did not yield any errors:
`Parsed with column specification:
cols(
  X1 = col_character()
)`


However, since my strings were not completely imported, I tried to switch back to the base R function "read.delim()"
```{r}
  data[[species]] <- read.delim(file = data.txt.names[index],
                                header = FALSE,
                                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)`
```

This import is successful and the full line could be imported. nchar() shows there are 199 characters in one of these aforementioned lines. Hence, in view of this, are there some type of upper limit of the number of characters in each line that readr could import? 

Thanks,
Jason.

title: read_csv: skip ignores quote
description:
One would expect that the quote parameter is respected even when skipping lines, but the current implementation doesn't work this way.
Instead, read_csv cuts half way through reading a cell when `skip` is specified, even though `quote = "\""` is set by default.

```R
# works
readr::read_csv(paste0("Col A, Col B\n",
                       "\"entry a\n\n\na\",\"entry b\nb\"\n",
                       "some 1,some 2\n"),
                col_names = FALSE)

# skips half way through "entry a a", results in 2 instead of 1 row
readr::read_csv(paste0("Col A, Col B\n",
                       "\"entry a\n\n\na\",\"entry b\nb\"\n",
                       "some 1,some 2\n"),
                col_names = FALSE,
                skip = 2)


# results in expected behavior (without \n's): 1 row with "some 1, some 2"
readr::read_csv(paste0("Col A, Col B\n",
                       "\"entry a a\",\"entry b b\"\n",
                       "some 1,some 2\n"),
                col_names = FALSE,
                skip = 2)
```

```
# A tibble: 3 x 2
                X1           X2
             <chr>        <chr>
1            Col A        Col B
2 "entry a\n\n\na" "entry b\nb"
3           some 1       some 2

# A tibble: 2 x 2
      X1           X2
   <chr>        <chr>
1  "a\"" "entry b\nb"
2 some 1       some 2


# A tibble: 1 x 2
      X1     X2
   <chr>  <chr>
1 some 1 some 2
```

title: parse_factor implicitly relevels empty string "" and actual NA to factor "NA"
description:
`readr_1.1.1` and `tidyverse_1.2.1`

I want to convert a string column to factors, taking `"NA"` as an actual factor level (say `"NA"` means "North America"), and also taking `""` as an actual factor level. However, both `""` and `<NA>` are mapped to `"NA"` by `parse_factor`, while `NC` is mapped to `<NA>`.

``` r
library(tidyverse)

df <- tibble(
  id = 1:5,
  group = c('NA', 'NB', 'NC', '', NA)
)

df %>%
  mutate(f = parse_factor(group,
                          levels = c('', 'NA', 'NB'),
                          na = character()))
#> Warning: 1 parsing failure.
#> row # A tibble: 1 x 4 col     row   col expected           actual expected   <int> <int> <chr>              <chr>  actual 1     3    NA value in level set NC
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>      id group f    
#>   <int> <chr> <fct>
#> 1     1 NA    NA   
#> 2     2 NB    NB   
#> 3     3 NC    <NA> 
#> 4     4 ""    NA   
#> 5     5 <NA>  NA
```

But I expected

``` r
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>      id group f    
#>   <int> <chr> <fct>
#> 1     1 NA    NA   
#> 2     2 NB    NB   
#> 3     3 NC    <NA> 
#> 4     4 ""    ""
#> 5     5 <NA>  <NA>
```

title: add n_max parameter into read_csv_chunked function
description:
Working with huge files I want to process them in chunks. Sometimes files have header rows to be ignored and footer rows to be ignored. There is an option in `read_csv` function to specify `skip` and `n_max` however there is no `n_max` in chunked functions. 

So I can't process huge file with standard `read_csv_chunked` function if I need to ignore footer lines.

title: Tabs are not trimmed when trim_ws = TRUE
description:
When using `read_csv` to read a CSV file that contains tabs on its rows, the `trim_ws` argument does not seem to have any effect. The tab characters do not get stripped anyway.
Take this CSV file for example
```
X,Y
x1,y1
x2	,y2
x3,y3	
x4,y4
```
There is a tab after `x2` and after `y3` (not visible). And the code below demonstrates the issue
```
> data <- read_csv("test.csv", trim_ws = TRUE, col_types = "cc")
> data[, 1]
# A tibble: 4 x 1
       X
   <chr>
1     x1
2 "x2\t"
3     x3
4     x4
> data[, 2]
# A tibble: 4 x 1
       Y
   <chr>
1     y1
2     y2
3 "y3\t"
4     y4
```
As you can see the tab characters are there and not trimmed.
I'm running the code using R 3.3.3 and readr 1.1.1. on macOS High Sierra.

title: parse_datetime() does not return real seconds
description:
Trying to read in a csv with `read_csv()`, I realized my datetimes were only read to the full second, when they have microsecond accuracy--the format is as in "2018-07-04 10:33:15.064859".

Trying to understand why this is happening, I realized that `parse_datetime()` does exactly the same thing--it gives back the datetime to the full seconds, even though %OS is specified in the format for real seconds.

```
parse_datetime("2018-07-04 10:33:15.064859", format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%OS")
[1] "2018-07-04 10:33:15 UTC"
```

`parse_time()` does work as @jimhester describes in his last comment in #379, but `parse_datetime()` does not work as expected.

title: Feature request: Silence warning about no newline at end of input
description:
As mentioned in #842, read_table gives a warning if the input does not end in a newline.
I think input not ending in newline should be accepted for consistency with `read.table`.

```r
read.table(textConnection("a b\nccc d"), header = TRUE)
#>     a b
#> 1 ccc d

readr::read_table2("a b\nccc d")
#> Warning: 1 parsing failure.
#> row col expected        actual         file
#>   1   b          embedded null literal data
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   a     b    
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 ccc   d

readr::read_table2("a b\nccc d\n")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   a     b    
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 ccc   d
```

A string-column containing double quotations is printed out to file with an extra set of quotes around the entire string when using `write_tsv` (I can't tell if this is because of `tibble` or `write_tsv`)

    df <- data.frame(A = paste("val is", dQuote("ok")))
    out1 <- "readr_out.tsv"
    out2 <- "baser_out.tsv" 
    write_tsv(df, out1, col_names=FALSE)
    # "val is ""ok"""

title: fwf_positions() should enforce col_names to be a character
description:
If the `col_names` argument to `fwf_positions()` is a factor, then the return value of that function has a column named `col_names` that is also a factor, which causes `read_fwf()` to throw the error

```
Error: `col_names` must be TRUE, FALSE or a character vector
``` 

### Reproducible example

```r
# 1. Create a tibble with col_names as a factor
library(readr)
start_posns <- c(1, 2, 4, 8)
end_posns <- c(1, 3, 7, 15)
col_names <- factor(letters[1:4])
fwf_col_info <- fwf_positions(start_posns, end_posns, col_names)

glimpse(fwf_col_info)
## Observations: 4
## Variables: 3
## $ begin     <dbl> 0, 1, 3, 7
## $ end       <dbl> 1, 3, 7, 15
## $ col_names <fct> a, b, c, d

# 2. Write some data to file
tfile <- tempfile()
writeLines(
  c("1AA1111aaaaaaaa", "2BB2222bbbbbbbb", "3CC3333cccccccc", "4DD4444dddddddd"),
  tfile
)

# 3. Try to import it
read_fwf(tfile, fwf_col_info)
## Error: `col_names` must be TRUE, FALSE or a character vector
```

## Thoughts on fixes

Either `fwf_positions()` should convert factor `col_names` to character, or `read_fwf()` should allow factors and do the conversion itself, or both.

title: `read_csv()` cannot handle file paths with characters outside of the default locale (Windows)
description:
(Originally reported here: https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/834#issuecomment-415298952)

On Windows, it seems `read_csv()` cannot handle the file path that contains character outside of the default locale.

For example, in my locale, CP932 (Shift_JIS), `长` is not representable.

``` r
readr::read_csv("萼片长.csv")
#> Error in guess_header_(datasource, tokenizer, locale) : 
#>   Cannot read file C:/Users/hiroaki-yutani/Documents/repo/R/ggplot2/萼片<U+957F>.csv: (...snip...)
```

For another example, in CP1252 (latin1), all of `萼` and `片` and `长` are not representable:

```r
# change locale to latin1
rlang::mut_latin1_locale()

readr::read_csv("萼片长.csv")
#> Error in guess_header_(datasource, tokenizer, locale) : 
#>   Cannot read file C:/Users/hiroaki-yutani/Documents/repo/R/ggplot2/<U+843C><U+7247><U+957F>.csv: (...snip...)
```

In the defense of readr, base R also fails to handle them. For example, `saveRDS()`.

``` r
saveRDS(iris, file = "萼片长.rds")
#> Error in gzfile(file, mode) : cannot open the connection
#> In addition: Warning message:
#> In gzfile(file, mode) :
#>   cannot open compressed file '<U+843C><U+7247><U+957F>.rds', probable reason 'Invalid argument'
```

But, I have no idea how boost can handle this, since they requires the file path in the native locale...

title: Have read_csv and friends understand international characters
description:
Modern R handles UTF-8 characters well, including the Norwegian `æøå`. However, `read_csv` returns a `tibble` which displays these characters as unicode escape codes. This is ugly, e.g. when knitting international rmarkdown documents.

read.table handles international input without problems, and the result can be converted to a tibble without the ugly escaping. I wish `read_csv` and other readr functions would behave similarly.

Small reproducible example:

```r
readr::read_csv(file="x\næøå")
## # A tibble: 1 x 1
##   x             
##   <chr>         
## 1 "\xe6\xf8\xe5"

tibble::as_tibble(read.table(textConnection("x\næøå"), header=TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
## # A tibble: 1 x 1
##   x    
##   <chr>
## 1 æøå
```

title: write_csv treatment of "small" numerical values
description:
This is similar to #671 but I don't think it's the same. The issue is using scientific notation when there's no reason to do so. Specifically, if a "small" integer in the data is formatted as numeric, then write_csv uses scientific notation even when not necessary.

`write_csv(data.frame(a=c(2999, 3000, 3001)), 'test.csv')` 
produces
```
a
2999
3e3
3001
```
If the first occurrence of scientific notation is past row 1000, then read_csv can't read what write_csv just wrote.

On the other hand,
`write.csv(data.frame(a=c(2999, 3000, 3001)), 'test.csv', row.names=FALSE)`
produces
```
"a"
2999
3000
3001
```
This seems more reasonable.

Simple example:

```
library(readr)

2  5678
3     1
```

title: length of NULL cannot be changed errors on installing R 3.5.0
description:
Hi,

I'm in the early stages of trying to track this down - asking in case it is 'known' or anyone has any ideas before I spend too long on hunting it down. 

I installed R 3.5.0 today and reinstalled packages along with it. I'm using readr 1.2.0, tibble 1.4.2.9001, rlang 0.2.0.9001.

My code sits in a package for loading my dataset. The code is 'known working' on my 3.4.4 machine and has been for some time so it looks like a regression which has occurred somewhere.

I've narrowed it down to calling read_csv which is generating the warnings (>50 warnings).

I'm using defined import columns. Because the column list is large,  I'm managing it by splitting it into two definitions (columnTypes and followupColumnTypes), and then calling read_csv:

```
  columnTypes <- readr::cols(
    ProClinV1Id = readr::col_integer(),
    PatientId = readr::col_integer(),
    TeamCode = readr::col_character())

  followupColumnTypes <- readr::cols(
    LockedS8 = readr::col_skip(),
    LockedS8DateTime = readr::col_skip(),
    LockedS8UserName = readr::col_skip(),
    S8Status = readr::col_skip(),
    S8FollowUp = readr::col_factor(c('Y', 'N', 'NB', 'ND', NA)),
    S8FollowUpType = readr::col_factor(c('IP', 'T', 'O', 'P', NA)))

  importColumns <- columnTypes
  importColumns$cols <- c(columnTypes$cols,
                          followupColumnTypes$cols)

  importedData <- readr::read_csv(filename,
                                    col_names = TRUE,
                                    col_types = importColumns)

```

I'm getting >50 warnings of:

```
In read_tokens_(data, tokenizer, col_specs, col_names,  ... :
  length of NULL cannot be changed
```

Haven't yet managed to distill the example down further into a reprex - if it doesn't ring any bells with anyone I'll try to do that.

The imported data itself seems fine so whatever is going on isn't affecting the output (but is screwing up my debug as I can't see the wood for the trees! I can workaround by disabling warnings on input - but that is ignoring the issue really!)

The only major R thing I can think of is the byte-compiling by default causing a problem somewhere.

title: Option to ignore unparsable lines?
description:
I first posted this in webtools' queue (https://github.com/Ironholds/webtools/issues/1) and we came to the conclusion that this is actually a readr feature request.

The problem occurs when you have a field in double quotes, that contains an unescaped/unencoded double quote inside it. read_delim unsurprisingly gets confused when the delimiter character does not occur directly after the second double quote.

Here's an example of what I ran into using only read_delim:

``` r

library("readr")

lines <- c(
  '10.44.74.181 - - [20/Mar/2015:21:20:23 +0000] "GET http://www.example.com/fonts/webfont.eot?)%20format("eot") HTTP/1.1" 200 234'
)

temp_path <- tempfile()
conn <-file(temp_path)
writeLines(lines, conn)
close(conn)
temp_path

names <- c("ip_address", "remote_user_ident", "local_user_ident", "timestamp",
           "timestamp_junk","request", "status_code","bytes_sent")
data <- read_delim(temp_path, delim = " ", col_names = names)

```

This results in:

`Error: At [1, 6] expecting delimiter or quote but found 'e'`

Similar to https://github.com/hadley/readr/issues/94, I think it'd be good to have an option to warn/drop these rows that are unparsable.

title: Allow human readable date formats like "dddd d mmmm yyyy"?
description:
Would it be an idea to allow human readable date and time formats?

I would assume almost anybody could understand that `dddd d mmmm yyyy` would result in `Monday 1 January 2018`, but I can't make a lot of the equivalent `%A %e %B %Y`, it has an almost flat learning curve.

I wrote a function myself, but I think others could benefit from it as well. An idea for `readr`? Or do you know a better place?

```r
date_generic <- function(format) {
  if (!grepl('%', format, fixed = TRUE)) {

    # first months and minutes, after that everything is case INsensitive
    format <- gsub('mmmm', '%B1', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- gsub('mmm', '%b', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- gsub('mm', '%m', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- gsub('MM', '%M1', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- format %>%
      tolower() %>%
      gsub('%b1', '%B', ., fixed = TRUE) %>%
      gsub('%m1', '%M', ., fixed = TRUE)

    # dates
    format <- gsub('dddd', '%A', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- gsub('ddd', '%a', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- gsub('dd', '%!', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- gsub('d', '%e', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- gsub('%!', '%d', format, fixed = TRUE)

    format <- gsub('ww', '%V', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- gsub('w', '%V', format, fixed = TRUE)

    format <- gsub('yyyy_iso', '%G', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- gsub('yyyy', '%Y', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- gsub('yy_iso', '%g', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- gsub('yy', '%y', format, fixed = TRUE)

    # time
    format <- gsub('hh', '%H', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- gsub('h', '%k', format, fixed = TRUE)
    format <- gsub('ss', '%S', format, fixed = TRUE)

    # seconds since the Epoch, 1970-01-01 00:00:00
    format <- gsub('unix', '%s', format, fixed = TRUE)
    # Equivalent to %Y-%m-%d (the ISO 8601 date format)
    format <- gsub('iso', '%F', format, fixed = TRUE)

  }
  format
}

format(as.Date('2018-01-01'), date_generic("mmm/yyyy"))
# "Jan/2018"

# For weeks:
format(as.Date('2018-01-01'), date_generic("yyyy-ww"))
# "2018-01"
```

title: read_*() mangles file paths by converting them to UTF-8 and fails to read the resulting paths
description:
On Windows, the `read_*()` functions, e.g. `read_csv()`, converts the `file` argument to an UTF-8 byte sequence before trying the read the file. If the path contains non-ASCII characters, the resulting path no longer corresponds to an existing file, so reading the file fails.

Note that the `write_*()` functions do not have this bug, and successfully writes file and folder names containing non-ASCII charcters. Here’s a reprex for both writing and reading a file:

 ```r
library(readr)
fname = "h:/tmp/r/test-æøå.csv" # Replace h:/tmp/r/ with an existing folder

# Saving a file works fine
file.exists(fname)
#> [1] FALSE
write_csv(iris, fname)

# But reading the resulting file doesn’t
file.exists(fname)
#> [1] TRUE
> read_csv(fname)
#> Error in guess_header_(datasource, tokenizer, locale) : 
#>  Cannot read file h:/tmp/r/test-Ã¦Ã¸Ã¥.csv: Systemet finner ikke angitt fil.
```

Note that the file name `test-æøå.csv` has been converted to `test-Ã¦Ã¸Ã¥.csv`. This latter is an UTF-8 byte sequence interepreted as being in the native encoding (Windows-1252).

(The error message ‘Systemet finner ikke angitt fil.’ means ‘The system cannot find the file specified.’ and comes from Windows (since it’s translated).)

title: read_fwf does not interpret fwf widths correctly on utf8 encoded input with special characters
description:
Under certain circumstances the widths of fwf columns are not interpreted correctly when `file` is a character vector, rather than a file path. 

This bug was a bit hard pinpoint. I did not seem to occur on utf8 encoded input (e.g. when I construct the text string directly in the R-script). I tried this with the latest readr version from cran as well as github (1.1.1 and 1.2.0)

[test.txt](https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/files/2003627/test.txt)

``` r
col_positions <- readr::fwf_widths(
  c(5, 30, 4, 7, 6, 1, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 14, 12, 6, 4)
)

col_types <- "icicccddiiccccc"



# This works:

r1 <- readr::read_fwf(
  "test.txt",
  locale = readr::locale(encoding = "latin1"),
  col_types = col_types,
  col_positions = col_positions
)

as.data.frame(r1)
#>     X1           X2  X3     X4   X5   X6   X7 X8 X9 X10   X11         X12

#>       X13   X14 X15
#> 1 xxxxxxx xxxxx  11
#> 2    <NA> xxxxx  11
#> 3    <NA> xxxxx  11


# This doesn't:

x <- readr::read_lines(
```

title: read_csv column type guess for 1000 rows of "NA" is logical - should be character?
description:
If `col_types = NULL`, and a column has the first 1000 rows with a value of NA, `read_csv` specifies the column as logical. 

(As an aside, this seems to have changed in the last several months, as I discovered this with old code that used to yield these columns as character type).

This seems like a behavior that is prone to errors.  If we only know that the first 1000 are NA, there is no reason to assume what comes later will be logical. The most robust handling of this situation would be to treat it as character so that there is no risk of parsing failures that coerce values to fit some other class.

Here's a test file - basically just CSV with 1200 rows of "NA" then a row with "TEST"
[natest.csv.zip](https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/files/1968787/natest.csv.zip)

``` r



require(readr)
#> Loading required package: readr
read_csv("~/temp/natest.csv")
#> Parsed with column specification:
#> cols(
#>   numbers = col_double(),
#>   testcol = col_logical()
#> )

#>  row     col           expected actual                file
```

title: Possible memory leak when user interrupts a read
description:
I'm a little beyond my depth, so I apologize if I'm just misinterpreting the output from the `top` command, but I think that if a user interrupts while a large file is being read, there is a memory leak. 

```r
# Steps to reproduce:
# 1) Run code to write large text file
# 2) Restart R session
# 3) Run read_lines command below, but interrupt during the progress bar
# 4) Even though R seems to think there's nothing loaded, when I look at 
#     system resources using Windows Task Manager or Linux `top` command
#     it appears that R has a higher memory usage until I restart the R 
#    session again (`gc()` does not fix). If I do this a second time, I can use even 
#    more memory.
# 5) If I don't interrupt the read, and then remove the object and gc(), top
#     doesn't show this memory usage.

library(readr)
library(magrittr)

# Make file big enough that progress bar shows up
n_lines <- 50000000

sample(0:9, 70, replace = TRUE) %>%
  paste0(collapse = "") %>%
  rep(n_lines) %>%
  write_lines("test_file.dat")


# Restart R session here (and then interupt while progress bar is showing)
test <- readr::read_lines("test_file.dat")
ls()
gc()
# Still have high memory usage


# Works as expected if I don't interrupt (restart session again)
test <- readr::read_lines("test_file.dat")
rm(test)
gc()
# Memory usage appears to have gone down
```

title: Consider using read_private instead of read_only for SourceFile
description:
I don't have much background with R but I noticed this while trying to get some R code running in our sandbox which (for better or worse) uses a FUSE filesystem.

`read_delim()` was failing with `ENODEV`, which I tracked down to `SourceFile` attempting to mmap the file with `MAP_SHARED`. I'm fairly sure this would fail on a network filesystem too, as well as FUSE?

Is there any reason this needs to be a shared mapping? Could you use `MAP_PRIVATE` (via `boost::interprocess::read_private`) instead?

e.g.
https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/compare/master...groklearning:mmap-private?expand=1

Thanks

title: Read bz2 anx xz compressed URLs
description:
Currently only remote gz files are supported (added in https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/commit/22d60358ad22379f81de06a7b5af400fc6de0270 / https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/163).

From a user standpoint, it'd be nice to also be able to read xz and bz2 compressed files from URLs. Pandas (python) now supports reading tables from compressed URLs. Not sure if R base is equally capable?

title: Read from clipboard
description:
I was wondering if reading from a clipboard will be supported in the future? There was an [earlier issue](https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/112) which provided a work-around, but it doesn't seem to work anymore.

```
> x <- readr::read_csv(file("clipboard"))
Error in read_connection_(con) : can only read from a binary connection
> x <- readr::read_csv(file("clipboard", open = 'rb'))
Error in file("clipboard", open = "rb") : 
  'mode' for the clipboard must be 'r' or 'w'
```

read_csv can only read from a binary connection while the connection itself only allows for non-binary connections.

Using the base functions, this is quite straightforward.

```
> x <- read.csv("clipboard", sep = '\t')
> x
  a b c
1 1 2 3
2 4 5 6
```

title: [Feature] Standardize column names
description:
Very often, column names are not standardized. Some of them include blank spaces (eg "height of father"), some include accents (eg "Départements", "Région" in French datasets), etc. Those column names are not easy to manipulate in R and have to be standardized. 

I've developped  `set_standard_names()`, a function which I find very useful to remove all non ascii characters and blank spaces in column names.

The code behind the function is [here](https://github.com/pachevalier/tricky/blob/master/R/tibbles.R#L89) and it relies on  [`str_standardize`](https://github.com/pachevalier/tricky/blob/master/R/strings.R#L17). The documentation is [here](http://pachevalier.github.io/tricky/reference/set_standard_names.html).

For now, the function is in my personal package and therefore hardly discoverable. Do you think it would be relevant to include those functions in the `readr` package or in any other package of the `tidyverse` ?

title: `cols()` does not accept a named list
description:
Specifying column types with a named list inside `cols()` and `cols_only()` only works when the list is explicitly defined within `cols()` and `cols_only()`. Passing a named list created separately (e.g. loaded from a separate CSV of metadata) raises an error about collector objects.

``` r
mtcars_csv <- system.file("extdata", "mtcars.csv", package="readr")

# The named list of column types can be moved into a separate list, both with
# column objects or abbreviations:
col_types_list <- cols_only(
  mpg = col_double(),
  cyl = col_integer(),
  disp = col_double(),
  hp = col_integer()
)

col_types_list_abbr <- cols_only(
  mpg = "d",
  cyl = "i",
  disp = "d",
  hp = "i"
)

# And then it can be used in read_csv:
df1 <- read_csv(mtcars_csv, col_types=col_types_list)
df2 <- read_csv(mtcars_csv, col_types=col_types_list_abbr)

# However, passing a named list object to cols() or cols_only() will not work,
# raising an error about collector objects:
col_list <- list(mpg = col_double(),
                 cyl = col_integer(),
                 disp = col_double(),
                 hp = col_integer())

col_list_abbr <- list(mpg = "d",
                      cyl = "i",
                      disp = "d",
                      hp = "i")

df3 <- read_csv(mtcars_csv, col_types=cols_only(col_list))
#> Error: Some `col_types` are not S3 collector objects: 1
df4 <- read_csv(mtcars_csv, col_types=cols_only(col_list_abbr))
#> Error: Some `col_types` are not S3 collector objects: 1
```

title: Default col_double is overridden with col_integer
description:
When default column type is explicitly set to `col_double`, `read_tsv` overrides it with `col_integer` if it determines that first 1000 values are integers. (Note: write_tsv saves 1000 as '1e3', which triggers an error when column type is set to `col_integer`.)

    dsOut <- data_frame(A = c(rep.int(1, 1000), 1000))
    write_tsv(dsOut, "a.txt")
    dsIn <- read_tsv("a.txt", col_types=c(.default = col_double()))

That results in a warning ("number of columns of result is not a multiple of vector length") and the column type is integer.

    spec(dsIn)
    # cols(
    #   A = col_integer()
    # )

If there is a double ('1e3' in this case) within the first 1000 values, everything works properly without warnings and the column is double.

    dsOut <- data_frame(A = c(rep.int(1, 999), 1000, 1000))
    write_tsv(dsOut, "b.txt")
    dsIn <- read_tsv("b.txt", col_types=c(.default = col_double()))
    spec(dsIn)
    # cols(
    #   A = col_double()
    # )

title: Feature request: more powerful `col_*()` functions
description:
This might be beyond the scope of readr, but is it being considered to introduce more powerful column specification?

Things I have in mind include:

- per column `na` parameter: we might want, for example to have `0` be a `NA` for one but not for other columns
  ```r
  col_spec(
    colA = col_integer(na = c("", "NA", "0")),
    colB = col_double()
  )
  ```
- guarantees: e.g. that a column contains no `NA` or no negative values
  ```r
  col_spec(
    colA = col_character(allow_na = FALSE),
    colB = col_integer(gte(0L))
  )
  ```
  the column parser would then thrown an error if any assertion fails.
- renaming a column: i.e.
  ```r
  col_spec(
    OrigColA = col_character(name = "new_col_a"),
    OrigColB = col_integer(name = "new_col_b")
  )
  ```

Of course all of this can be achieved after reading in the data with readr (or by reading everything as `.default = col_character()` and then using `parse_*()`), but then again, readr is all about simple and robust data import, so I feel like this could be useful to some.

title: Setting record delimiters
description:

``` R
  col_names=c("tax_id", "X2", "name_txt", "X4", "unique_name", "X6", "name_class", "X8"),
  col_type="iccccccc",
  quote=""
)[, c(1,3,5,7)]
```

title: guess_max = Inf
description:
Almost always when I read text files I want it to use all the rows to infer types. However, setting guess_max to Inf, NA, or -1 causes errors:

```
> orpha_genes = read_csv(orpha_genes_disk_file, guess_max = Inf)
Error in .Call("readr_guess_types_", PACKAGE = "readr", sourceSpec, tokenizerSpec,  : 
  negative length vectors are not allowed
In addition: Warning message:
In guess_types_(datasource, tokenizer, locale, n = n) :
  NAs introduced by coercion to integer range
> orpha_genes = read_csv(orpha_genes_disk_file, guess_max = NA)
Error in .Call("readr_guess_types_", PACKAGE = "readr", sourceSpec, tokenizerSpec,  : 
  negative length vectors are not allowed
> orpha_genes = read_csv(orpha_genes_disk_file, guess_max = -1)
Error in .Call("readr_guess_types_", PACKAGE = "readr", sourceSpec, tokenizerSpec,  : 
  negative length vectors are not allowed
> orpha_genes = read_csv(orpha_genes_disk_file, guess_max = NULL)
Error in guess_types_(datasource, tokenizer, locale, n = n) : 
  expecting a single value
```

Note that the error for NA is incorrect. NA is not a negative vector.

Instead I do something like this:

`orpha_genes = read_csv(orpha_genes_disk_file, guess_max = 999999)`

One has to be careful about how many 9's one adds, because if one adds too many one gets:

```
> read_csv("data/affy_diseases.csv", guess_max = 999999999999999999999999999)
Error in .Call("readr_guess_types_", PACKAGE = "readr", sourceSpec, tokenizerSpec,  : 
  negative length vectors are not allowed
In addition: Warning message:
In guess_types_(datasource, tokenizer, locale, n = n) :
  NAs introduced by coercion to integer range
```

I tried reducing the number of 9's until I stopped getting that error. At some point, my entire system crashed instead! Unfortunately, I don't know how many 9's I tried, so now I'm weary about trying again. I tried this one both my virtual Ubuntu 16.10 machine and on my Windows 8.1 host. Both systems crashed.

In general, this parameter seems to be bug-prone.

title: Consider promotion of integer -> double tokenizers
description:
For certain numeric columns, it's possible that the first entries are representable as integer, with only the later entries being representable as double. In such a case, calls to `read_csv()` can fail as the inferred integer tokenizer will fail to tokenize those later entries.

Would it be possible for `readr` to instead just promote the tokenizer from integer to double on the fly in such a case?

title: Updating the multiple columns' spec via assignment
description:
I was wondering if there was a way to mass edit column specs programmatically.  Hopefully the below provides a sufficient example.  I acknowledge I am likely doing it wrong.  Also, maybe this use case isn't supported, which is fine, but it seemed like a weird result when I came across it, so I thought I'd post.  

``` r

library(tidyverse)

example <- tribble(
  ~x, ~y, ~x_DT, ~pay_DT, 
  1, "a", "20170101", "20170201", 
  2, "z", "20170101", "20170201"
)

readr::write_csv(example, ("example.csv"))
test_spec <- readr::spec(readr::read_csv("example.csv"))
#> Parsed with column specification:
#> cols(
#>   x = col_double(),
#>   y = col_character(),
#>   x_DT = col_integer(),
#>   pay_DT = col_integer()
#> )

# That looks good, but those last two DT columns are %Y%m%d dates.
# I want to edit the spec so that all columns ending in DT are made into date format 
selected <- names(test_spec$cols) %>% regmatches(regexpr(".*_DT$", .))
selected
#> [1] "x_DT"   "pay_DT"

# Here I try to assign the column format, and come close, but get a weird spec back.
test_spec$cols[selected] <- col_date(format = "%Y%m%d")
test_spec
#> cols(
#>   x = col_double(),
#>   y = col_character(),
#>   x_DT = character(%Y%m%d = "%Y%m%d"),
#>   pay_DT = character(%Y%m%d = "%Y%m%d")
#> )

# single signment to cols works though.
test_spec$cols$x_DT <- col_date(format = "%Y%m%d")
test_spec
#> cols(
#>   x = col_double(),
#>   y = col_character(),
#>   x_DT = col_date(format = "%Y%m%d"),
#>   pay_DT = character(%Y%m%d = "%Y%m%d")
#> )

# double square brackets don't work either
test_spec$cols[[selected]] <- col_date(format = "%Y%m%d")
test_spec
#> Error in vapply(cols[[i]], deparse, character(1)): values must be length 1,
#>  but FUN(X[[2]]) result is length 2
```

title: col_guess doesn't handle zero-inflated data well
description:
I work with several large data sets with data on species abundances (with one column for each species), that frequently have large numbers of zeros. This means that `read_csv` will frequently parse the column as an integer, as the bulk of the rows at the start of the entry are zero, even when the non-zero entries are doubles. These data sets often have too many columns for it to be efficient to specify the type of each one when coding, and can have enough data in them that increasing guess_max can slow things down.

Would it be possible to give parse_guess an option to be more conservative? For instance, specifying that it treats all numeric values as double, or all strings as character (to avoid automatically parsing things into dates)?

title: Leading whitespace causes header row duplication

title: `parse_factor` trims x automatically but not levels
description:
`parse_factor(x, levels)` trims `x` automatically but not `levels`.
It is inconsistent with the `factor` function.
I don't know if this behavior should be fixed or documented but it can be confusing.

```r
library(readr)

factor(c("a", "a "), levels = c("a")) %>% as.integer() # 1 NA
parse_factor(c("a", "a "), levels = c("a")) %>% as.integer() # 1 1

factor(c("a", "a "), levels = c("a ")) %>% as.integer() # NA 1
parse_factor(c("a", "a "), levels = c("a ")) %>% as.integer() # NA NA

factor(c("a", "a "), levels = c("a", "a ")) %>% as.integer() # 1 2
parse_factor(c("a", "a "), levels = c("a", "a ")) %>% as.integer() # 1 1

factor(c("a", "a "), levels = c("a ", "a")) %>% as.integer() # 2 1
parse_factor(c("a", "a "), levels = c("a ", "a")) %>% as.integer() # 2 2
```

title: "Special" characters encoding issues with write_* and read_*
description:
EDIT: Skip to [my third post](https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/697#issuecomment-335440296), everything else are bugs in `base`. 

There is something wrong in the way `readr`'s `write_*` and `read_*` functions deal with "special" characters (on Windows).

```r
x <- c("€", "–", "¼", "⅛", "℅", "‰", "ö")
Encoding(x)

# "latin1" "latin1" "latin1" "UTF-8"  "UTF-8"  "latin1" "latin1"

df <- data.frame(x, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

print(x)
# "€" "–" "¼" "⅛" "℅" "‰" "ö"

print(df)
#          x
# 1        €
# 2        –
# 3        ¼
# 4 <U+215B>
# 5 <U+2105>
# 6        ‰
# 7        ö
```

So apparently `print()` cannot deal with `⅛` and `℅` when they are in a data.frame? 


Anyway, this is what `readr` does

```r
library("readr")
write_csv(df, "df_readr.csv")
read_csv("df_readr.csv")

# Parsed with column specification:
# cols(
#   x = col_character()
# )
# # A tibble: 7 x 1
#          x
#      <chr>
# 1 "\u0080"
# 2 "\u0096"
# 3        ¼
# 4 <U+215B>
# 5 <U+2105>
# 6 "\u0089"
# 7        ö
```

Interesting. Even more so when we look at the output of `write_lines()` 

```r
write_lines(df$x, "df_readr_lines.txt")
read_lines("df_readr_lines.txt")
# "\u0080" "\u0096" "¼"      "⅛"      "℅"      "\u0089" "ö"     
```

This is equivalent to what `write_lines()` does and what I see in Notepad++ (well kinda). 

So both write functions can deal with things like `⅛` and `℅` but not with the Euro-symbol or the en-dash (U+2013). 

Finally, the output of `format_csv` is rubbish.

```r
cat(format_csv(df))

# x
# Â€
# Â–
# Â¼
# â…›
# â„…
# Â‰
# Ã¶
```

For comparison now `utils`

```r
write.csv(df, "df_utils.csv", fileEncoding = "UTF-8", row.names = FALSE)
read.csv("df_utils.csv", fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
#          x
# 1        €
# 2        –
# 3        ¼
# 4 <U+215B>
# 5 <U+2105>
# 6        ‰
# 7        ö
```

This looks the same in Notepad++. 

So `utils::write.csv()` writes the same as what `print(df)` shows in the console. I'd expect this kind of consistency from `readr`, too.

title: readr - parse_date - date_names
description:
There are different month names for January is in Austria and Germany ("Jänner"/"Januar").
The solution is to build my own data_name object for Austria.

> mon <- c("Jänner", "Februar", "März", "April", "Mai", "Juni", "Juli", "August", "September", "Oktober", "November", "Dezember")
> monab <- c("Jän", "Feb", "Mrz", "Apr", "Mai", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Okt", "Nov", "Dez")
> day <- c("Sonntag", "Montag", "Dienstag", "Mittwoch", "Donnerstag", "Freitag", "Samstag")
> dayab <- c("So", "Mo", "Di", "Mi", "Do", "Fr", "Sa")
> deAT <- date_names(mon, monab, day, dayab)

<date_names>
Days:   Sonntag (So), Montag (Mo), Dienstag (Di), Mittwoch (Mi), Donnerstag
        (Do), Freitag (Fr), Samstag (Sa)

        (Jun), Juli (Jul), August (Aug), September (Sep), Oktober
        (Okt), November (Nov), Dezember (Dez)

It seems to be a correct data_name object.

row # A tibble: 1 x 4 col     row   col            expected          actual expected   <int> <int>               <chr>           <chr> actual 1     1    NA date like %d. %B %Y 24. Jänner 2014

title: Provide lists / vectors of col_types to cols function to support versioned CSVs
description:
Hi,

Apologies if this is already implemented differently and I just can't find it...

Many thanks for the rlang package - it's extremely useful!

I've got a CSV file with multiple different versions in use where I'm writing a package to load the file in painlessly, tidy and aggregate it ready for analysis. Full files can be 300MB in size with 300 columns - I don't have control over the changes made to the CSV format.

I can establish which version is in use by doing a quick test read and checking the position and naming of certain columns.

With ~300 fields in the file, and probably 10 (and potentially more in future with a factorial combination of columns added or removed) different CSV versions in existence what I would prefer to do is to break up my cols specification into groups of cols definitions.

Let's say that version 1 just has MyColumn; and version2 has MyColumn and MyNewColumn in.

To load version 1 files, we would just load the columnTypes definitions. But for version 2 files we want to also include the column definitions in columnTypes2.

I was hoping that the cols syntax would be behaving list-like or vector-like, so I've tried the following examples:

```
columnTypes <- readr::cols(
MyColumn = readr::col_integer())
columnTypes2 <- readr::cols(
MyNewColumn = readr::col_character())

 importedData <- readr::read_csv(filename, col_names = TRUE, col_types = c(columnTypes, columnTypes2))
```

I've also tried:

```
columnTypes2 <- readr::cols(
MyNewColumn = readr::col_character())

columnTypes <- readr::cols(
MyColumn = readr::col_integer(),
columnTypes2)
 importedData <- readr::read_csv(filename, col_names = TRUE, col_types = columnTypes)

```

The other nice syntax way (which I appreciate doesn't work as it's not NSE) would be to use rlang features:
```

columnTypes <- readr::cols(
MyColumn = readr::col_integer(),
!!! columnTypes2)

```

Am I missing a neat way to achieve this? If it's not possible, do you think any of the methods above could be considered in future? Or any suggestions on suitable workarounds for the problem?

title: Option for thousands separator in read_csv()
description:
Several times while working with datasets using readr's read_csv() function, I've had parse errors thrown because of unexpected commas being used as thousands separators. After guessing the column types to be doubles from the first 1000 rows, the function comes across a large numeric value which doesn't fit as a double because it has commas! To get around this, I have to specify the column type using the col_types argument. But sometimes it is not convenient to manually type out the column types for each feature.

In my case, the solution was to go upstream to my database manager and change the settings so that it does not write in thousands separators. But this isn't always possible for datasets someone might find in the wild.

The [pandas read_csv](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/generated/pandas.read_csv.html) command has an option to specify a thousands separator. I've found this extremely convenient for many datasets now, and frequently eliminates all parse errors. Is it possible to include a similar feature?

title: White space definition differs between read.csv() & read_csv()
description:
There appears to be a difference in the way Base R `read.csv()` and `readr::read_csv()` define "white spaces". `help(read.csv)` and `help(scan)` provide a Base R white space definition but I could not find anything similar for `readr::read_csv()` (perhaps I missed it).

In the reprex example below there is space after each `,` (comma) in the csv file. `read.csv()` counts this towards what it reads in whereas `readr::read_csv()` does not. Both approaches have their logic but are they different by design?

Note: Below I am using `readr` version ‘1.2.0’ installed using `devtools::install_github("tidyverse/readr")`

```
library(tidyverse)
csvFile <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
csvSpace <- c('Date, City, Temp
"18/06/2017", "Lisbon", 23
"18/06/2017", "  Rome", 25
"18/06/2017", "Oslo", 12\n')
write_file(csvSpace, csvFile)

# `readr::read_csv()`
# Without trimming white spaces variable `Temp` is character.
space_csv_F <- readr::read_csv(csvFile, trim_ws = FALSE)
glimpse(space_csv_F)

space_csv_T <- readr::read_csv(csvFile, trim_ws = TRUE)
glimpse(space_csv_T)

# Base R `read.csv()`
# Temp is integer with or without stripping white spaces.
space.CSV.F <- read.csv(csvFile, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, strip.white = FALSE)
glimpse(space.CSV.F)

space.CSV.T <- read.csv(csvFile, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, strip.white = TRUE)
glimpse(space.CSV.T)
```

title: Feature Request: Give the Option of Reading Only Specific Columns in read_* Function Family
description:
Imagine I have a 22 GB CSV, with 20 Columns, but I am only interested in 3 of them.

It would be useful to give the option in _readr_ package functions that:
* Although all columns are read at time of processing the data.
* Only "some" of them are saved into RAM memory, in order to save memory space.
* And the remaining columns are considered "dummy" variables, and are not imported into RAM (Although yes processed).

This could be easily achieved with an optional clause in read_* functions. e.g:
read_csv2("file.csv", restrict_columns = c("MyColumn_Name1", ..., "MyColumnNameN"))

In MySQL, for example, you can easily do this by assigning some of the CSV columns to dummy variables, which are overwriten with each register read, and not saved. 

It is fairly easy to implement, anyone interested in collaboration?

Thank you.
Juan

I think things are a bit more readable if you do:

```
options(digits = 3)

  base = read.csv('factors.csv', header = FALSE, nrows = n,

  datatable = fread_factors('factors.csv', header = FALSE,

  times = 10L 
)
```

I'd also think about testing with 1e5 rows - that's still big enough to get a decent estimate of the speed, but makes the benchmark process a little faster.

Finally, it'd be nice if the benchmarks automatically created the data when needed:

``` R
if (!file.exists("factor.csv")) make_factors(nr = 1e5)
```

title: Decouple MMapReader
description:
Too much logic in `MMapReader` perhaps it should just exhibit: 
- int get_int
- double get_double
- String get_String
- String get_line

and higher level algorithms can be defined elsewhere, e.g. things like read, get, count_lines, ...

This way we can separate the algorithm from low level stuff. So that supporting other connections would only be a matter of implementing these low level stuff.

title: arbitrary connection support
description:
We need to leverage this: https://gist.github.com/romainfrancois/6119995

so that we can read a stream from an arbitrary connection. We would still use mmap for speed when it makes sense, but otherwise we can process the stream from a buffered connection. 

In a threaded world we can imagine to separate the work into:
- buffering data from the connection
- process data

so that the thread(s) processing the data would not have to wait to process. 

But before threads, we can sequentially retrieve data from the connection and process. 

The problem I suppose is that I guess we can only read once from some connections, which might render difficult a two steps algorithm like counting the number of lines and then allocate data ...

title: Enumerate design principles
description:
When designing fastread functions, it's useful to have some design principles to adhere to. Here's my thoughts:
- Fail early: fastread functions should fail early, as soon as they discover there is something wrong with the input. fastread should make reasonable default guesses, but if it guesses wrong (e.g. a column turns out to be character, not integer) it shouldn't automatically coerce, but should raise an error indicating what the problem is. The user always know best about their data, so if a column type (or name) conflicts between the file and specification, then we should throw an error so that the user can resolve the problem (This also means providing informative diagnostics so they can see exactly where the problem was).
- Fast: the goal of fastread is to be fast. If adding a rarely used feature would result in a significant slow down, we should reconsider how important it is. Users can always fall back to the slow built in functions if they need to parse an unusual format. fastread should be competitive with the best file readers from other programming languages.

Once we've iterated on these a couple of times, they can go in the readme.
