title: File specification
description:
If the user doesn't supply any classes, we should run something like `guess_classes(file, n = 10)` which would inspect the first `n` lines to guess the classes for each line:
- integer and double: straightforward
- date/time: recgonise a few standard unambiguous formats (e.g. `%Y-%m-%d`) and selection of most common ISO_8601 formats
- factor: never guessed
- character: anything else

`guess_classes()` would return a vector of parsers, as well as printing a message informing the user what it guessed. The message would be designed so that you could copy and paste into a new `read_csv` call.  (The message is always printed to encourage the user to incorporated into the `read_csv` call, making code more robust to changes in the underlying data).

``` R
guess_classes("iris.csv")
#> Guessing column types:
#> colclasses(double(), double(), double(), double(), character())
```

(although obviously those function names don't work because they're already claimed by R)

For user specification we might want a richer form that let you supply a default and exceptions:

``` R
read_csv("iris.csv", colclasses(.default = double(), Species = character())
```

Maybe thinking about it as a column specification would be better. Then you could supply column names:

``` R
# Read from first line
colspec(names = firstline(), classes = list(Species = character()), default_class = double())
# Make default names
colspec(names = default(prefix = "X"))
# Supply explicit names (if not present)
colspec(names = c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width", "Petal.Length", "Petal.Width", "Species"))
```

The big advantage in assuming that we always have some specification of column names is then we can specify classes by name, which makes code more robust (it would be an error to specify the class for a column name that doesn't exist in the data).

`spec()` is probably sufficient for a name, so we'd have a `spec()` for user supplied specifications and `guess_spec()` to automatically determine. Then we need some way of describing the individual classes. I think it's relatively straightforward to see what each class needs (e.g. format for dates/times, levels for factor), the main problem is coming up with succinct yet clear function names that don't conflict with existing names.

I also wonder if we could deal with missing values through a column specification: `double(na.value = 99)` etc. The downside is that we'd need a special way of describing a global missing value setting, but it would make the specification more flexible.  A complete set of arguments that we could move from `read_csv` to column specifications is:
- na.strings
- strip.white
- allowEscapes

I'm imagining that the column specifications (e.g. `spec_double()` (which needs a better name)) would generate a RC object that's bound to a C++ object which defined parsing behaviour. Does that make sense?

title: benchmark reading / vs parsing
description:
Here are some simple benchmarks for read_csv of [http://cran-logs.rstudio.com/2014/2014-01-27.csv.gz](http://cran-logs.rstudio.com/2014/2014-01-27.csv.gz) for now setting all columns to character

```
path <- "/tmp/2014-01-27.csv.gz"
junk <- read_csv( file(path, open = "r"), n = 115829, classes = rep("character", 10) )
```

nore that we assume we know in advance the number of rows (115829). 
The times below are milli seconds, split into 3 parts
- alloc: time R takes to allocate the data. nothing we can do here. 
- process: parsing the feed and assigning chunks into the vectors
- read: reading from the connection  

```
    what      time percent
1 process 157.90994   71.38
2   alloc  17.95150    8.11
3    read  45.36878   20.51
```

It takes more time to read than to process. I think that's a good thing. When we move to threading, it means we can essentially anticipate reading. 

Here is a raw comparison of read_csv and read.csv using a gz connection: 

```
> system.time( read_csv( file(path, open = "r"), n = 115829, classes = rep("character", 10) ) )
utilisateur     système      écoulé
      0.203       0.005       0.207
> system.time( read.csv( file = file(path, open = "r"), nrows = 115829, colClasses = rep("character", 10) ) )
utilisateur     système      écoulé
      1.285       0.010       1.308
```

title: Source adapters
description:
We can read from arbitrary connections now and make the data read in the connection available as a `Source`. 

Would be interesting to have a `Source` implementation that filters data. This `FilteredSource` would read from the underlying connection, process each line and decide if it keeps it or not. 

Interesting filters can be: 
- based on line numbers. For example expressing reading one line every 10 lines
- based on string matching. perhaps we can process the line through a regex. Or simpler things like starts_with, ends_with, contains. 

What's interesting about this is that this is independant from the parsing done in `read_csv` or other consumers of `Source`. 

Of course, depending on the underlying source, it might be possible or not to calculate the number of lines in advance.

title: All parsers need invalid argument
description:
e.g. `invalid = c("error", "warning", "silent")`:
- error = throw error message with field/line number and abort parsing
- warning = warning with field/line number and replace with NA
- silent = just replace with NA.

title: use custom allocators
connection pushback
description:
We need to consider the connection push back. 

When we read from a connection: there might be data in the push back, we need to read this first

Because we use `->read` to buffer data, we need to put data back into the push back if we exit. For example if we read 3 lines, we need to put data in the push back so that it starts at the start of the 4th line.

title: Growing vector strategy.
description:
Sometimes we don't know the final size and it is too expensive or perhaps impossible to calculate it in advance. For example when we read from several files or connections, I don't think we can realistically assume that users will give us the number of lines in each file. 

So we can use `std::vector` to accumulate data or perhaps use `R_alloc` to get some buffer garbage collected memory, or perhaps both (see http://blog.r-enthusiasts.com/2014/01/21/r-transient-allocator.html which can be easily extracted out Rcpp11 if needed).

title: Read multiple files into one data frame
description: A common use case is reading multiple files using `lapply` + `read.csv` and then combining them into one file with `rbind/rbind.fill/rbind_list`. It would be nice if there was some way to do this in one step to avoid a copy.

title: Fast writers
description:
We may also want to consider having fast writers.  `write.table` generates the complete output before saving it to disk, so it's not suitable for saving large files.  For a recent problem I had to write

``` R
n <- 10000L
m <- floor(nrow(logs) / n)
for (i in seq(0, m, by = 1)) {
  start <- i * n + 1
  end <- pmin((i + 1) * n, nrow(logs))

  write.table(logs[start:end, ], "logs.csv", row.names = FALSE, 
    sep = ",", append = i != 0L, col.names = FALSE, na = "")
  cat(".")
}
```

That's obviously not ideal.

title: Suppress "" in write_csv
description:
write.csv has the quote parameter that controls whether or not the values are wrapped in "quotes". I suggest adding this to write_csv. 

I just used readr (and dplyr) to consolidate a huge data file into something smaller and more useful (thank you!). It's mostly two- and three-letters codes, and they all ended up wrapped in quotes when they didn't need to be. It would be nice to be able to turn this off when desired.

title: Columns are read even if not mentioned in col_types in read_tsv
description:
From ?read_tsv:

> col_types 
> [...]
> If a list, it must contain one "collector" for each column. If you only want to read a subset of the columns, you can use a named list (where the names give the column names). If a column is not mentioned by name, it will not be included in the output. [...]

Bug reproduction steps

```
read_tsv("1\t2\n3\t4\n",col_names=c("X","Y"),col_types=list("X"=col_integer()))
```

Expected result

```
  X
1 1
2 3
```

Observed result

```
  X Y
1 1 2
2 3 4
```

Sidenote: `read_tsv("1\t2\n3\t4\n",col_names=c("X","Y"),col_types=c("i_"))` yields the correct result.

title: read_csv support escape_backslash
description:
Although not hard to figure out that it can be down by `read_delim` with `delim = ","`, It seems more user friendly if `read_csv` support `escape_backslash`.

If it's not supported, it's helpful to document that read_csv doesn't support `escape_backslash` and redirect users to `read_delim`.

title: read_csv coerces all column values to NA if 100 first observations are missing
description:
If the first 100 observations of a variable are missing, `read_csv` overwrites _all_ column values with NAs (unless the column is boolean). Ideally, column type should be determined using the first 100 _non-missing_ values of each column.

```
library(readr)
x = data.frame(matrix(rnorm(1000), ncol=5))
x$X1[1:100] = NA
write.csv(x, file='test.csv', row.names=FALSE)
y = read_csv('test.csv')
y$X1
problems(x)
```

title: Desired: read_csv equivalent of read.csv's colClasses="character" to read all columns as character
description:
Hi,

I think all data analysts should be paranoid, and assume that data are coded improperly. Thus I want to read all data, including numeric data, in as character values until I convince myself that I am not losing important information by converting to numeric. (Example: I once had data that was supposed to be coded (1 or 2) for (male or female), but some rows erroneously were coded (M or F). Reading the data as numeric would have lost the information in the M, F rows, converting them to NAs.)

Specifying column types for each individual column is fine if there are only a few columns, but if there are hundreds, it would be nice to have an easy way to make them all the same type, just as colClasses="character" allows for read.csv.

The code below shows what I mean.

Many thanks for considering this.

Don

```
> library(readr)
> 
> data <-"sex,age,income\n1,20,40e3\n2,40,60000\nM,30,80000"
> 
> # read all columns as character using read.csv
> df1 <- read.csv(textConnection(data), colClasses="character") # only have to specify character once
> df1
  sex age income
1   1  20   40e3
2   2  40  60000
3   M  30  80000
> str(df1)
'data.frame':   3 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ sex   : chr  "1" "2" "M"
 $ age   : chr  "20" "40" "30"
 $ income: chr  "40e3" "60000" "80000"
> 
> # The following read_csv statements will produce the same results, but I would prefer not to have to
> # specify col_types for EACH column
> 
> # read all columns as character using read_csv
> df2 <- read_csv(data, col_types="ccc") # must specify each column
> df2
```

title: make.names
description: It doesn't seem readr by default creates syntactically valid names. It is easy to implement it and may be worthwhile to do it. Or certainly provide it as an option.

title: write_csv should save POSIXct as ISO8601 times
write_csv truncating numbers?
description:
In the simple example below, there is a difference between df01 and df02:

``` R
library(readr)

set.seed(1234)
n <- 1e3
dat <-  data.frame(a=as.integer(sample(1:1000,n,replace=TRUE)),
                 b=rnorm(n),
                 c=sample(c("foo","bar","baz","qux","quux"),n,replace=TRUE),
                 d=sample(c(TRUE,FALSE),n,replace=TRUE), 
                 stringsAsFactors=FALSE)

write.csv(dat,"test.csv",row.names = FALSE)
write_csv(dat,"test1.csv")

df01 <- read_csv("test.csv")
df02 <- read_csv("test1.csv")
```

title: datetime columns are treated like date columns in read_csv
description:
I have some columns in which all values are in the format "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S".  However, read_csv seems to expect that this column be inthe format "%Y-%m-%d" (i.e. it assumes that my datetime is a date).  Reproducible example follows:


title: Mimic `base::read.table()` variable name fixing
description:
Consider if `readr::read_xxx()` should have a parameter (possibly `make_names=F`) that specifies if unconventional variable names should be renamed in the same way as `base::read.xxx()` does.  Admittedly it's minor, but it would allow the readr functions to be drop-in compatible in more code.    

My guess is that compatibility could be accomplished by calling [`base::make.names()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/make.names.html) somewhere near the bottom of [`readr::read_delimited()`](https://github.com/hadley/readr/blob/master/R/read_delim.R)

As a small example, I'm working with code that needed to change from

``` r
ds <- plyr::rename(ds, replace=c(
    "Subject." = "subject_id"
  , "Art." = "ff_art" 
))
```

to

``` r
ds <- plyr::rename(ds, replace=c(
   "Subject#" = "subject_id"
  , "Art " = "ff_art" #Be careful of the trailing space after 'Art '
))
```

In other words, somewhere `readr::read_delimiter would do something like this, and copy over the data.frame colnames.

``` r
> make.names(c("Subject#", "Art "))
[1] "Subject." "Art."  
```

We've certainly all been given datasets with many more violating variables than two.

title: Cover all variations of csv formats
description:
It would be nice if read_csv could cover the great variety of (fuzzily) defined csv formats, at least if the filespec is known. Automatic detection is less important and can build on this. Here is what I know about csv-file variation:
- BOM or not
- character encoding
- row separator[s](one or two and which ones, file might come from unix/win/mac)
- list separator
- decimal separator
- quoting character {",'}
- how to escape the quoting character in strings (\" \' "" '' etc. )
- whether strings are quoted {never|always|only if needed}
- whether numbers are quoted
- whether row- and column-separators are escaped within strings
- allow/disallow multi-lines in quoted strings (disallowing is a precondition for skipAbytes= and abytes below)
- different ways to code multi-lines in quoted strings {hard break, soft break}
- different NA strings, possible with multiple of them possible each with more than one character
- header {yes|no}
- header {quoted|unquoted}
- comment characters marking lines to skip
- whether to interpret (and count) empty lines as completely missing record or to skip it. 
- whether to strip white space around unquoted strings

title: Connection broken after reading first chunk of rows
description:
``` R
# lets create data
write_csv(iris, "iris.csv")
con <- file("iris.csv", "rb")
# reading the first chunk from a connection works
read_csv(con, n_max=50)
# but autsch: can't continue reading from the connection
read_csv(con, n_max=50)
close(con)
```

Reading chunks from a connection (#16) is important (and read.csv can do it).
I know that there is a performance trade-off:
reading line-by-line with readLines() is slower than reading bigger chunks of bytes
but reading bigger chunks will usually read beyond the desired line break
and putting back to connections is costly and doesn't work everywhere (see #19).
A solution is adding a parameter for specifying _approx_ chunk size

``` R
read_csv(con, read_approx_bytes=5000)
```

So you can read a binary chunk of that size and then continue reading single bytes until the row is exhausted. For compatibility with read.csv you could actually allow both parameters, read_approx_bytes= and nrows= or n_max=. If someone asks for a precise number of lines, the slower readLines() (or a similar functionin C++) could be used.

title: read_csv from R readr treats imported data differently than generated data
description:
I had an issue using ifelse() in a function which was initially solved in this [stackoverflow thread](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/31325531/r-ifelse-evaluates-a-condition-and-returns-match). After implementing the suggestions the code performed exactly as desired. The code is below 

```
country_panel <- function(x, y) {
  ifelse(cnames$time < y, 
    cnames[match(x, cnames$country),]$panel,
    cnames[match(x, cnames$country),]$standardize
 )
 }
```

Generate the fake data with this

```
 countryname <- c("Viet Nam", "Viet Nam", "Viet Nam", "Viet Nam", "Viet Nam")
year <- c(1974, 1975, 1976, 1977,1978)

df <- data.frame(countryname, year, stringsAsFactors=FALSE)

country <- c("Vietnam, North", "Vietnam, N.", "Vietnam North", "Viet Nam",   "Democratic Republic Of Vietnam")
standardize <- c("Vietnam, Democratic Republic of", "Vietnam, Democratic Republic of", "Vietnam, Democratic Republic of", "Vietnam, Democratic Republic of", "Vietnam, Democratic Republic of")
panel <- c("Vietnam", "Vietnam","Vietnam","Vietnam","Vietnam")
time <- c(1976,1976,1976,1976,1976)

cnames <- data.frame(country, standardize, panel, time, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

Evaluate using the function using

```
 d1 <- df %>% 
   mutate(new_name = country_panel(countryname, year))
```

However, when I went to implement the suggestions with the real data the problem returned where the function does not evaluate the condition in the `ifelse` statement and only returns the `$panel` value. 

Because using `stringsAsFactors = FALSE` in the `data.frame` worked with the fake data I thought that using `read.csv(PATH, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)` would work instead of using `read_csv` but they both perform equally. 

I should also note that I checked the attributes of each vector in the data frame using `str()` and forced them to match what I found in the fake data. 

The real data and scripts to replicate everything can be found on GitHub [here](https://github.com/dsself/StandardCountries/tree/master/paneldev)

title: Looking for dates where there are none
description:
I have been trying to integrate `readr` into several workflows where it would bring a real speed gain, but I am facing just one issue that makes it risky for me to do so.

It has to do with `readr` looking for dates where there are none. Here's an example:

``` r
y = c("1989-90", "1990-91", "1991-92", "1992-93", "1993-94", "1994-95", 
      "1995-96", "1996-97", "1997-98", "1998-99", "1999-00", "2000-01", 
      "2001-02", "2002-03", "2003-04", "2004-05", "2005-06", "2006-07", 
      "2007-08", "2008-09", "2009-10", "2012-13", "2013-14", "2014-15", 
      "2015-16")
y = cbind(not_dates = y, x = 1)
write.csv(y, "test.csv", row.names = FALSE)
readr::read_csv("test.csv")
```

When faced with that example, `readr` 0.1.1 tries to interpret the first column as dates, fails to find a format, and thus returns `NA`.

The same problem arises if the data are of the form `"1989-1990", "1990-1991", ...`

Now, I know how to use `col_types`, but some of my workflows contain dozens of I/O calls from/to CSV files that have tons of columns, so using `readr` would require going through a lot of checks.

This is the only real trouble that I have faced with the package, so I thought I would ask: would you consider it reasonable – would it be possible – to have `readr` _not_ try to recognise strings of the form `\\d{4}-\\d{2}` or `\\d{4}-\\d{4}` as dates?

title: Data package support?
description:
Whilst CSV etc is in part so flexible is because it's easy to use informally, the wide variety of conventions associated with X delimited files, and the lack of semantics or typing associated with column definitions, (though conventions can go someway to addressing that, informally at least) means that parsers have to use all sorts of heuristics to parse the files sensible.

Tools like `readr` go a long way towards providing a means of getting data into a structured and typed data frame in a painless way (things like `pandas` provide similar tools in the `scipystack`) but more often than not we lose the typing and semantics when we save the data out again.

I wonder though if we should also be thinking about supporting and using packaging formats such as [data packages](http://data.okfn.org/doc/data-package) that augment CSV exports with JSON metadata files. I don't for one minute imagine that folk would start to use them widely, but as a transport format moving data files between systems and opendata portals such as CKAN powered ones, they do provide a relatively lightweight "progressive enhancement" to CSV files that can make it easier to load in a file that has already been saved from a structured, typed representation such as a dataframe.

There are already a few packages out there that seem to support this format - [RODProt](https://github.com/QBRC/RODProt) and [dpmr](https://github.com/christophergandrud/dpmr). Perhaps including support for the format in `readr` would be useful?

_Disclaimer - data packages and CKAN are Open Knowledge activities; I'm occasionally affiliated with that organisation._

title: read_delim fails on multibyte delimiters (at least this one.)
description:
Let's say you have to deal with weird data, and that data has basically every printable character under the sun embedded in it. No problem, you think to yourself, i'll just pick a unicode character as my delimiter.

I picked ❤ because I am a romantic at heart. I made this little file to test it:

```
$ cat sample.hsv
id❤name❤age
1❤ed❤36
2❤leigh❤NA 
3❤natha❤14
```

I then reached for readr's read_delim and used it in such a fashion (after installing the latest version from github):

```
> library(readr)
> dat <- read_delim("/tmp/sample.hsv", "❤")
```

Unfortunately, it does this:

```
> str(dat)
Classes ‘tbl_df’, ‘tbl’ and 'data.frame':   3 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ id          : int  1 2 3
 $ ��name: chr  "\x9d\xa4ed" "\x9d\xa4leigh" "\x9d\xa4natha"
 $ ��age : chr  "\x9d\xa436" "\x9d\xa4NA" "\x9d\xa414"
```

Should I not be using multibyte delimiters? (I mean, I know I shouldn't, but I guess I _really_ shouldn't?) I also was surprised that it worked to figure out the columns, but it didn't strip them from the data, so I figure perhaps not all is lost?

In a perfect world, of course, this would just return a data frame with the 3 columns: c("id", "name", "age") with the appropriate data.

Here are two possibilities to implement this:
1) `col_types` accepts as "collector" function as an argument such as `col_types = col_character()` or `col_types = col_integer()`. All columns are processed in this way.
2) If a character of length 1 is passed to `col_types` (e.g. `col_types = "c"`), this type is used for all columns.

title: Check for interrupts even when progress bar is off
problems() warning workflow with skip
description:
if I ever call `problems()` I tend to call `read_lines()` on the file and pull out the lines of interest to see what's what. However, if I had specified `skip` in `read_tsv()` to get the actual lines I want I need to add `skip` to `problems()$row`. 

This is fine if I am reading in one file but in reality I'm reading in 100s and `skip` is actually computed for each file according to a simple guessing function (see end of this post)...which means I have to keep `skip` around for each file.

**issues:**
1. Would be possible to add to `problems()` so that I could have the `$row` and the `read_lines()[row_idx]` equivalent right there. An alternative solution would be to have a `skip` parameter in `read_lines(..., skip = )` (I prefer this actually since it's consistent with all the other `read_*`.
2. It would be awesome to be able to pass the problematic line indices directly to `read_lines()`; so that you could do `read_lines(..., sub = 10:20)` and `read_lines(..., sub = c(1,5))` to get lines 10:20 and c(1,5), respectively. A naive implementation could be where `n_max` is computed from `max(sub)` and `sub` is just used to subset the result e.g.:`read_lines(n_max = max(sub))[sub]`.

---

the simple guessing function:

``` r
#' guess how many lines to skip by looking for the first line that has the expected number of
#' delimiters. 
#'
#' @param expect_delim delimiter to expect
#' @param expect_n_vars number of vars (cols) to expect
#' @param n_max passed to read_lines's n_max
guess_skip <- function(file, expect_delim, expect_n_vars, n_max = 100) {
  lines <- readr::read_lines(file, n_max = n_max)
  delims_per_line <- stringi::stri_count_fixed(lines, expect_delim)
  first_data_line <- which.max(delims_per_line)
  stopifnot(delims_per_line[first_data_line] == expect_n_vars - 1)
  first_data_line - 1
}
```

title: Horrible CSV: Can readr deal with the full spectrum of horrible files?
description:
Originally posted as a comment to https://github.com/hadley/readr/issues/94. Opened new issue as requested. 

Fantastic package! Please excuse if this is out of scope, but there are all sorts of horrible source CSV that I find myself having to deal with by pre-processing outside of R with something like Perl. Totally ok if you think that's still probably the best way to do this.

The way you've got this package set up however, makes me think that perhaps other forms of CSV lunacy could be dealt with by simply writing a new tokenizer.

The specific things that I have trouble dealing with entirely within R include:
1. Mismatched encoding/locale, usually something that has been declared explicitly or implicitly as UTF-8 but is actually ISO-8859-1, which has consequences for interpreting newlines and EOF. (There are R solutions for this, including the excellent `rvest` package, but this really needs to be dealt with right at the file level before throwing it at a parser.)
2. Embedded but unescaped newlines.
3. Embedded but unescaped delimiters.
4. Embedded but unescaped quotes.
5. Undeclared/inconsistent padding whitespace (Pretty sure `readr` can handle this already, but included in the list for completeness)

If you've already got or are working on auto-detect/guessing for the number of fields, the delimiter, the quote character and the newline code, you can potentially fix all of these annoying issues (with or without fanfare, as the case may be).

On a high level, you would add a check (probably just for string or unknown col types) for the number of fields in the current line and if it doesn't match what was auto-detected or declared in the call, jump to a special tokenizer for that line and any subsequent lines until you get a single parsed record that makes sense, then jump back to your standard tokenizer. Optionally, you spit out a warning (or error) for the line(s) and the problem.

If the file is so messy that it can't even get past auto-detect, then you exit and throw an error that the file isn't valid CSV (or delimited) of any flavour, and this is also useful information.

Are my assumptions here about how readr works and/or is planned reasonable?

title: Inconsistent behaviour with read_csv and skip > #rows
description:
1. When `col_types` is specified and `skip` is equal to or greater than the number of actual rows, `read_csv()` returns a data.frame with 1 row.
2. When `col_types` is _not_ specified and `skip` is equal to or greater than the number of actual rows, `read_csv()` throws an error.

I think Case1 is wrong to return a row of results when there aren't any, and should probably return a zero-row data.frame.

EDIT: Case 2 is handled OK i.e. If column types aren't specified, and there are no rows from which to infer type, you can't really return anything sensible.

I found this inconsistency when doing chunked reads from a large CSV file, and a zero-row data.frame was going to be an indicator that I'd run out of data.

``` r
> read_csv("1,2\n3,4", col_names=c('a', 'b'), col_types='ii')
Source: local data frame [2 x 2]

  a b
1 1 2
2 3 4
> 
> read_csv("1,2\n3,4", col_names=c('a', 'b'), col_types='ii', skip=2)
Source: local data frame [1 x 2]

   a  b
1 NA NA
> 
> read_csv("1,2\n3,4", col_names=c('a', 'b'), skip=2)
Error: You have 2 column names, but 0 columns
```

title: Tokenizer needs to handle nulls
description:
After attempting to read a file with nulls fails (different issue), the datafile is locked. It is not being shown as an open connection by `showConnections(all=TRUE)`, and I know no other places to check for known open/locked connections.

The file, call it `abc.txt`:

```
ab\x00c,def
abc,def
```

(That's a null character, not the literal characters ... I don't know another way to depict it in GH.)

``` r
read_delim('abc.txt', delim=',')
## Error in collectorsGuess(source, tokenizer, n = 100) : 
##   embedded nul in string: 'ab\0c'

read_delim('abc.txt', delim=',', col_names=FALSE, col_types='cc')
## Error in read_tokens(ds, tokenizer, col_types, col_names, n_max = n_max,  : 
##   embedded nul in string: 'ab\0c'
```

The fact that it cannot read a null is not the issue here (though to some people it may be a problem). More the point is that the file is locked and cannot be changed/over-written by anything. (By "anything", I tested emacs/ESS, RStudio text editor, notepad++, even some of _R_'s base file-writing functions.) Tested combinations of `read_delim` arguments, plus the row of the datafile containing the null character:

| file row | `col_names` | `col_types` | read file correctly? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 |  | "cc" | yes |
| 1 |  |  | yes |
| 1 | FALSE | "cc" | error |
| 1 | FALSE |  | error |
| 2 |  | "cc" | error |
| 2 |  |  | error |
| 2 | FALSE | "cc" | error |
| 2 | FALSE |  | error |

When it fails, subsequent calls to one of the two "good" combinations above works fine, though the file is still locked to outside editors. Closing the session of _R_ is the only way I was able to unlock the file for editors to be able to save/over-write the file.

Done on win81_64 using emacs/ESS and RStudio. Attempted it on linux (ubuntu 14.04.2 with R-3.2.0) and none of these argument combinations resulted in a locked file. Not tested on mac.

title: Handle also when header and data rows have different number of columns
description:
# Case 1: More column names than data columns

`read.table()` has `fill=TRUE` to handle the case for when there are more column names than columns in the data rows, e.g.

``` r
> read_tsv("a\tb\tc\n1\t2\n")
Error: You have 3 column names, but 2 columns

> read.table(text="a\tb\tc\n1\t2\n", fill=FALSE)
Error in scan(file, what, nmax, sep, dec, quote, skip, nlines, na.strings,
  line 2 did not have 3 elements
> read.table(text="a\tb\tc\n1\t2\n", fill=TRUE)
  V1 V2 V3
1  a  b  c
2  1  2
```

Looking at the help, I don't think there is way to use `read_tsv()` to deal with this case.

WISH: Make it possible "fill" _data rows_ with empty values/NAs, when data rows lack trailing cells.  This would assume the missing ones are at the end, cf. argument `fill` of `read.table()`.
# Case 2: Fewer column names than data columns

`read.table()` does not handle this.  I don't think `read_tsv()` does either.

``` r
> read.table(text="a\tb\n1\t2\t3\t4\n", header=TRUE, fill=FALSE)
Error in read.table(text = "a\tb\n1\t2\t3\t4\n", header = TRUE, fill = FALSE) :
  more columns than column names
> read.table(text="a\tb\n1\t2\t3\t4\n", header=TRUE, fill=TRUE)
Error in read.table(text = "a\tb\n1\t2\t3\t4\n", header = TRUE, fill = FALSE) :
  more columns than column names
> read_tsv("a\tb\n1\t2\t3\t4\n")
Error: You have 2 column names, but 4 columns
```

WISH: Make it possible "fill" _column names_ with empty values/NAs, when header lack trailing column names.  This would assume the missing ones are at the end, cf. argument `fill` of `read.table()`.
## Background

For a real-world example, please see https://gist.github.com/HenrikBengtsson/dabc383aaa958c0ed49a.  The above examples are never ending stories in my life.

title: read_csv: Set collector for column with first 100 rows blank as character collector
description:
Hi Hadley,

Is it possible to either (1) create an option to set all column collectors as character collectors or (2) when imputing 100 blank rows, set the collector as a character collector instead of a logical collector?

Often times my data has the first 100 rows blank; there are also too many columns for me to set each column type manually, so I use the default column collection imputer. What I found is that with 100 blank rows, read_csv interprets these as NA, a logical, and thus uses the logical collector. However, the actual data (characters) are not logicals and are coerced into NAs because they're not TRUE or FALSE. Thus, the entire column is read in as NAs, which may not be a bug but is an insidious effect that's not immediately obvious because suddenly a column of expected data of unknown type is read in as a blank column.

Thus, can you either make it such that it is easy to set all column collectors as character collectors, or edit the imputer such that 100 blank rows triggers the character collector and not the logical collector?

My current workaround has been to first read in 0 rows, count the number of columns, and read in all the data with col_types = str_dup("c", [number of columns]).

Thanks!

```
Alternatively, you can use a compact string representation
```

```
c = col_character(),
D = col_date(),
```

title: parsing failure when integers are expected but see a numeric value
description:
Here is an example I constructed from a real problem:

``` r
library(readr)
library(data.table)
library(dplyr)

sim = function(n) {
    df = data.frame(key   = 1:n,
                    value = c(rep(3, n-1), 54.0000019783304))
    write_csv(df, "test.csv")

    df.base = read.csv("test.csv") %>% rename(value_base = value)
    df.readr = read_csv("test.csv") %>% rename(value_readr = value)
    df.DT = fread("test.csv") %>% rename(value_DT = value)

    df.joined = df %>%
        left_join(df.base) %>%
        left_join(df.readr) %>%
        left_join(df.DT)

    tail(df.joined)
```

title: read_csv chokes on negatives and decimals
description:
This is probably related to https://github.com/hadley/readr/issues/376, https://github.com/hadley/readr/issues/308, and https://github.com/hadley/readr/issues/358. 

read_csv(2) doesn't work with decimals which are non-locale, and also on negatives. 

Check the following two examples. It's temperature data for Germany. url3 is March, and some months have negative temperatures. Data is imported as character, at least preserving the negatives and decimals. A `mutate(column = as.numeric(column))` "fixes" the problem. For month April data (url4), there are no negative temperatures, and the data is imported as numeric, but dropping the decimal (so, `5.6` is converted to `56`). 

Expected outcome: temperature data should be imported as numeric, with correct decimal and negative values. 

```
url3 <- paste0(
  "ftp://ftp-cdc.dwd.de/pub/CDC/",
  "regional_averages_DE/monthly/air_temperature_mean/",
  "regional_averages_tm_", sprintf("%02i", 3), ".txt"
)
url4 <- paste0(
  "ftp://ftp-cdc.dwd.de/pub/CDC/",
  "regional_averages_DE/monthly/air_temperature_mean/",
  "regional_averages_tm_", sprintf("%02i", 4), ".txt"
)

## note: ignore the parsing warnings, it's the last line that is messing it up. Can be avoided by setting n_max
dd3 <- read_csv2(url3, skip = 1, dec = ".")# temp data is as expected, but as.character(): "x.y" 
dd4 <- read_csv2(url4, skip = 1, dec = ".")# temp data is messed up: xxx
```

I "fixed" it by using `read_lines` and piping that into `read.csv2(text = read_lines(...), dec = ".", ...)`, so that could be used as a test-case.

title: Error when trying to convert data frame created by readr to spatial object
description:
Hello,

I am finding problems when trying to convert data frames (produced by `readr::read_csv`, `readxl::read_excel`, or `dplyr`) to spatial objects using `sp::coordinates`. I have seen other people have the same problem (e.g. https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/1267, http://blog.dominodatalab.com/applied-spatial-data-science-with-r/), so I thought it might be worth asking here.

An example:

```
    library(sp)
    library(readr)

    # Use reduced 'meuse' dataset
    data(meuse)
    meuse <- meuse[1:10, 1:3]

    # write data as CSV to read them later
    write_csv(meuse, "meuse.csv")

    meuse.imported <- read_csv("meuse.csv")
    str(meuse.imported)

```

The imported data frame has classes 'tbl_df', 'tbl' and 'data.frame'. Now when I try to convert it to a spatial object, it gives error:

```
coordinates(meuse.imported) <- c("x", "y")
## Error in (function (classes, fdef, mtable)  : 
##  unable to find an inherited method for function ‘coordinates<-’ for signature ‘"tbl_df"’
```

This error does not happen when reading the data using `read.csv`:

```
    meuse.imported <- read.csv("meuse.csv")
    str(meuse.imported)

    ##   ..@ coords.nrs : int [1:2] 1 2
    ##   ..@ coords     : num [1:10, 1:2] 181072 181025 181165 181298 181307 ...
    ##   .. ..- attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2
    ##   .. .. ..$ : NULL
```

So I guess the problem is with the classes `tbl_df` and `tbl` created by `readr`, `readxl` and `dplyr`... Is there an easy way to overcome this? Any advice would be much appreciated.

>  $ description_c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9)  : chr  NA NA NA NA ...

```
badCols
[1] "X4" "X4"
unique.bad.cols <- unique(badCols)

Warning message:
The following named parsers don't match the column names: unique.bad.cols
```

title: Speed vs LaF for pulling a few columns from a large file, FYI
description:
Hi,

Thank you for readr. It is almost always my goto tool for getting data from csv files. Recently I have had a need to pull selected columns from large csv files (the Census Bureau's American Community Survey for the U.S., 5-year data). I have compared readr to the package LaF (Large Ascii Files) and found LaF to be about 2-4 times as fast as readr for this purpose. This is not an issue or a problem, of course, but I thought I should let you know, in case you want to investigate what makes LaF faster for this purpose.

Here is a small reproducible example, once you download the Census file (url given below); it uses one of the 4 files that make up the 2013 5-year sample. On my machine, the LaF version reads the file in 53 seconds and the readr version reads it in 117 seconds.

Again, not a problem or issue, but enough of a difference for me to use LaF for this purpose. I would rather use readr for everything.

Many thanks.

Don

```
# comparison of readr and LaF - reading a few columns from a large file

# get the data ####
fnz <- "csv_pus.zip"
webdir <- "http://www2.census.gov/acs2013_5yr/pums/"

localdir <- "e:/temp/"

fna <- "ss13pusa.csv" # about 4.4gb, 4.6m rows, 295 columns - 1 of 4 files in zip archive

# uncomment this next line to download the data
# not tested because I did this manually
# download.file(paste0(webdir, fnz), paste0(localdir, fnz), mode="wb")
unzip(paste0(localdir, fnz), files=fna, exdir="e:/temp")

library("dplyr")
library("readr")
library("LaF")


# first, LaF ####
cnames <- names(read_csv(paste0(localdir, fna), n_max=1)) # get the column names using readr
cnames

dat.laf <- laf_open_csv(paste0(localdir, fna), column_names=cnames, column_types=rep("string", length(cnames)), skip=1)
keepvars <- c("serialno", "PUMA10", "ST", "ADJINC", "PWGTP", "AGEP", "WAGP", "HISP", "RAC1P", "SEX", "SCHL")
dat.laf[1:20, keepvars]
system.time(df.laf <- dat.laf[, keepvars])
glimpse(df.laf)


# now readr ####
system.time(df.rr <- read_csv(paste0(localdir, fna), col_names=TRUE, 
                col_types=cols_only(serialno="c", PUMA10="c", ST="c", ADJINC="c", PWGTP="c",
                                    AGEP="c", WAGP="c", HISP="c", RAC1P="c", SEX="c", SCHL="c")))
glimpse(df.rr)

```

title: Expand to parallel chunk reading
description:
In #206 I have suggested to allow a aprox chunk size parameter read_approx_bytes=.
An extension of this logic even allows _parallel_ reading from a csv-file
(Some people have fast SANs that support parallel read-processes, even consumer PCIe SSDs are there now, e.g. Intel SSD 750)

process 1
read_csv(con, skip_approx_bytes=0, read_approx_bytes=5000)
process 2
read_csv(con, skip_approx_bytes=5000, read_approx_bytes=5000)

Here an additional challenge is that process 2 can't wait until process 1 figured out the exact position of the next row-break
however, if we read an csv format that disallows line-breaks in strings we can simply move from the specified skip_approx_bytes position until we find the next line-break, there the process starts reading read_approx_bytes, and then continues reading until the row is exhausted
A separate function which does just the position finding is useful

approx_csv(file, approx_bytebreaks) -> returns exact_bytebreaks
for example
approx_csv(file, c(0, 5000)) -> returns e.g. c(0, 5003)

this allows for example preparing an ffdf file of appropriate size
and all parallel processes can independently write their read data.frame into their section of the ffdf
this gives completely lock-free parallelism.
Note that sizing an ffdf only works because ffdf has constant record-size, i.e. factors instead of character (see #161)

title: read_delim comment: invert, vector, or regex
description:
Use cases:

A. Multiple comment characters present in the file, perhaps due to inconsistent file creation formatting.

B. (Specific to me, not the majority use.) Some of my input files (that I don't control) are technically not proper CSV: the first field indicates the number and type of the remaining fields. I need to eventually read all of them (into separate data.frames), so multiple reads are required.

My current workaround is via `grep` and/or `sed` with tempfiles, and though this is generally safe for all dev systems except Windows without Rtools, it also introduces an external pipe.

Options:
1. Provide an `invert_comment` option to _only_ accept the "commented" lines (which seems a little counter-intuitive, perhaps). This is perhaps the simplest to implement.
2. Allow a vector for `comment`. A little more work, this has a broader use-case I think with poorly-constructed CSV files. (I don't know that anybody else has the pleasure of dealing with the poorly-constructed data files I'm dealing with ... ;-)
3. Regular expressions. This is a _lot_ more work, I admit. Since you're already using Boost, it should be feasible to use `boost/regex.hpp` ([example at Rcpp](http://gallery.rcpp.org/articles/boost-regular-expressions/)).

I don't know that I'm the best to work on it, but I'm familiar enough with Rcpp to give the first two a try. I can try the third, but I admit it will take perhaps more Rcpp expertise than I have. If you are amenable and think one of these is the right direction, I can work on a PR.

``` R
end  =c(2,5,6)
col_names=c('A','B','C')
col_positions <- fwf_positions(start, end, col_names = col_names)
col_types <- list(A=col_integer(),B=col_integer())

d1 <- read_fwf(x,col_positions = col_positions,col_types = col_types)

col_positions <- fwf_positions(start[1:2], end[1:2], col_names = col_names[1:2])
d2 <- read_fwf(x,col_positions = col_positions,col_types = col_types)
```

This worked fine with readr 0.1.0. I suspect that the following is to blame:

> read_fwf() is now much more careful with new lines. If a line is too short,
> you'll get a warning instead of a silent mistake (#166, #254). Additionally,
> the last column can now be ragged: the width of the last field is silently
> extended until it hits the next line break (#146). This appears to be a
> common feature of "fixed" width files in the wild.

I don't think you can detect if the fwf really is ragged or not. You cannot assume it is since you will never be able to read a subset of columns. A possible solution would be to assume ragged fwf if the last `end` in `fwf_positions` is Inf  OR  the last `width` in `fwf_widths` is Inf  OR  the last `end` in `fwf_positions` is not supplied (`length(start)-length(end)==1)`).

title: Dates should use double type
description:
This is really esoteric but caused a test of mine to fail in a very puzzling way. Dates created by `readr` are different from those created all other ways (integer vs double).

``` r
library(readr)
xbase <- data.frame(d = as.Date(c("2016-02-02", NA)))
xdplyr <- dplyr::data_frame(d = as.Date(c("2016-02-02", NA)))
xreadr <- read_csv("d\n2016-02-02\nNA")
```

These appear to be the same, up to `tbl_df`-ness.

``` r
str(xbase)
#> 'data.frame':    2 obs. of  1 variable:
#>  $ d: Date, format: "2016-02-02" NA
str(xdplyr)
#> Classes 'tbl_df', 'tbl' and 'data.frame':    2 obs. of  1 variable:
#>  $ d: Date, format: "2016-02-02" NA
str(xreadr)
#> Classes 'tbl_df', 'tbl' and 'data.frame':    2 obs. of  1 variable:
#>  $ d: Date, format: "2016-02-02" NA
```

But the `readr` product stores its dates as integer vs numeric for the other two.

``` r
dput(xbase[2, , drop = FALSE])

dput(xdplyr[2, ])

#> "data.frame"), row.names = c(NA, -1L))
```

title: Parsing time with format 04:00:00
description:
Hello. 

When time is entered in the format of HH:MM:SS, I think readr wants to parse this as a date, which in turn leads to a parsing error. 

```
x <- c("04:00:00", "04:30:00", "14:00:22")

parse_time(x) # OK

>  [1]  4:00:00  4:30:00 14:00:22

parse_date(x) # Parsing error

>  Warning: 3 parsing failures.
>  row col           expected   actual
>    1  -- date like %Y-%m-%d 04:00:00
>    2  -- date like %Y-%m-%d 04:30:00
>    3  -- date like %Y-%m-%d 14:00:22

write.table(x, "times.csv", sep = ",", row.names = FALSE)

read_csv("times.csv") # Parsing error

>  Warning: 3 parsing failures.
>  row  col   expected   actual
>   1 time valid date 04:00:00
>   2 time valid date 04:30:00
>   3 time valid date 14:00:22

```

The problem is resolved by specifying the column type.

This means I either need to know what the col_types are in advance (which is often not the case when working with collaborators who have sent me a large number of large spreadsheets), or to make them all character, which then creates more work on the other side and defeats the purpose of the smart things that readr does. type_convert is useful, but will still set the offending column to NA. Is it possible in the presence of this kind of parsing error for readr to set that col_type to character as a default? Perhaps this is working as intended, but I thought I would point it out. 

Many thanks.

title: type_convert only touches character columns; doesn't check/subset col_types accordingly
description:
``` r
library(readr)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
```

If you can use `read_csv()`, the automatic variable type detection is great.

``` r
read_csv("integer,logical\n1,TRUE\n2,FALSE\n")
#> Source: local data frame [2 x 2]
#> 
#>   integer logical
#>     (int)   (lgl)
#> 1       1    TRUE
#> 2       2   FALSE
```

I understand `type_convert()` is meant to do similar when you're stuck with a _data frame_ that needs Hadleyverse type (re-)conversion.

``` r
(df <- data_frame(integer = c(1, 2),
                  logical = c("TRUE", "FALSE")))
#> Source: local data frame [2 x 2]
#> 
#>   integer logical
#>     (dbl)   (chr)
#> 1       1    TRUE
#> 2       2   FALSE
```

Right now, only character columns are re-processed. Could all columns be re-processed? At least when `col_types = NULL`?

``` r
type_convert(df)
#> Source: local data frame [2 x 2]
#> 
#>   integer logical
#>     (dbl)   (lgl)
#> 1       1    TRUE
#> 2       2   FALSE
```

Also, if you specify `col_types`, it's not actually checked/subsetted against the character columns, so you get warnings and an incorrect result.

``` r
type_convert(df, col_types = "il")
#> Warning: Insufficient `col_names`. Adding 1 names.
#> Warning in type_convert_col(char_cols[[i]], col_types[[i]],
#> which(is_character)[i], : [0, 2]: expected an integer, but got 'TRUE'
#> Warning in type_convert_col(char_cols[[i]], col_types[[i]],
#> which(is_character)[i], : [1, 2]: expected an integer, but got 'FALSE'
#> Source: local data frame [2 x 2]
#> 
#>   integer logical
#>     (dbl)   (int)
#> 1       1      NA
#> 2       2      NA
```

Current workaround is to make sure everything is character prior to use of `type_convert()`.

``` r
df[] <- lapply(df, as.character)
type_convert(df)
#> Source: local data frame [2 x 2]
#> 
#>   integer logical
#>     (int)   (lgl)
#> 1       1    TRUE
#> 2       2   FALSE
```

This may be related to what this person was talking about? Hard to tell. https://github.com/hadley/readr/pull/160

title: Performance when reading a large number of smaller files
description:
This is not a bug, but we noticed a significant decrease in performance with readr between versions 0.1.0 and 0.2.2 when reading in a large set of smaller files. Turns out `default_local` is quite slow compared to the other fast `readr` functions.

Perhaps the below example can be captured somewhere in the documentation.

``` r
x <- paste0(paste0(1:1000,',',rep(letters,length=1000)),collapse = '\n')
# Version 0.1.0
t1 <- system.time(l <- lapply(rep(x,1000),FUN = read_lines))
#user  system elapsed
#0.19    0.03    0.22
```

That is fast!, now the same with readr 0.2.2

``` r
# Version 0.2.2
t2 <- system.time(l <- lapply(rep(x,1000),FUN = read_lines))
#user  system elapsed 
#8.67   19.06   27.86 
```

That is over 100 times slower. The way to fix this is by making a single call to default_local

``` r
t3 <- system.time({locale=default_locale();l <- lapply(rep(x,1000),FUN = read_lines,locale=locale)})
#user  system elapsed 
#0.17    0.01    0.19 
```

Back to the old readr 0.1.0 performance (perhaps even a hair faster) Nice!

title: Quoted values are never turned into missing values
description:
As mentioned in a comment on #111, if a cell value is quoted it can never be a null value:

```
> unquoted.csv <- "1,2,3\n4,Unknown,6"
> quoted.csv <- '1,2,3\n4,"Unknown",6'
> read_csv(unquoted.csv, na="Unknown", col_names=F)
  X1   X2 X3
1  1    2  3
2  4 <NA>  6
> read_csv(quoted.csv, na="Unknown", col_names=F)
  X1      X2 X3
1  1       2  3
2  4 Unknown  6
```

I think the second call to `read_csv` should result in the `"Unknown"` cell being converted into a `NA` value — that is, the output of both calls to `read_csv` should be identical. It's probably good practice to ignore quotes when typing variables (as mentioned in a comment on #155).

This is causing problems parsing the Guardian's [The Counted data](http://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2015/jun/01/about-the-counted), where all CSV fields are quoted and null values are specified using `Unknown`.

title: (Enhancement Request) Additional documentation about column parsing
description:
Many thanks for this excellent package Hadley. I'm probably slower than most, but it took me a while to parse the documentation and build out a general process for building a spec to process large text files that I process each day within a batch job. I wrote this example up below if it might be helpful for, e.g., a vignette example. All the best, Derek

```
# Spec a CSV file
example <- mtcars

# Build some intentionally bad data to review problems()
example$date <- rep_len(c("2016-09-31", "2016-09-30", "2015-02-29"), length.out=nrow(example))
example$mpg[2] <- "twenty-one"

write_csv(example, "test.csv")

# Check the entire file, so get line count minus header and pass this value to the parser:
rowstocheck <- as.numeric(gsub('^\\s+(\\d+) .*', '\\1', 
                         system("wc -l test.csv", intern=T), perl = T)) - 1

# View col specs as a starting point for building, e.g., a template that reads
#  a large text file that may contain (new/unexpected) formatting errors:
spec_csv("test.csv", col_names = TRUE, na = c("", "NA"), guess_max = rowstocheck) # Add applicable NA strings

## Output:
# cols(
#     mpg = col_double(),
#     cyl = col_double(),
#     disp = col_double(),
#     hp = col_double(),
#     drat = col_double(),
#     wt = col_double(),
#     qsec = col_double(),
#     vs = col_double(),
#     am = col_double(),
#     gear = col_double(),
#     carb = col_double(),
#     date = col_date(format = "")

# Use the above output of spec_csv to build your import process
z  <- read_csv("test.csv", col_types = cols(
                              mpg = col_double(), # expected a number here, substantively
                              cyl = col_double(),
                              disp = col_double(),
                              hp = col_double(),
                              drat = col_double(),
                              wt = col_double(),
                              qsec = col_double(),
                              vs = col_double(),
                              am = col_double(),
                              gear = col_double(),
                              carb = col_double(),
                              date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"), # Modify to suit your format
                              .default = col_character())) # Loads unexpected new fields in your batch as char

# Now process/review the invalid dates in your file:
as.list(problems(z))
```

``` r
colLabs <- ""

cols(colLabs)
```

```
Error: Unknown shortcut:
```

``` r
lapply(strsplit(colLabs, split = "")[[1]], readr:::col_concise)
```

title: Make it easy to catch mutations in the data by emitting col_types string
description:
One of the nice features of readr is that it introspects column types and gives you data frames with columns of "appropriate" data types. This is cool. It does so heuristically by reading a bunch of rows (but not all) and guessing.

This is very nice for interactive use, however I think it could be made into a neat feature to catch data schema mutation.

I would like to propose a new function which reads a _whole_ CSV file, and from the entire file returns a col_types string. A user can then take that string and put it in their production script's read_csv ca;;, so that in the future, if a new data file comes in which has different data types, instead of (for example) silently returning a data frame which has chars where a date once was, it will now give a proper error.

title: Optional `make.names` arg to preserve `as.formula` functionality
description:
`readr` preserves colnames as per https://github.com/hadley/readr/issues/165 but this makes working with `as.formula` expressions complicated (/I didn't get this to work).

Here's a reproducible and fairly common problem:

``` r
library(readr)
library(plotly)
desktop_itmes <- read_csv("https://ndownloader.figshare.com/files/6452595")
desktop_itmes %>% 
  select(`Desktop Items`, `Operating System`, University) %>%
  group_by(University, `Operating System`) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(`Desktop Items`)) %>%
  plot_ly(x = ~mean,
          y = as.formula("~`Operating System`"),
          colors = ~University,
          type = "bar")
```

Of course this all fixed with 

``` r
colnames(desktop_itmes) <- make.names(colnames(desktop_itmes))
desktop_itmes %>% 
  select(Desktop.Items, Operating.System, University) %>%
  group_by(University, Operating.System) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(Desktop.Items)) %>%
  plot_ly(x = ~mean,
          y = ~Operating.System,
          type = "bar",
          orientation = "h")
```

However, I feel that many users will plug away for ages trying to shoehorn `variable name` into formula. It might be inappropriate to add an option for the function, but some comment on this somewhere in the `tidyverse` would be useful for many users - IMO.

title: Change default locale
description:
I was wondering how to change the default locale. My understanding is that `stringi` provides encoding defaults, but I couldn't find marks_ defaults.

I noticed that decimal and grouping marks are wrong in French. `locale("fr")` should be `Numbers:  123 456,78` rather than `Numbers:  123,456.78`. 

`parse_number("3 456.234 4", locale=locale("fr"))` should be equal to `parse_number("3 456,234 4", locale=locale("fr", grouping_mark = " ", decimal_mark=","))`

Also, following (ISO 31-O)[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_31-0#Numbers] I wonder if multiple decimal separators could be allowed (e.g. `c(".", ","), or using regexp`"[.,]"`) ? 

I'm pretty sure many people could raise issues on which defaults `locale` to use and endless debates could ensue, apologies for that !

title: Files encoded with UTF-8 BOM are (still) not supported
description:
I was encouraged to file this bug report by https://blog.rstudio.org/2016/08/05/readr-1-0-0/#comments. Basically, bug #263 is not fixed in `readr` 1.0.0, despite being closed as fixed. Files encoded with UTF-8 with BOM (e.g. CSV files saved by Excel) are not correctly read:
1. The BOM character is not being discarded.
2. It the column names are quoted, the quotes are not being removed from the _first_ column.
3. The character encoding name `UTF-8-BOM`, introduced in R 3.0.0, is not recognised.

Here’s an [an example](https://github.com/hadley/readr/files/407456/utf8-bom.zip) (ZIP file containing an UTF-8-BOM-encoded CSV file). The file looks like this (with an embedded BOM):

```
"foo","bar","b☺z"
1,3,5
2,4,6
```

Reproducible example:

```
library(readr)
d = read_csv("utf8-bom.csv")
d
```

This is shown as

```
Source: local data frame [2 x 3]

  ﻿"foo"   bar   b☺z
  <int> <int> <int>
1     1     3     5
2     2     4     6
```

when run under an UTF-8 locale. On other locales (e.g. Windows), the name of the first column is instead shown as `<U+FEFF>"foo"` (though some other ways of showing the column hides the U+FEFF character reference). In any case, it contains an embedded BOM character, as witnessed by

```
> charToRaw(names(d)[1])
[1] ef bb bf 22 66 6f 6f 22

> nchar(names(d))
[1] 6 3 3
```

under both Windows and Linux.

Expected results: The BOM and the two quote characters should be discarded, so the above commands should result in:

```
> charToRaw(names(d)[1])
[1] 66 6f 6f

> nchar(names(d))
[1] 3 3 3
```

Also, trying to explicitly use the UTF-8-BOM encoding results in an error message:

```
> d = read_csv("utf8-bom.csv", locale = locale(encoding = "UTF-8-BOM"))
Error: Unknown encoding UTF-8-BOM
```

While the base `read.csv()` function works fine:

```
> d = read.csv("utf8-bom.csv", fileEncoding="UTF-8-BOM")
> nchar(names(d))
[1] 3 3 3
```

(Here **not** specifying a `fileEncoding` argument also may or may not work, depending on which platform you’re on. It works on my UTF-8-based Linux box.)

title: slow with small datasets
description:
I made small package that guesses the formatting of flat/tabular files: https://github.com/lukas-rokka/readrGuess 

It tests different combinations of formatting, altogether `readr::read_delim()` is called 18 times. But the performance for small datasets is not good. 

Following code takes roughly 1.5 seconds, while it should take just a few milliseconds from a computation point of view. 
```
readrGuess::read_guess(readr::format_delim(data.frame(a=1:1, b="a", c=1.1), ";"))
```

Doing the same thing with a big dataset only takes about 2 seconds
```
readrGuess::read_guess(readr::format_delim(data.frame(a=1:10000, b="a", c=1.1), ";"))
```

When checking with profiling it appears that `read_delim()` has a quite big overhead. `gc` (memory clean up I believe) is running most of the time when using it with small datasets. 

Is it possible somehow use the functionalities of the `read_delim()` for small datasets without causing `gc()` calls, or is it an unavoidable trade off that comes with using rcpp?

title: function to guess encoding from character vector
description:
Would it make sense to have a function that can guess the encoding from a character vector?
for example...
```
guess_encoding_from_chr_vector <-
  function (chr_vector, ...) 
  {
    file <- charToRaw(paste(unique(chr_vector), collapse = ''))
    readr::guess_encoding(file, ...)
  }

df <- readr::read_csv('http://databank.worldbank.org/data/download/GDP.csv', skip = 3)
guess_encoding_from_chr_vector(df$Economy)
```

`readr::guess_encoding()` goes line by line through a file. Imagine a file with 500,000+ lines (well over the default n_max of 10,000) where the first non-ASCII character appears far below the 10,000th line, and there are **many** columns filled with numeric data and only one column with characters (i.e. country name). One could progressively increment `n_max` using `readr::guess_encoding()` and eventually find the first non-ASCII character to get an appropriate encoding guess, but wouldn't it be more efficient, especially if a `readr::read_csv()` had already been attempted and the data was in memory as a data.frame, to try to guess the encoding based only on the data/column/vector that contains the character strings (and only unique values of such)?

title: calling locale() is slow
description:
Based on issue #555 

Calling locale() is slow. Not a big issue if calling a large file once, but if calling small files many times it matters. This example takes 1.5 second to run
```
system.time(replicate(18, read_delim(
  "c1;c2\n1,0;2,0", ";", locale=locale(decimal_mark = ","))))
```

While if the locale is set just once, it only takes about 0.05 seconds.

It is the call to `OlsoNames()` from `check_tz()` at line 115 in locale.R that is the cause to the slowness. 
```
system.time(replicate(18, "UTC" %in% OlsonNames()))
```

title: read_csv() outputs the tibble multiplication sign as invalid UTF-8 character
description:
read_csv() version 1.0 outputs the tibble multiplication sign as invalid UTF-8 character. Typical example output are at
http://readr.tidyverse.org/reference/read_delim.html :

#> # A tibble: 32 × 11

The multiplication sign character in read_csv outputs such as above is extended ASCII but it should be either in plain ASCII or in Unicode UTF-8. In UTF-8 encoding, the character is displayed as xD7 but pandoc gives the error message

"Cannot decode byte '\xd7': Data.Text.Internal.Encoding.Fusion.streamUtf8: Invalid UTF-8 stream"

This is a problem for pandoc on Windows only. I tried pandoc version 1.13.1 and 1.18. I mentioned the problem on Statalist and wondered if it was a problem with Stata's user-written program "Markdoc", which is Stata's equivalent program to R Markdown. The user-programmer of MarkDoc concluded that read_csv should have avoided the invalid UTF-8 character, and I agree. The Statalist URL is [http://www.statalist.org/forums/forum/general-stata-discussion/general/1355554-markdoc-manual-gui?p=1362612#post1362612](http://www.statalist.org/forums/forum/general-stata-discussion/general/1355554-markdoc-manual-gui?p=1362612#post1362612)

What is the rationale for using extended ASCII instead of plain ASCII or UTF-8 for the tibble multiplication sign? Given (1) the compatibility problems with pandoc on Windows and with dependent programs such as Stata's markdoc, (2) the no need for extended ASCII, and (3) having an obvious easy fix, I assume this issue was simply overlooked. The problem does not occur with R's read.csv, only with your read_csv (and partially also with fread).

description:

```r
# MAKE SOME TOY DATA AND SET read_delim PARAMETERS

n <- 1000
write.table(data.frame(a=1:n,b=1:n,c=runif(n),response=sample(c(0,1),n,TRUE)),

                   b=col_integer(),

batchsize=100
```

title: `read_table` can't read from pipes
description:
The following does not work:

```
con <- pipe("perl -le 'print qq{x $_} for 1..5'")
read_table(con)
## Error in isOpen(con) : invalid connection
```

The reason seems to be that `read_table` first calls `fwf_empty`, which opens the connection and reads from it; then it calls `col_spec_standardise`, which also tries to open the same connection & read from it.  The latter fails because it's already been read from and can't be re-opened.

There's also another subsequent call to `datasource` (on line 47 in the current Git `master` of `read_table.R`) that would fail after this one.

In general, to support connections & pipes, each reading function should ensure that its file/connection is opened exactly once.  Avoiding these re-opens should give better performance too.

title: ListCallback to complement SideEffect and DataFrame callbacks
description:
Related to (PR) #520.

There are times where it's useful for the chunked callback to return a list (that is combined into a single list at the end).
An example is when processing a large JSONL file with purrr functions: (1) read file chunk, (2) use purrr to transform, filter, reduce, etc. as needed, and (3) combine into a final list, call that final object `my_data`.
_My_ specific use-case is to filter the data to discard irrelevant data such that the final object can fit into memory for interactive work/exploration.

When downstream functions expect `my_data` to be a data frame, then DataFrameCallback works just fine.

But if there already exist some downstream functions written to deal with `my_data` as a list (e.g. prepared purrr-enabled pipelines), the DataFrameCallback must be written to return a single list-column data frame, then extract that single list-column, and finally pass the now-extracted list to the downstream functions.

It seems silly to return a single-column data frame, just to then extract that single column later, when we know we'd like have a list in-hand at the end of the chunked reading/processing phase.

Minor suggestion, but certainly not a blocker/bug/etc. (since the work-around is described above).
In all other aspects, readr's great!

title: delim = "" should generate clear error
description:
Consider this minimal example with a classic CO2 dataset:

base R version works fine:

```r
co2 <- read.delim("ftp://aftp.cmdl.noaa.gov/products/trends/co2/co2_mm_mlo.txt",
                  sep = "", comment = "#", 
                  col.names = c("year", "month", "decimal_date", "average", "interpolated", "trend", "days"),
                  na.strings = c("-1", "-99.99"))
co2 %>% head()
```

readr function not so much

```{r}
co2 <- read_delim("ftp://aftp.cmdl.noaa.gov/products/trends/co2/co2_mm_mlo.txt", trim_ws = TRUE,
                  delim = "", comment = "#", 
                  col_names = c("year", "month", "decimal_date", "average", "interpolated", "trend", "days"),
                  col_types = c("iiddddi"),
                  na = c("-1", "-99.99"))
co2 %>% head()
```

The problem seems to be in the file being whitespace delimited, `read.delim` seems to interpret `sep=""` somewhat surprisingly (but conveniently in this case) as "any number of spaces".  `read_delim` does not. 

I haven't figured out a way to parse this file with `readr` functions, though I could be missing something obvious.  It seems like an option for `delim_whitespace` (as in `pandas`), or perhaps better, the ability to use regex expressions for delimiters would help?

(A bit unrelated, but it might also be convenient for the comment symbol to permit regex patterns?)

I made a [gist of the problem](https://gist.github.com/pe3/ec4216acabfbe5034f5a29dfc9625344) with sample files in UTF-8 and iso-8859-1.

```
library("readr")
library("dplyr")

#####################################################################
# works as expected when column types are chr and file is iso-8859-1

read_delim(
  "scandinavian.csv",
  ";",
  locale = locale("fi", encoding = "iso-8859-1"),
  escape_double = FALSE,
  col_names = FALSE,
  trim_ws = TRUE
) %>% glimpse() %>% select(X11,X12)

#      X11   X12
#    <chr> <chr>
#  1   VAS VÄNST

#####################################################################
# works as expected when column types are fctr and file is UTF-8

read_delim(
  "scandinavian-utf.csv",
  ";",
  locale = locale("fi", encoding = "UTF-8"),
  escape_double = FALSE,
  col_names = FALSE,
  col_types = cols(X11 = col_factor(c("VAS")), X12 = col_factor(c("VÄNST"))),
  trim_ws = TRUE
) %>% glimpse() %>% select(X11,X12)

#      X11   X12
#    <chr> <chr>
#  1   VAS VÄNST

#####################################################################
# works unexpectedly when column types are fctr and file is iso-8859-1

read_delim(
  "scandinavian.csv",
  ";",
  locale = locale("fi", encoding = "iso-8859-1"),
  escape_double = FALSE,
  col_names = FALSE,
  col_types = cols(X11 = col_factor(c("VAS")), X12 = col_factor(c("VÄNST"))),
  trim_ws = TRUE
) %>% glimpse() %>% select(X11,X12)

#      X11   X12
#    <chr> <chr>
#  1   VAS    NA

# should see:
#      X11   X12
#    <chr> <chr>
#  1   VAS VÄNST
```
scandinavian-utf.csv
```
K ;01;091;A;001A;HEL;HEL;06;01;01;VAS ;VÄNST ;0002;Kruununhaka A ;Kronohagen A ;Riku ;Ahola ;1;031;valtiotieteiden kandidaatti
```
scandinavian.csv
```
K ;01;091;A;001A;HEL;HEL;06;01;01;VAS ;VÄNST ;0002;Kruununhaka A ;Kronohagen A ;Riku ;Ahola ;1;031;valtiotieteiden kandidaatti
```

The data is from the Finnish ministry of justice election results. The test files used in the above code can be generated this way: 

```
curl -O http://tulospalvelu.vaalit.fi/K2012/data/k-2012_ehd_maa.csv.zip
unzip k-2012_ehd_maa.csv.zip
head -n 1 kv-2012_teat_maa.csv > scandinavian.csv
iconv -f ISO-8859-1 -t UTF-8  scandinavian.csv  > scandinavian-utf.csv
$ file -I scandinavian.csv 
scandinavian.csv: text/plain; charset=iso-8859-1
$ file -I scandinavian-utf.csv
scandinavian-utf.csv: text/plain; charset=utf-8
```

**Is This Signed Arithmetic Overflow?**
[4.1.3 Trapping arithmetic functions](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gccint/Integer-library-routines.html) says: _“The following functions implement trapping arithmetic. These functions call the libc function abort upon signed arithmetic overflow.”_ `__mulvdi3` is one such a function and the observed signal matches the documented one.

**readr version**
The development release, commint n°`5e2ad90bc7a66e7cd8eaedd3b43afdb520fcf265`.

See also #562

title: problems() not pulling up the exact text of a parsing failure
description:
The example:

```
library(tidyverse)
x <- tribble(
  ~unit, ~value,
  "a"  ,    "1",
  "b"  ,     "(NA)")
write_tsv(x, path = "test.tsv")
```
Now try and parse with the incorrect NA specification (in the real application it's not obvious exactly what represents NA).
```
new_x <- read_tsv("test.tsv",
                  na = "",
                  col_types = cols(
                      unit = col_character(),
                      value = col_number()
                    ))
file.remove("test.tsv")

problems(new_x)
# A tibble: 1 × 4
#     row   col expected actual
#   <int> <chr>    <chr>  <chr>
# 1     2 value a number       
```

I would have expected this to come up:
```
# A tibble: 1 × 4
#   row     col expected actual
# <int>   <chr>    <chr>  <chr>
# 1   2   value a number   (NA) 
```
Is this the expected behavior?

This inconsistency my cause problems. title: Read_table reads long files incorrectly due to wrong columns width guessing
description:
See the example code below, which makes use of the attached file, specifically the first column.
The last members of the first column, which should be `c(1005:1010)`, are instead `c(5:10)` when read by `read_table()` without skipping anything.

It seems that `read_table()` looks for the first 100 rows when reading, and finds that the first column only has a three digits number. However, later in the file the number becomes 4-digits.

```
testfile <- "https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/files/847495/testfile.txt"
com <- read_table(testfile, col_names=FALSE); tail(com$X1)
# [1]  5  6  7  8  9 10
com <- read_table(testfile, col_names=FALSE, skip=20); tail(com$X1)
# [1] 1005 1006 1007 1008 1009 1010
```

How can I avoid this, without using `read_fwf()` (which is not doable for me because this script must be able to read a large number of differently formatted files)?
Would it be possible to add a tuning parameter that specifies how many rows are checked to choose the column width?

Thanks in advance.

[testfile.txt](https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/files/847495/testfile.txt)

title: `read.delim` can read from process substitution handle but `read_tsv` can not
description:
I'd like to read a table from a process substitution handle provided as argument

```
echo "test" > test.tsv
R --args <(cat test.tsv)
```

However when using readr this fails. Most likely because readr will jump back in forth in the file. However, also the recommended stackoverflow solution to fix the same issue for `read.csv` fails for `read_tsv`

```
inputFile <- commandArgs(T)[1]
require(readr)

## does not work (most likely because random access when parsing file)
#read_tsv(inputFile)
# > Error: Cannot read file /dev/fd/63


#try solution from http://stackoverflow.com/questions/15784373/process-substitution
OpenRead <- function(arg) {

    if (arg %in% c("-", "/dev/stdin")) {
        file("stdin", open = "r")
    } else if (grepl("^/dev/fd/", arg)) {
        fifo(arg, open = "r")
    } else {
        file(arg, open = "r")
    }
}

fileHandle <- OpenRead(inputFile)


#readLines(inputFile) ## does not work either
#readLines(fileHandle) ## works

## does also not work
#read_tsv(fileHandle)
# > Error: can only read from a binary connection

#read.delim(inputFile, header=F) ## also does not work directly...

## ...but works as expected when using connection handle:
read.delim(fileHandle, header=F)
```

Somehow `readr` seems to consider the connection as a binary stream even if it's just a plain text file handle.

```
  0.19  0.08  0.07  0.19  0.23  0.24  0.26  0.25  1.00  
  0.30  0.27  0.24  0.21  0.32  0.34  0.54  0.46  0.28  1.00  
  0.37  0.35  0.37  0.29  0.36  0.37  0.32  0.29  0.30  0.35  1.00  
  0.21  0.20  0.18  0.16  0.27  0.40  0.58  0.45  0.27  0.59  0.31  1.00
```

Based on this [SO answer](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/13863569/reading-a-symmetric-matrix-from-file-that-omits-upper-triangular-part) I can read this in with base R's `read.table` if I specify `fill=TRUE`, and my matrix has fewer than 5 columns since, from the docs, "The number of data columns is determined by looking at the first five lines of input..."

So if my matrix is greater than 5 columns, and I don't know this in advance (and therefore can't correctly set the length of `col.names`) then I am SOL.

I was hoping that `readr::read_table` might be robust enough to handle this sort of issue especially since I can choose `guess_max` arbitrarily, but I have not had any luck. 

Docs say that `read_table2` can handle rows of different lengths, but I am having trouble doing so.

```{R}
# file is the same as the above data
readr::read_table2(paste0("data-raw/", file), col_names = FALSE, guess_max = 100)
```
This gives me the first two columns plus warnings about additional columns in certain rows. 

Since the documentation says that `readr::read_table2` can handle rows of different lengths, I am guessing there is something equivalent to `read.table`'s `fill` parameter, but perhaps I am misunderstanding something.

Kind Regards,
Carl

```
# this is the source code for write_bib
x = "readr" 
file = ""
tweak = TRUE # default is true
width = NULL 
prefix = getOption("knitr.bib.prefix", "R-")
bib = NULL # I've added this 

  idx = mapply(system.file, package = x) == ""
  if (any(idx)) {
    warning("package(s) ", paste(x[idx], collapse = ", "), 
            " not found")
    x = x[!idx]
  }
  x = setdiff(x, knitr:::.base.pkgs)
  bib = sapply(x, function(pkg) {
    cite = citation(pkg, auto = if (pkg == "base") 
      NULL
      else TRUE)
    if (tweak) {
      cite$title = gsub(sprintf("^(%s: )(\\1)", pkg), "\\1", 
                        cite$title)
      cite$title = gsub(" & ", " \\\\& ", cite$title)
    }
    entry = toBibtex(cite)
    entry[1] = sub("\\{,$", sprintf("{%s%s,", prefix, pkg), 
                   entry[1])
    entry
  }, simplify = FALSE)
  
# at this point we have  everything ok:
  
#  $readr
#  @Manual{R-readr,
#    title = {readr: Read Rectangular Text Data},
#    note = {http://readr.tidyverse.org, https://github.com/tidyverse/readr},
#  }

  
  if (tweak) {
    for (i in intersect(names(knitr:::.tweak.bib), x)) {
      message("tweaking ", i)
      bib[[i]] = knitr:::merge_list(bib[[i]], knitr:::.tweak.bib[[i]])
    }
    bib = lapply(bib, function(b) {
      b["author"] = sub("Duncan Temple Lang", "Duncan {Temple Lang}", 
                        b["author"])
      b["title"] = sub("'RStudio'", "RStudio", b["title"])
      if (!("year" %in% names(b))) 
        b["year"] = knitr:::.this.year
      idx = which(names(b) == "")
      if (!is.null(width)) 
        b[-idx] = stringr::str_wrap(b[-idx], width, 2, 
                                    4)
      structure(c(b[idx[1L]], b[-idx], b[idx[2L]]), class = "Bibtex")
    })
  }
  
  # but now it is broken, with a line of NA:
  
#  $readr
#  @Manual{R-readr,
#    title = {readr: Read Rectangular Text Data},
#    note = {http://readr.tidyverse.org, https://github.com/tidyverse/readr},
#    NA
#    year = {2017},
#  }
  
  
   
  bib = bib[sort(x)]
  if (!is.null(file) && length(x)) 
    knitr:::writeUTF8(unlist(bib), file)
  invisible(bib)
```

The workaround is to set 'tweak' to FALSE in a bookdown index.Rmd file, like this:

````r
```{r  include=FALSE}
# automatically create a bib database for R packages
knitr::write_bib(c(
  .packages(), 
  'bookdown', 
  'knitr', 
  'rmarkdown'), 
  'packages.bib',
  tweak = FALSE) # because readr gets an NA if TRUE

```
````
